浑水盖住她的嘴和鼻子，她在吸气时呛进水，猛烈咳嗽，身体不断抽动。她继续一边扯动安全带，一边拼命抬高下巴，试图把嘴伸到水面上方。每当水面稍微退下，她立刻张大嘴抢一口空气；下一股浑水又盖住她的脸，她再次呛咳。

He remains focused on the telephone and equipment, NOT on the Engineer. — ELSEWHERE IN THE ROOM: Two workers are urgently studying large printed technical diagrams and plant schematics spread across a desk. One worker points rapidly at different locations on the schematic with his finger while explaining something to the other. The second worker follows the diagram, checks another sheet, then points toward a different section as if correcting him. They are trying to determine the condition or configuration of part of the cooling system. Their discussion is fast, technical and tense. They do NOT stop when the Engineer passes. — FARTHER IN THE BACKGROUND, AT ANOTHER CONTROL PANEL: Two other workers are having a tense technical disagreement while operating the controls. One points at the panel and insists: 「この系統を切ります！」 The other immediately objects: 「待て！冷却が落ちる！ They gesture toward different instruments and controls while arguing about the correct response. They are not having an emotional personal argument. It is a rapid professional disagreement under extreme pressure, with both workers still actively operating the equipment. — THROUGHOUT THE ROOM: Other workers move quickly between consoles, check gauges, write readings on paper, exchange documents, call information across the room and operate switches. Some workers are seated at consoles, others are standing or moving between stations. Nobody is idle. Nobody poses for camera. Nobody turns to watch the Engineer simply because he is the protagonist. The Engineer moves THROUGH an already functioning emergency response rather than entering a room full of people waiting for him. The background activity should feel layered, messy and partially unreadable, like a real workplace emergency: several conversations and tasks happening simultaneously under the continuous emergency alarm.

The Engineer keeps moving rapidly through the room as the camera does a 360 turn around him as he walks, ending behind his back again. 

Without stopping, the Engineer turns his head and upper body toward the first WORKER he passes.

浑水不断从前方流入，水线在她身上逐渐升高。她被刚才扑面的水呛得咳嗽，一边扯动安全带，一边抬高下巴寻找空气。随着水位上涨，每次挣扎激起的水花都会扑到她嘴边，她咳嗽着把脸抬起，大口喘息。

摄影机始终留在她肩膀后方的同一个车内位置。上涨的水面逐渐触及镜头下缘，再慢慢升到镜头中央。画面下半部分浸在灰褐色污水中，受到泥沙、气泡和折射干扰；上半部分仍能看到她抬起的脸和挣扎的肩膀。水线在同一个镜头前真实晃动。

Photorealistic product / asset photograph of an industrial MANUAL SHUT-OFF VALVE WITH A LARGE DISHED HANDWHEEL, the kind found in a Japanese nuclear power plant of the 2000s, isolated on a plain, even, medium-grey seamless studio background.

THE HANDWHEEL — THE KEY PART, DESCRIBED PRECISELY: a large horizontal handwheel about 50 cm in diameter, of the DISHED, CONE-SHAPED type. Its RIM is a wide FLAT band of cast steel — about 4–5 cm wide and only about 1 cm thick, flat on top like a ring-shaped plate, NOT a thin round-section bar. From the underside of this rim, THREE straight spokes slope DOWNWARD and inward at an angle, meeting a solid central hub set about 15 cm BELOW the rim, so the whole wheel forms a shallow inverted cone / funnel shape — the rim floats high, the hub sits low. Mounted on the top of the rim, standing straight UP from it, a single revolving GRIP HANDLE: a black rubber-covered cylindrical spinner handle about 12 cm long and 3 cm thick on a steel pin, the kind used to spin the wheel fast. The wheel painted industrial SAFETY RED — a true, pure red enamel (approximately #B8231B, like a fire-extinguisher red), NOT orange, NOT orange-red, NOT vermilion; the paint old — worn to bare grey metal on top of the rim where hands slide over it, chipped, matte, a little rust at the chips, the red itself slightly dulled and dusty but still clearly red; the handle black, scuffed.

THE VALVE BELOW: from the hub a bare steel threaded rising stem drops through a cast-iron yoke into the valve — a heavy cast-steel gate valve about 70 cm tall overall: a tall bonnet with a packing gland and four studs, a bulbous round body, mounted on a short horizontal section of steel pipe with bolted flanges at both ends. Body and pipe painted a worn pale grey-green, grimy, faint oil streaks, dust in the recesses; flanges bolted with hex nuts, dull steel, some rust. A small blank rectangular steel tag hung from the yoke on a wire, no text.

CAMERA: single view, three-quarter angle slightly from above — high enough to see the top of the flat rim and the cone of spokes falling to the hub, low enough to see the grip handle standing up in profile; the stem, bonnet, body and pipe all visible; the whole valve fully in frame with margin around it; lens about 85 mm equivalent, everything in sharp focus.

LIGHT: neutral, even, shadowless studio light — a large soft source from above and slightly in front, plus fill from both sides, neutral daylight-white, no colour cast, no warm tint that would push the red toward orange. Only a soft faint contact shadow beneath the pipe; no hard shadows, no rim light, no reflections of a room, no glare on the paint.

COLOUR: true to material — pure safety-red wheel, black handle, grey-green body, bare steel and rust as they are; white balance strictly neutral; the background a flat neutral mid-grey, evenly lit edge to edge, no gradient, no vignette.

女员工的表演有三个连续阶段：跑向汽车、上车和启动发动机时，她紧张、急躁、拼命赶时间，呼吸短促，动作迅速；看见近在眼前的海啸时，她突然僵住，身体和呼吸短暂冻结；海水撞上她以后，冲击打破僵直，她立即拼命挣扎逃生，却始终无法脱困。

全片是一个连续长镜头，没有剪辑、隐藏剪辑、时间跳跃或瞬移。摄影机从厂房走廊穿过出口进入停车场，再通过敞开的驾驶座车门进入汽车。门框、人物身体、曝光变化和运动模糊都不能掩盖转场。

只有工程师段落使用一次连续的光学推近与拉远：从汽车旁推近二楼玻璃后的工程师，再拉远回到同一扇敞开的驾驶座车门。其余段落依靠摄影机实际移动改变构图。

开场是几乎不透明的棕灰色浑水，泥沙与气泡贴着镜头翻滚。摄影机猛然穿出水面，紧接着用约一秒沿近处金属楼梯的斜扶手和立柱向上移动，同时绕平台靠近工程师的一侧完成约90度的短弧，连续落到他双手和侧脸的近景。上升与绕行是同一个紧凑流畅的动作：近处扶手、楼梯钢构先后擦过画框，红色警示灯从极近前景虚化掠过，带出清楚的视差和湿红反光，最后让出他的脸。摄影机沿构件之间真实的开放间隙通过，短弧在到达面部时自然结束。平台地板起初比水面高约一米，镜头上升时连续看到水面、露出的支撑结构和上方的黑色系带工作鞋，清楚建立他此刻站在水面之上的高度。此时鞋面和蓝色长裤裤脚仍基本干燥，脚下平台尚未被水漫过。

逃生路线由真实连在一起的不同标高构成：阀门平台后方几级楼梯先向下进入更低的淹水连接通道，通道另一端再经带转角的楼梯向上，到更高处的金属出口门。要到对面上层，必须先下降经过水中，再爬升。楼梯、扶手、平台的相对位置始终固定，洪水水位持续升高。

他侧身双手抓住管道上的阀门手轮，用肩背猛拧，迅速换握再试。阀门彻底卡死，手轮、轮毂和轮辐始终停在同一角度，连一点转动都没有；只有他的手臂、肩背和身体因用力而绷紧、颤动，双手始终抓牢轮缘。摄影机从湿手沿前臂移到咬紧的嘴和近侧眼睛，再沿耳侧绕向肩后，始终跟着发力的身体。阀门旁、靠近他脸侧略高的位置安装一盏红色警示灯。它闪烁时，近距离红光明确扫过他的脸颊、额头和鼻侧，在眼镜镜片与湿皮肤上留下移动的红色反光；每次变暗，另一侧脸重新沉入阴影。附近冷白工业灯不规则闪断，与红灯交错，远处灯点柔化成散景。上方水流穿过格栅倾泻，失焦水帘掠过前景，警笛与洪水声持续。

在他连续用力时，下方水面迅速沿刚才露出的支撑立柱升高，漫到平台上。他感觉到脚边进水，低头，摄影机紧随他的视线，从脸部猛然向下俯摇（tilt-down），清楚看见水已经盖过鞋底、涌上黑色鞋面，原本干燥的裤脚被浸湿、颜色变深。摄影机随即连续抬回他的转身动作。他立即回头看向身后的逃生通道，镜头从肩侧短暂读到先下后上的路线和正在被淹没的下层台阶。他松开手轮，转身急步走向下行楼梯。

他抓着扶手沿楼梯向下快走，脚每降一级，水就从小腿升到膝盖、再到腰部，明确读到他必须先下降进入齐腰深的低连接通道。摄影机贴着侧脸和肩一起降低，水线及扶手从画框下缘掠过；这条通道另一端的阶梯将带他重新升出水面。就在他仍踩着下行楼梯、换脚向前时，整栋建筑突然发生猛烈地震式震动：地面与楼梯先横向一挫，接着数次快速左右摇晃并伴随短促竖向颠震。固定管道、梁、楼梯和扶手同时震颤，连接件发出金属呻吟，水面向相反方向滞后涌动。这是整座建筑的地震，直接改变他脚下支撑。他的黑色工作鞋被横移的湿台阶带滑，身体因惯性失衡，抓握脱开，跌入下面的水中。主照明和红色警示灯随这次地震熄灭。摄影机受到同样的横甩和竖震，接着沿他的跌落轨迹没入浑水，再立即随他冲回水面。落水、短暂没顶、重新抓住支撑和浮出是一口气完成的连续动作。

黑暗只是一段极短的动作过渡：水下闷响迅速变回急促吸气和拍水声。浮出时他左手已经摸到固定扶手，右手紧接着从黑暗中取出手电并按亮，身体始终朝出口移动。取物来源藏在阴影里。手电亮起后，近处湿金属反射出他的脸，摄影机立刻落在极紧的面部特写，脸占画面约95—100%，额头、下巴或一侧脸颊可被裁切。近侧眼睛和嘴是清楚的视觉落点，保持自然面部透视。他张口连续急吸气，胸肩快速起伏，边喘边拉着扶手前进。他随即低头缩肩，从横在路径上方的一段破损管道下面挤过去，脚步持续向前。破口涌出的水紧贴他的额头和脸前倾泻，水帘从镜头与面部之间掠过，打在眼镜和脸颊上。他眯眼侧过脸，继续拉着扶手穿过水流。摄影机跟随他低头、侧身，始终保持几乎填满画面的面部大特写；管道只在画框上缘以失焦碎片掠过，眼睛、嘴和掠过脸前的水流构成这一动作。

摄影机刚从水里出来，前端保护玻璃挂着不规则水滴和细水膜，随重力、奔跑和震动慢慢滑落，局部折射脸和光。弱手电在他转腕寻找落脚点时扫向周围，偶尔斜擦镜头，照亮水滴并产生短促的局部光晕；光移开后眼睛重新可读。周围维持深黑，面容只在照到附近湿表面的反射中短暂显现。贴近镜头的一两次重呼气带来极淡、立刻散开的湿气柔化，流动水滴是主要的湿镜头质感。

一次向侧方的扫光擦到水边死鱼的一小段银色躯体和破损鳍。它近乎仰面漂在低通道水面，大部分浸水，只随水被动移动。摄影机继续以他的极近面容为主体，鱼只从画框边缘柔焦出现。他注意到意外轮廓，眼神短暂绷紧，急吸一口气，立刻把注意力收回前方扶手，保持动作的控制，继续迅速向前。恐惧体现在急促呼吸、紧张目光与果断的抓握中，他努力控制住慌乱，鱼留在下面的水中。

他一手举灯，一手沿扶手拉着自己通过低通道，脚踩住对面的第一阶，猛然把沉重身体拖出深水。摄影机随身体升起，继续贴着占满大部分画面的侧脸，水从嘴角、下颌和衣领滴下。他接着连续跑上一段台阶，转过中间平台，再向更高的门冲去。弱光在台阶与管道之间急晃，左臂不断拉住扶手，湿衣紧贴身体滴水，眼镜和安全帽保持在位。镜头在眼、嘴和耳侧之间短幅绕行，手与扶手掠过边缘，身后水吞没刚离开的台阶。

门在上行楼梯顶端。他左手压下机械把手、肩膀推门，门卡住。他马上站稳再次压把手、用身体推，金属门摩擦着打开。摄影机与他一起穿过门框，继续贴着侧前方的脸陪他急走两三步。技术走廊的金属地板、钢丝网和管线只从画框边缘虚化掠过，脚步回响改变。最后仍是湿脸、急吸气和寻找前方的眼睛，玻璃上的水滴继续滑落，近距离的一次重呼气短暂柔化局部光线。

摄影机从开始就有明显而强烈的手持颠簸，跟着用力、步伐和洪水失衡；地震时振幅骤然增强，多个不规则横向冲击与竖向颠震同时作用于建筑、人物和镜头，之后转为落水、涉水和奔跑的沉重摇晃。每次恢复都带真实惯性，关键的眼神和接触有短暂清楚的落点。前半通过近景建立动作，第二次出水后以95—100%面部构图持续陪伴，空间由边缘物体、动作方向和声音传递。浅景深、克制的变形宽银幕散景与细腻颗粒保留湿皮肤细节。

声音突出频繁急吸气、克制的吃力呼气、地震的低频轰鸣与钢构连续震颤、洪水、水下闷响、手电开关、湿脚步和开门摩擦。远处警笛持续。极低的紧张音乐脉冲在背景加压，落水时短暂让出急喘的位置，上楼时重新追紧。动作从出水到穿门始终连贯紧迫。

写实灾难电影，一条实时连续长镜头。摄影机紧跟工程师，用强烈、不规则的手持震动、真实的运动惯性和近距离面部表演呈现求生过程。

正面倒退跟拍时，窗户在画面左侧。工程师全身湿透，脸颊流着水，湿衣领贴着脖子，眼镜片上有不均匀水珠，眼睛仍然可见。他急促呼吸，肩膀随奔跑冲击起伏。摄影机紧紧跟住湿脸，强烈颠簸中持续修正位置，不使用平稳滑轨效果。

固定红色警报灯内部的反射器持续旋转，红色扫光掠过墙壁、安全帽与湿脸；上方灯具不规则闪烁。冷灰窗光保持面部与环境可读。走廊已有损坏和地面杂物，过程中没有东西从天花板掉下来。

工程师起初一直看着前方的行进路线，专注于奔跑，不看镜头，也不提前盯着侧面的窗户或汽车。头部基本朝向前进方向，急促而沉重地呼吸，表现出此前已经跑了很远的疲惫。

跑动途中，窗外移动的红色汽车进入他的余光，他这时才注意到它。先是眼睛向窗口转动，随后头逐渐跟着转过去，目光锁住刚刚发现的东西。认出异常之后他才开始减速，不是在开场就一边跑一边持续看窗外。

他的减速分布在连续几个步伐中，步幅逐渐缩短，速度逐渐降低，没有突然刹停。摄影机同时逐渐减缓倒退，并持续缩短与他脸部的距离，从极近的湿脸慢慢逼近眼镜。人物减速和摄影机靠近同步发生，是一个连续过程，没有突然冲向眼镜或停下来等他。

临近停下时，他仍向前迈出几步缓慢、沉重的小步，身体保留前冲惯性。他一直喘着粗气，胸口与肩膀随呼吸起伏，嘴微张，不能突然屏息或变得平静。目光越来越专注，眉间逐渐绷紧，让观众看出他已经意识到窗外发生了悲惨的事情。

直到摄影机已经非常接近一只眼睛和湿眼镜片时，才让红车的反射变得可辨。先前的镜片只有自然的环境反光，不提前持续展示汽车。随着最后几步缓慢前行、头部角度和摄影机距离的变化，浑浊水面中一小块红色车顶逐渐出现在镜片反射里，让观众短暂看清后再离开。

反射很小、半透明，属于真实窗外环境在镜片上的反光，不是贴上的汽车图像。眼睛仍在镜片后方可见，曲率与水珠使反射局部弯曲和遮挡，不让每颗水珠都复制一辆车，不让反射发光、铺满镜片或像视频屏幕。工程师自然完成减速，在窗边停下，仍然沉重喘息；摄影机始终保留细微位移与强烈手持摇晃，没有完全停住。

只有在摄影机到达湿眼镜的极近距离、观众已经短暂辨认出红色车顶之后，摄影机才开始缓慢向画面左侧转向，朝他正在看的窗户连续摇摄。不要在接近眼镜途中提前向左转，也不要省略反射被辨认的短暂瞬间。靠近眼镜与随后向左转向自然衔接，中间没有静止等待。不绕过头部，不经过耳朵，不移动到肩后。工程师的脸逐渐从画面右侧退出，窗玻璃自然进入画面。主体转向缓慢连续，同时始终保留强烈、不规则的手持震动与摇摆。缓慢的是摄影机转向路线，不是动作慢放。

转向过程中，焦点先短暂落在近处窗玻璃的裂纹、水珠和少量污水痕上。裂纹位于右上角或画面外缘，作为次要前景，不占据中心，不挡住窗外运动路径。随着向左转向继续，焦点从近处玻璃连续转移到窗外被洪水推动的汽车。不是停下来展示玻璃再重新开始移动。摄影机始终留在室内，不穿窗，不切换室外角度。

窗外运动方向明确固定：红车位于画面右侧，作为碰撞目标的建筑混凝土墙位于它前进方向的左侧。汹涌的褐色水流从画面右侧涌向左侧，推动同一辆红车沿画面从右向左移动约五米，连续缩短它与左侧墙面的距离。不要让车向右移动、原地摇摆或突然改变方向。

汽车几乎完全沉在浑浊水下，只露出极小的一块红色车顶边缘，其余车顶、车窗、车门、引擎盖、后备厢和车轮全部被水遮住。不能出现完整汽车轮廓，也不能让车辆升起露出完整车身。通过这一小块红色车顶辨认它就是参考中的同一辆车。

一股从右向左推进的浪涌压过并覆盖汽车，露出的车顶边缘被水间歇遮住又短暂显露，同时持续向画面左侧位移。覆盖汽车的浪与推动汽车的水流是同一股运动。周围泡沫与杂物沿同一主流方向经过，强调车顶相对固定建筑的真实移动。汽车不是停在原地上下晃动，也不是一块脱落车顶独自漂浮；它始终是整辆车几乎完全浸没后唯一可见的部分。

洪水把几乎完全浸没的汽车从右向左猛烈推撞在左侧建筑的混凝土墙上。碰撞瞬间，那一小块可见的红色车顶边缘在墙根突然停止向左移动，剧烈震颤并局部折皱，伴随同步的沉重金属压溃声。汽车主体和主要接触部位始终隐藏在水下，不为了展示撞击而露出车窗、车门或整个车顶。

紧随其后的浪继续从右向左压来，覆盖剩余的红色车顶。通过车顶边缘的连续左移、突然撞停和局部变形，让观众清楚理解水下汽车狠狠撞上建筑。不能在接触前长时间完全遮住车顶，也不能只表现水浪撞墙而汽车没有位移。撞击后更多水覆盖它，露出的部分进一步减少。无爆炸、火球、穿墙、玩具式反弹或慢动作。

背景只有少量灰、银、白色汽车被水推移，其中一两辆与障碍物或其他车辆挤撞，不能抢走红车的主体位置。摄影机观察时持续移动、强烈震动与摇摆，但小块红色车顶、前进路径和建筑位置仍然可辨。裂纹留在边缘失焦，不在撞击时重新抢走焦点。

撞击之后，工程师从画面侧边进入这个仍朝着窗户的构图，先看见他近距离的侧脸。他仍望着水下汽车撞击的位置，湿眼睛绷住，嘴唇微张，沉重的呼吸变得不均匀。摄影机不绕回去寻找他，而是在他进入画面的同时，将焦点从窗外转移到他的脸。窗外洪水退入背景，他的湿脸、眼镜和安全帽边缘成为近景主体。这个焦点变化与他的入画动作连续发生，摄影机始终保持移动与手持摇晃。

他强迫自己离开窗口，沿刚才奔跑的原方向继续前进，不掉头。摄影机随着他的起跑转向并跟上，让他从近距离侧面构图向前跑过，随后自然落到他的背后。整个过程依靠他的前进和摄影机的跟随完成，不绕着他做圆弧展示，不停下来重新构图。

背后跟拍时窗户自然在画面右侧，对应开场正面跟拍时的画面左侧，建筑空间不镜像。摄影机保持极近距离，主要看见安全帽后部、湿脖颈和湿背。奔跑震动持续，摄影机逐渐追近，湿蓝色工作服越来越大，最终背部完全遮住镜头。结束在真实衣料全遮挡与持续运动中，不停步、不定格、不人工淡出，不提前显示控制室。

真实皮肤、湿衣料、水珠和自然面部比例，克制的变形宽银幕镜头特征。避免全身镜头和宽阔环境展示。声音包括急促呼吸、湿脚步、警报、员工模糊喊声、洪水及接触同步的沉重金属压溃声。无额外清晰台词、配乐、字幕、旁白或转镜whoosh音效。

21:9超宽画幅，写实电影质感，实时动作，一个连续长镜头。全段使用紧密近景与极近景，摄影机持续有强烈、不规则的手持震动、摇摆和真实惯性。摄影机的主体路线连贯明确，震动叠加在连续运动上。摄影机始终保持移动，没有突然刹停、静止等待或停下后重新启动。无可见剪辑、跳机位或穿模。

全片是一个连续长镜头，没有剪辑、隐藏剪辑、时间跳跃或瞬移。摄影机从走廊穿过出口进入停车场，再通过敞开的驾驶座车门进入汽车，始终沿连续可见的空间路线移动。曝光调整、人物、门框和运动模糊都不能成为转场。

只进行一组光学变焦：推进二楼玻璃后的工程师，再连续拉远回到汽车。其余摄影机运动均为真实的空间移动。

正面倒退跟拍时，窗户在画面左侧。工程师全身湿透，脸颊流着水，湿衣领贴着脖子，眼镜片上有不均匀水珠，眼睛仍然可见。他急促呼吸，肩膀随奔跑冲击起伏。摄影机紧紧跟住湿脸，强烈颠簸中持续修正位置，不使用平稳滑轨效果。

他的目光突然被窗外吸住，头随眼睛转向窗口，脚步急停。摄影机从已经很近的脸部继续实际靠近一只眼睛和湿眼镜片。嘴微张，吸气骤停。在摄影机开始向左转向之前，让观众先看见约一秒钟的自然镜片反射：浑浊水面中一小块红色车顶随水流移动。这个反射很小、半透明，属于整个窗外环境在镜片上的真实反光，不是一张单独贴上的汽车图像。保留镜片后的眼睛、镜片曲率和表面水珠，反射随头部与摄影机的细微晃动自然变化；水珠只局部折射和遮挡它，不把每颗水珠都变成一辆车。不要让反射铺满镜片、发光或像视频屏幕一样清晰平整。摄影机在这一短暂辨认期间仍有手持摇晃，但尚未开始向左摇摄。

短暂的眼镜反射被看清之后，摄影机才从当前正面位置缓慢向画面左侧转向，朝他正在看的窗户连续摇摄。不绕过头部，不经过耳朵，不移动到肩后。工程师的脸逐渐从画面右侧退出，窗玻璃自然进入画面。主体转向速度缓慢而连续，同时保留强烈、不规则的手持震动与摇摆；缓慢的是转向路线，不是动作慢放，也不是稳定器式平滑运动。

转向过程中，焦点先短暂落在近处窗玻璃的裂纹、水珠和少量污水痕上。裂纹位于右上角或画面外缘，作为次要前景，不占据中心，不挡住窗外运动路径。随着向左转向继续，焦点从近处玻璃连续转移到窗外被洪水推动的汽车。不是停下来展示玻璃再重新开始移动。摄影机始终留在室内，不穿窗，不切换室外角度。

窗外运动方向明确固定：红车位于画面右侧，作为碰撞目标的建筑混凝土墙位于它前进方向的左侧。汹涌的褐色水流从画面右侧涌向左侧，推动同一辆红车沿画面从右向左移动约五米，连续缩短它与左侧墙面的距离。不要让车向右移动、原地摇摆或突然改变方向。

撞击之后，工程师从画面侧边进入这个仍朝着窗户的构图，先看见他近距离的侧脸。他仍望着水下汽车撞击的位置，湿眼睛绷住，嘴唇微张，呼吸短暂卡住。摄影机不绕回去寻找他，而是在他进入画面的同时，将焦点从窗外转移到他的脸。窗外洪水退入背景，他的湿脸、眼镜和安全帽边缘成为近景主体。这个焦点变化与他的入画动作连续发生，摄影机的手持摇晃始终存在。

他强迫自己离开窗口，沿刚才奔跑的原方向继续前进，不掉头。摄影机随着他的起跑转向并跟上，让他从近距离侧面构图向前跑过，随后自然落到他的背后。整个过程依靠他的前进和摄影机的跟随完成，不绕着他做圆弧展示，不停下来重新构图。

背后跟拍时窗户自然在画面右侧，对应开场正面跟拍时的画面左侧，建筑空间不镜像。摄影机保持极近距离，主要看见安全帽后部、湿脖颈和湿背。奔跑震动持续，摄影机逐渐追近，湿蓝色工作服越来越大，最终背部完全遮住镜头。结束在真实衣料全遮挡与持续运动中，不停步、不定格、不人工淡出，不提前显示控制室。

真实皮肤、湿衣料、水珠和自然面部比例，克制的变形宽银幕镜头特征。避免全身镜头和宽阔环境展示。声音包括急促呼吸、湿脚步、警报、员工模糊喊声、洪水及接触同步的沉重金属压溃声。无额外清晰台词、配乐、字幕、旁白或转镜whoosh音效。

Photorealistic product / asset photograph of an industrial MANUAL SHUT-OFF VALVE WITH A LARGE DISHED HANDWHEEL, the kind found in a Japanese nuclear power plant of the 2000s, isolated on a plain, even, medium-grey seamless studio background.

THE HANDWHEEL — THE KEY PART, DESCRIBED PRECISELY: a large horizontal handwheel about 50 cm in diameter, of the DISHED, CONE-SHAPED type. Its RIM is a wide FLAT band of cast steel — about 4–5 cm wide and only about 1 cm thick, flat on top like a ring-shaped plate, NOT a thin round-section bar. From the underside of this rim, THREE straight spokes slope DOWNWARD and inward at an angle, meeting a solid central hub set about 15 cm BELOW the rim, so the whole wheel forms a shallow inverted cone / funnel shape — the rim floats high, the hub sits low. Mounted on the top of the rim, standing straight UP from it, a single revolving GRIP HANDLE: a black rubber-covered cylindrical spinner handle about 12 cm long and 3 cm thick on a steel pin, the kind used to spin the wheel fast. The wheel painted a dull ORANGE-RED safety colour, the paint old — worn to bare grey metal on top of the rim where hands slide over it, chipped, matte, a little rust at the chips; the handle black, scuffed.

THE VALVE BELOW: from the hub a bare steel threaded rising stem drops through a cast-iron yoke into the valve — a heavy cast-steel gate valve about 70 cm tall overall: a tall bonnet with a packing gland and four studs, a bulbous round body, mounted on a short horizontal section of steel pipe with bolted flanges at both ends. Body and pipe painted a worn pale grey-green, grimy, faint oil streaks, dust in the recesses; flanges bolted with hex nuts, dull steel, some rust. A small blank rectangular steel tag hung from the yoke on a wire, no text.

CAMERA: single view, three-quarter angle slightly from above — high enough to see the top of the flat rim and the cone of spokes falling to the hub, low enough to see the grip handle standing up in profile; the stem, bonnet, body and pipe all visible; the whole valve fully in frame with margin around it; lens about 85 mm equivalent, everything in sharp focus.

LIGHT: neutral, even, shadowless studio light — a large soft source from above and slightly in front, plus fill from both sides, neutral daylight-white, no colour cast. Only a soft faint contact shadow beneath the pipe; no hard shadows, no rim light, no reflections of a room, no glare on the paint.

COLOUR: true to material — orange-red wheel, black handle, grey-green body, bare steel and rust as they are; the background a flat neutral mid-grey, evenly lit edge to edge, no gradient, no vignette.

IN ITS PLACE, ADD A DEAD JUVENILE OARFISH (Regalecus glesne, "king of herrings") — ONLY ITS HEAD SHOWING. The species, described precisely: a long ribbon-like, laterally flattened, eel-shaped body only a few centimetres thick; skin bright metallic silver with a mirror-like sheen and scattered faint dark speckles and short dark dashes; no scales; a low crimson-red dorsal fin running the entire length of the body; on top of the head a crest of six to ten very long, thin, crimson-red fin rays, each up to 30–40 cm, with tiny flag-like tips; two long thread-thin red pelvic filaments trailing from below the head; a small head with a steep, short snout, a small protrusible mouth with no teeth, and a very large round silver eye with a black pupil.

Only the HEAD and the very first part of the body break the surface: the small pointed silver head lying flat on its side, one large round eye turned up toward the ceiling — dull, clouded, milky, unblinking — the small mouth hanging slightly open, the gill cover lifted a little; the tall crest of long red rays fallen limp, spread flat and floating on the water surface like wet threads, a few of them drooping under; the thin red pelvic filaments trailing loose in the water. Behind the head, the rest of the ribbon-like silver body sinks away below the surface: a short stretch of the flank just visible as a pale silver blur under the dark water, the body angling down and vanishing into the black, the low red dorsal fin faintly readable for a moment under the surface and then gone. No tail visible, no length on show — the fish reads as a dead head floating, body hanging beneath it. Obviously dead: no movement, slack fins, the silver skin dulled and blotched, a faint pale film on the eye, small bubbles and floating debris caught against the head.

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 21:9. Image 1 is the reference for the SCENE: the same reactor core — the same field of tall fuel assemblies, the same boiling water, the same steam — but photographed from a completely different camera position: the camera is INSIDE the reactor vessel, close to the assemblies, not looking in from the wall.

THE SCENE — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical fuel assemblies of Image 1 — tall, square-section steel channels packed in a tight regular grid, their faces lined with fine vertical rods and ribs, their tops finished with lifting handles and small square nozzles, cold dark steel, wet, scaled with grey deposits; the water around their bases boiling violently — foam, bursting bubbles, spray, a churning surface line; dense steam rising off the water and filling the space above; the assemblies' upper parts standing exposed above the surface, the water level dropped below their tops. Same materials, same detail, same scale relationship between the assemblies and the water. Nothing is redesigned.

CAMERA — INSIDE THE VESSEL, LOW AND CLOSE: the lens sits inside the reactor, just above the boiling water surface, at the outer edge of the core, among the outermost assemblies, looking across the core. Lens about 28 mm equivalent, natural perspective, no fisheye. A MEDIUM-WIDE SHOT, much closer than Image 1: the two or three nearest assemblies stand large in the foreground at the left and right edges of the frame, their wet ribbed faces filling the sides, their handles rising above the top of the frame; between and beyond them the rows of assemblies recede in steep perspective into the steam, each row softer and paler than the one before, the far core dissolving into grey-white; the churning water surface fills the lower third of the frame, running right up to the lens, foam and spray in the immediate foreground softly out of focus. The vessel wall is not in frame, or shows only as a faint curved shadow far behind the steam. Focus on the nearest assemblies; the foreground spray and the far rows fall out of focus. Strong depth: near steel sharp and dark, middle rows grey, far rows almost gone in the steam.

THE LIGHT — FLAT, DIFFUSED, FROM ABOVE: the only light comes from above, filtered through the steam — soft, non-directional, with no source, no hot spot, no bright patch; the steam at the top of the frame a dense, textured grey-white cloud held well below white, never burning out. The light falls from top to bottom: the tops of the assemblies and the foaming surface read lightest; the assembly faces darken steadily downward toward the water; the gaps between the rows sink into gloom, still readable, never black. No directional shadows, no hard edges, no rim light, no rays, no shafts through the steam, no bloom, no glow from the fuel.

THE COLOUR: materials carry their own muted colours: the assemblies a cold dark steel grey with a faint olive tint in the shadows, wet and dull; the water dull grey-green — never blue, never teal, never cyan; the foam and spray grey-white; the steam grey-white with a faint cool tint. No blue cast, no teal-and-orange, no golden or amber cast, no warm light anywhere. Overall saturation low and even.

THE TONE: low contrast, flat overcast-style curve, lifted shadows with detail, no crushed blacks; compressed highlights, the steam and the foam held below white; no glare, no halation except a faint softness on the brightest foam. Faint 35mm film grain, heaviest in the shadows. Slightly underexposed, dull and heavy rather than dramatic — restrained, documentary.

A long corridor with windows inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the REVERSE SHOT of Image 1: the same corridor photographed from its opposite end, looking back. March 11, 2011, late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. The earthquake has shaken the building, the lighting power is out, the red rotating alarm beacons are running — and outside, at this very moment, a tsunami surge is carrying a car straight at the wall of the next building, right below the nearest windows. Inside the corridor there is no water. No people.

REFERENCE ROLES: Image 1 = the corridor (materials, colours, fixtures; composition mirrored). Image 2 = ONLY the quay layout, the line of lamp posts, the breakwater and the sea — nothing else: the cars in Image 2, INCLUDING ITS RED CAR, are NOT used and do not exist in this scene; do not copy any car from Image 2. Image 3 = the red car — the ONLY source for the car: its exact design, body proportions, details and red paint. From Image 3 do NOT take the pose, the studio background, the studio lighting, or the lit headlights and tail lights.

COMPOSITION — MIRRORED DIAGONAL: the same long, straight, narrow corridor as in Image 1, but seen from the other end, so everything is reversed left-to-right: the WINDOW WALL now runs along the RIGHT side of the frame and the DOOR WALL along the LEFT. Camera at human eye level, standing close to the RIGHT wall, looking down the full length of the corridor toward a single vanishing point slightly LEFT of centre, where the corridor ends in a closed pale blue door with a small window. 女职员背对摄影机，朝他喊出日语：“家に帰らないと！” 她的声音因恐惧和喘息而绷紧，身体仍想转向出口。摄影机开始沿工程师侧面移动，但始终锁住他的超近面部：从接近正面的角度经过三分之二侧面直到侧脸，眼睛和嘴仍然清晰，保持相近的面部尺寸，绝不后退成双人中景。他盯住她，用日语说：“まだ津波警報が出てる！” 他的话逐渐变成恳切的阻止，眼中有对她可能遭遇死亡的担忧。

摄影机继续沿真实可通行的侧向弧线走到工程师肩旁，只有此时才从他的近侧脸连续转向女职员的脸，同时平滑转移焦点。工程师的脸从画框边缘退出，她的极近面部随即进入并填满画面。两个人距离近而略错开，摄影机从侧边绕行，不穿过身体；利用近处脸颊、帽沿或肩膀经过画面边缘形成连续视差，不做全黑遮挡切换。整个绕行只在一个人的超近脸与另一个人的超近脸之间转移，没有两人并排完整出现的中景。

完成绕行后，摄影机已经位于两人的另一侧，观看走廊的方向与刚才跟拍她迎面奔跑时相反。此时在女职员脸后方的虚焦空间里，员工持续面朝摄影机跑来，再从两侧经过。员工在建筑里的奔跑方向没有改变，改变的是摄影机的位置与朝向。不能沿用先前背对镜头跑远的背景。女职员的眼睛和嘴一起留在画面中，帽顶及部分下巴可以被裁切。她看着工程师，眼中有泪，胸口急促起伏但不需要拍到胸部。她努力在喘息中说清日语：“家族と連絡がつかないんです！” 说完停下来，目光仍抓住他的眼睛。她几乎无法承受继续等待，嘴唇颤动，像还有话却说不出来。让这次停顿真正存在：她在恳求，他在理解她已经被失去家人的恐惧击垮。不要立刻接点头，不添加解释台词。

工程师的后脑或帽沿仅留在极近前景边缘。他迟疑，最终给出一个很小、沉重的点头，随后主动松开她的肩膀，将阻拦的手收回，给她让出离开的空间。他知道危险仍在；这个动作不是保证她安全，更不是轻松同意。她不挣脱、不甩开他的手，也不在他松手前冲走。感受到他放开后，她仍短暂望着他的眼睛，眼神出现一个极细微的变化：在泪水与恐惧里透出无声的感谢，伴随几乎不可察觉的轻轻点头。摄影机保持她的极近面部，让观众从眼睛里读出“谢谢”，但她不说话，不用嘴型说谢谢，不露出灿烂笑容；对家人的恐惧仍在。这个短暂的感谢完成后，她才转身攥着钥匙继续跑。没有新增对白，没有“Go straight home”。钥匙始终由她持有，工程师不捡、不接、不递钥匙。

整段走廊始终有许多员工在紧急奔跑，但所有背景员工永远沿同一个物理方向前进，朝电站内部撤离。方向不因摄影机转向而改变，不出现逆行背景人群、随机来回奔跑或反复循环的同一个人。摄影机近旁和走廊后景不断有下一批员工接续经过，不能只在结尾才出现人群。女职员是唯一朝相反方向、向出口奔跑的人。即使在面部超近景里，画框边缘经过的模糊肩背、人物间隙中的移动和持续脚步声也让人感到人流没有停下。背景流动不遮住关键眼神与台词。

她转身后，摄影机只在工程师身旁迟留一瞬，感受他放手后的沉重，然后沿通道向前加速，追上她的后脑与肩膀近景。其他员工从她前方跑来，与她擦身而过，继续朝摄影机及工程师所在的方向前进。她独自逆流而行。摄影机在真实间隙中跟随，不撞穿人群，不通过突然变焦追上她，也不拉成远景。

她从走廊转入相连的楼梯，向下跑到转折平台，再转向下方出口。摄影机紧随其帽后与肩侧，真实降低高度并转过平台；扶手、阶梯和平台边缘在近景边缘连续经过，明确表现向下走，而不是沿水平走廊奔跑。出口距离短，人物动作正常速度。她推开下方门冲向明亮的室外，摄影机跟到门槛。强烈外光自然进入镜头，轮廓仍短暂可见，亮部逐渐过曝；不使用白色转场特效，不在白光里剪辑，整段连续运动直到结束。

A long corridor with windows inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the REVERSE SHOT of Image 1: the same corridor photographed from its opposite end, looking back. March 11, 2011, late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. The earthquake has shaken the building, the lighting power is out, the red rotating alarm beacons are running — and outside, at this very moment, a tsunami surge is carrying a car straight at the wall of the next building, right below the nearest windows. Inside the corridor there is no water. No people.

THE GLASS IS CRACKED BY THE QUAKE: several panes along the corridor carry fresh cracks — the nearest pane a large spider-web of radial cracks from an impact point near its lower corner, others long diagonal cracks running corner to corner, some branching, a few panes with only a single hairline — the cracked glass still held in its frames, no pane fallen out, no holes, no shards on the sill beyond a few tiny slivers; the cracks catch the grey daylight as thin bright lines and pick up the red beams as thin red threads. Between the cracks the glass is clean but not new, faint smears. No reflections of ceiling lights — they are dark.

THE VIEW THROUGH THE WINDOWS — THE TSUNAMI ON THE QUAY; LAYOUT FROM IMAGE 2, THE CAR FROM IMAGE 3: from this upper floor the windows look down onto the plant's waterfront quay of Image 2 — now under the tsunami. A highly realistic documentary-style photo, ultra-wide 21:9 cinematic frame, showing the inside of the Reactor Pressure Vessel of Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1, Japan, on 11 March 2011, during the early accident phase after automatic SCRAM, after loss of cooling has caused the reactor water level to fall dangerously low.

The scene must be technically grounded in a real BWR reactor vessel interior. This is not a giant open industrial hall and not a room full of separate columns. It is a cramped cylindrical steel pressure-vessel interior, with the camera positioned at core level, looking across a dense, tightly packed reactor core. The most important structural element is a compact array of many closely spaced square fuel assemblies inside the cylindrical core shroud, not a few isolated giant pipe bundles. The geometry should feel crowded, vertical, engineered, and physically plausible for a boiling water reactor.

The most important visual element: a clearly visible horizontal waterline cuts across the frame because the coolant level has dropped to a dangerously low point. The lower portions of the fuel assemblies remain submerged in dark, hot, violently turbulent reactor water. The upper portions of the fuel assemblies are now exposed above the water surface and are surrounded by extremely dense hot steam. The water surface is unstable, agitated, and harsh, with violent boiling, churning turbulence, flashing steam, foam, and continuous streams of bubbles rising between the tightly packed fuel assemblies.

The exposed upper core region must feel dangerous and overheated: dense white-grey steam, heat haze, condensation, moisture on metal surfaces, and a suffocating sense of thermal stress. The submerged lower part of the frame should feel darker, murkier, and more opaque than clear open water, with intense bubbling and disturbed flow rather than a clean aquarium-like underwater look.

Show authentic BWR core character: tightly grouped vertical fuel bundles, narrow spacing, hints of control-blade gaps between assemblies where visible, and the enclosing cylindrical reactor-vessel / shroud geometry around them. The space should feel physically constrained, metallic, and reactor-internal, not like a spacious chamber.

Lighting should be dim, cold, and diffuse through steam, with harsh highlights on wet metal and on the unstable water surface. The atmosphere should feel real, severe, and industrial, not stylized sci-fi.

Critical authenticity rules: no giant open room, no separate monumental columns, no walkable industrial hall, no decorative futuristic machinery, no huge readable wall text, no fantasy gauges, no oversized signage, no clean blue swimming-pool water, no calm ocean-like split-level surface. Everything must read as a real Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 BWR reactor pressure vessel interior in the early hours of the 11 March 2011 loss-of-cooling accident.

No people. No cinematic fantasy elements. No labels, no logos, no captions, no readable signage, no lettering, no numbers, no symbols.

A highly realistic documentary-style photo, ultra-wide 21:9 cinematic frame, showing the inside of the Reactor Pressure Vessel of Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1, Japan, on 11 March 2011, during the early accident phase after automatic SCRAM, after loss of cooling has caused the reactor water level to fall dangerously low.

The scene must be technically grounded in a real BWR reactor vessel interior. This is not a giant open industrial hall and not a room full of separate columns. It is a cramped cylindrical steel pressure-vessel interior, with the camera positioned at core level, looking across a dense, tightly packed reactor core. The most important structural element is a compact array of many closely spaced square fuel assemblies inside the cylindrical core shroud, not a few isolated giant pipe bundles. The geometry should feel crowded, vertical, engineered, and physically plausible for a boiling water reactor.

The most important visual element: a clearly visible horizontal waterline cuts across the frame because the coolant level has dropped to a dangerously low point. The lower portions of the fuel assemblies remain submerged in dark, hot, violently turbulent reactor water. The upper portions of the fuel assemblies are now exposed above the water surface and are surrounded by extremely dense hot steam. The water surface is unstable, agitated, and harsh, with violent boiling, churning turbulence, flashing steam, foam, and continuous streams of bubbles rising between the tightly packed fuel assemblies.

The exposed upper core region must feel dangerous and overheated: dense white-grey steam, heat haze, condensation, moisture on metal surfaces, and a suffocating sense of thermal stress. The submerged lower part of the frame should feel darker, murkier, and more opaque than clear open water, with intense bubbling and disturbed flow rather than a clean aquarium-like underwater look.

Show authentic BWR core character: tightly grouped vertical fuel bundles, narrow spacing, hints of control-blade gaps between assemblies where visible, and the enclosing cylindrical reactor-vessel / shroud geometry around them. The space should feel physically constrained, metallic, and reactor-internal, not like a spacious chamber.

Lighting should be dim, cold, and diffuse through steam, with harsh highlights on wet metal and on the unstable water surface. The atmosphere should feel real, severe, and industrial, not stylized sci-fi.

Critical authenticity rules: no giant open room, no separate monumental columns, no walkable industrial hall, no decorative futuristic machinery, no huge readable wall text, no fantasy gauges, no oversized signage, no clean blue swimming-pool water, no calm ocean-like split-level surface. Everything must read as a real Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 BWR reactor pressure vessel interior in the early hours of the 11 March 2011 loss-of-cooling accident.

No people. No cinematic fantasy elements. No labels, no logos, no captions, no readable signage, no lettering, no numbers, no symbols.

工程师就在近旁，追上一步，手掌进入画面落在她肩膀上将她拦住。她停顿并转身面对他，摄影机仍留在近处。她的后脑或帽沿只成为画面边缘的一小块模糊前景，工程师的脸占据画面。他带着真实恐惧急切说日语：“どこへ行くんだ？ ここにいた方が安全だ！” 这句话是在挽留一个可能走向死亡的人，不是训斥。他看着她，手的阻拦有分寸，不摇晃她、不粗暴拉扯。

摄影机随她拾起钥匙和起身的动作抬升、抬头，连续跟焦，迅速落到她的极近面部。碰撞打断两人的姿态：她被撞得侧转，起身时恢复自己原本朝出口奔跑的方向，朝已绕到工程师背后的摄影机跑来。她从工程师旁边的空隙穿过，不穿过他的身体。摄影机让出这个空隙并退行跟住她的脸。工程师在她从身旁通过时真实转身，改变自己的行进方向去拦住她，这个转身不是所有员工一起掉头。她一句话也不说，攥着钥匙立刻继续朝摄影机方向冲，摄影机退行跟住她的脸。此时员工从摄影机这一侧跑向走廊深处，与她迎面交错；镜头里看见的是员工离开摄影机的后脑和背部，从她脸的两侧失焦地掠过。她朝镜头跑，员工背对镜头跑远，两个方向必须清楚而相反，不能让背景员工跟她一起朝镜头跑。她呼吸急促，眼睛越过镜头寻找逃离方向，神情已经慌乱失控。不要在起身时拉远交代全身。

工程师就在近旁，追上一步，手掌进入画面落在她肩膀上将她拦住。她停顿并转身面对他，摄影机仍留在近处。她的后脑或帽沿只成为画面边缘的一小块模糊前景，工程师的脸占据画面。他带着真实恐惧急切说日语：“どこへ行くんだ？ ここにいた方が安全だ！” 这句话是在挽留一个可能走向死亡的人，不是训斥。他看着她，手的阻拦有分寸，不摇晃她、不粗暴拉扯。

女职员背对摄影机，朝他喊出日语：“家に帰らないと！” 她的声音因恐惧和喘息而绷紧，身体仍想转向出口。摄影机开始沿工程师侧面移动，但始终锁住他的超近面部：从接近正面的角度经过三分之二侧面直到侧脸，眼睛和嘴仍然清晰，保持相近的面部尺寸，绝不后退成双人中景。他盯住她，用日语说：“まだ津波警報が出てる！” 他的话逐渐变成恳切的阻止，眼中有对她可能遭遇死亡的担忧。

摄影机继续沿真实可通行的侧向弧线走到工程师肩旁，只有此时才从他的近侧脸连续转向女职员的脸，同时平滑转移焦点。工程师的脸从画框边缘退出，她的极近面部随即进入并填满画面。两个人距离近而略错开，摄影机从侧边绕行，不穿过身体；利用近处脸颊、帽沿或肩膀经过画面边缘形成连续视差，不做全黑遮挡切换。整个绕行只在一个人的超近脸与另一个人的超近脸之间转移，没有两人并排完整出现的中景。

完成绕行后，摄影机已经位于两人的另一侧，观看走廊的方向与刚才跟拍她迎面奔跑时相反。此时在女职员脸后方的虚焦空间里，员工持续面朝摄影机跑来，再从两侧经过。员工在建筑里的奔跑方向没有改变，改变的是摄影机的位置与朝向。不能沿用先前背对镜头跑远的背景。女职员的眼睛和嘴一起留在画面中，帽顶及部分下巴可以被裁切。她看着工程师，眼中有泪，胸口急促起伏但不需要拍到胸部。她努力在喘息中说清日语：“家族と連絡がつかないんです！” 说完停下来，目光仍抓住他的眼睛。她几乎无法承受继续等待，嘴唇颤动，像还有话却说不出来。让这次停顿真正存在：她在恳求，他在理解她已经被失去家人的恐惧击垮。不要立刻接点头，不添加解释台词。

工程师的后脑或帽沿仅留在极近前景边缘。他迟疑，最终给出一个很小、沉重的点头，随后主动松开她的肩膀，将阻拦的手收回，给她让出离开的空间。他知道危险仍在；这个动作不是保证她安全，更不是轻松同意。她不挣脱、不甩开他的手，也不在他松手前冲走。感受到他放开后，她仍短暂望着他的眼睛，眼神出现一个极细微的变化：在泪水与恐惧里透出无声的感谢，伴随几乎不可察觉的轻轻点头。摄影机保持她的极近面部，让观众从眼睛里读出“谢谢”，但她不说话，不用嘴型说谢谢，不露出灿烂笑容；对家人的恐惧仍在。这个短暂的感谢完成后，她才转身攥着钥匙继续跑。没有新增对白，没有“Go straight home”。钥匙始终由她持有，工程师不捡、不接、不递钥匙。

整段走廊始终有许多员工在紧急奔跑，但所有背景员工永远沿同一个物理方向前进，朝电站内部撤离。方向不因摄影机转向而改变，不出现逆行背景人群、随机来回奔跑或反复循环的同一个人。摄影机近旁和走廊后景不断有下一批员工接续经过，不能只在结尾才出现人群。女职员是唯一朝相反方向、向出口奔跑的人。即使在面部超近景里，画框边缘经过的模糊肩背、人物间隙中的移动和持续脚步声也让人感到人流没有停下。背景流动不遮住关键眼神与台词。

她转身后，摄影机只在工程师身旁迟留一瞬，感受他放手后的沉重，然后沿通道向前加速，追上她的后脑与肩膀近景。其他员工从她前方跑来，与她擦身而过，继续朝摄影机及工程师所在的方向前进。她独自逆流而行。摄影机在真实间隙中跟随，不撞穿人群，不通过突然变焦追上她，也不拉成远景。

她从走廊转入相连的楼梯，向下跑到转折平台，再转向下方出口。摄影机紧随其帽后与肩侧，真实降低高度并转过平台；扶手、阶梯和平台边缘在近景边缘连续经过，明确表现向下走，而不是沿水平走廊奔跑。出口距离短，人物动作正常速度。她推开下方门冲向明亮的室外，摄影机跟到门槛。强烈外光自然进入镜头，轮廓仍短暂可见，亮部逐渐过曝；不使用白色转场特效，不在白光里剪辑，整段连续运动直到结束。

摄影以自然的面部比例、皮肤细节、湿润眼睛和嘴部呼吸为主，近乎微距的亲密感，但不使用贴脸广角畸变。不要为了让整顶帽子、完整肩膀或两人关系入画而后退。焦点跟随当前重要的脸或手，背景柔化而有层次。顶灯与实际侧面灯光塑造明暗，保留自然肤色和有方向的阴影，走廊没有窗户、海景和窗光。碰撞时短促震动，随后是有重量、有惯性的跟随，不持续随机甩镜。

声音是沉重喘息、同向奔跑的许多脚步、衣料摩擦、钥匙撞击和门声，以及远处不可辨的紧急工作喊声。只有上述四句日语对白，由指定人物各说一次，声音与口型一致。没有旁白、字幕、音乐、额外对白、whoosh或swish。保留请求之后的情绪停顿，人群与危机在停顿中仍然继续。

A photo, Ultra-wide 21:9 cinematic shot from inside a Japanese boiling water nuclear reactor pressure vessel during an emergency shutdown, Fukushima Daiichi, March 2011.  The camera is positioned inside the enormous reactor pressure vessel, looking horizontally and slightly downward across the upper section of the nuclear fuel assemblies. Dense rows of long, precisely arranged vertical fuel assemblies and metallic structural components extend deep into the frame, industrial, complex, heavy, realistic nuclear engineering, no futuristic design.

The reactor has already been SCRAMmed, but decay heat continues to generate intense heat. The cooling system has failed after a total station blackout.

The most important visual element: the reactor water level has fallen dangerously low. A clearly visible horizontal waterline cuts across the frame. The lower portions of the fuel assemblies remain submerged in dark, turbulent water, while the upper portions are beginning to emerge above the water surface and are surrounded by extremely dense hot steam.

The water is violently agitated by residual heat, turbulent and unstable, with streams of bubbles and vapor rising between the fuel assemblies. It should NOT look like a cooking pot or an explosion. It is a huge pressurized industrial system undergoing loss of cooling.

Above the waterline, the exposed metal is wet, dark and extremely hot, partially obscured by thick white-gray steam. Subtle heat distortion in the air and steam. No flames. No visible radiation. No blue Cherenkov glow. No glowing green material. No molten lava. The fuel rods are NOT bright red or orange.

Lighting is extremely realistic and motivated only by the environment: dim, oppressive industrial darkness, faint cold gray-blue ambient light filtering through the dense steam, subtle metallic reflections from wet stainless steel surfaces. Most of the reactor interior falls into deep shadow. The steam catches the limited light and creates volumetric depth, but the image must not look stylized or theatrical.

Color palette: desaturated steel gray, dark graphite, dirty silver, cold gray-blue water, pale steam. Almost no saturated colors. Natural photographic contrast, slightly underexposed, realistic dynamic range, subtle film grain.

The composition should communicate scale: the fuel assemblies dominate the foreground and middle distance, disappearing into steam and darkness. The visible waterline is unmistakable and dramatically low, suggesting that the water is continuing to recede and expose the reactor core.

Documentary realism, historical disaster reconstruction, grounded Japanese industrial engineering, physically plausible materials, physically plausible lighting, physically plausible steam and water behavior. Shot as if for an expensive serious historical drama, not a disaster blockbuster.

35mm cinema lens, low camera position close to the water surface, strong foreground depth, subtle atmospheric perspective, restrained cinematic composition, photorealistic, extremely detailed, natural textures, realistic stainless steel, realistic water physics, realistic condensation.

Mood: silent, mechanical, inevitable, deeply unsettling. Nothing is exploding yet. The horror comes entirely from understanding that the cooling water is disappearing while the reactor continues producing decay heat.

NO people, NO control room, NO text, NO warning graphics, NO gauges, NO sci-fi reactor glow, NO flames, NO explosion, NO dramatic orange lighting, NO fantasy machinery, NO cyberpunk elements, NO Chernobyl-style graphite blocks, NO visible molten core.

March 11, 2011, late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. The earthquake has shaken the building, the lighting power is out, the red rotating alarm beacons are running — and outside, at this very moment, the TSUNAMI has drowned the quay below the windows and is driving a car into the wall of the next building. Inside the corridor there is no water. No people.

The window wall recedes in steep perspective on the right, the door wall on the left. Wide lens, natural perspective, no fisheye. Every material, colour and fixture is identical to Image 1 — only the direction of view is reversed, and the earthquake has left its traces.

THE WINDOW WALL (RIGHT): a continuous band of large sliding windows in slim aluminium frames exactly as in Image 1, sill at about waist height, running the whole length of the corridor; cream-painted wall beneath, a red steel handrail on brackets along it. THE GLASS IS CRACKED BY THE QUAKE: several panes along the corridor carry fresh cracks — the nearest pane a large spider-web of radial cracks from an impact point near its lower corner, others long diagonal cracks running corner to corner, some branching, a few panes with only a single hairline — the cracked glass still held in its frames, no pane fallen out, no holes, no shards on the sill beyond a few tiny slivers; the cracks catch the grey daylight as thin bright lines and pick up the red beams as thin red threads. The parking lot is completely under water — no bays, no dry ground, no rows of parked cars; the other cars of the lot are gone under or reduced to a few dark drifting shapes and debris. The guard rail is under. Only the single straight line of identical grey street-lamp posts still stands out of the water at equal spacing along the quay edge, one sodium luminaire each, lit warm amber, receding along the waterfront. The water is a violent, restless mass in the minutes right after the wave struck: dirty grey-brown, churned with foam, silt and debris — planks, plastic, torn sheet metal — heaving, surging, crossed by fast currents, spray in the air. Beyond it the harbour is a heaving grey-green mass; across it the long straight rubble-mound breakwater with grey concrete tetrapods on its seaward face is still being hit — waves slamming into it and pouring over its crown, grey-white spray bursting high, its small red marker lights and the green light at its end showing between the bursts; the open grey-green sea with white caps and a flat grey horizon beyond, the dark headland far off, flattened by haze. 35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint, dull overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, small red alarm lamps flash on the steel structure of the hall, one more red alarm lamp glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark, heavily overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken dark-grey smears, the small red lamps on the structure as thin trembling red streaks scattered where the lamps stand above the water, and the near lamp at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the few nearest the left edge catch a faint red glint from the near lamp; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — MAIN LIGHTING DEAD, A FAINT DULL WINDOW FILL, SMALL PRACTICALS:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight.
- THE WINDOWS — DULL, DARK, OVERCAST, VERY WEAK: outside it is a dark, heavily overcast afternoon, and it is that weather that is seen through the glass: low, dense, dark grey storm cloud fills every pane, textured, with no bright patch. The panes are DIM — mid-to-dark grey, dirty, salt-streaked, only a little lighter than the grey wall panels around them, about as bright as the small screens on the cabinets, and far darker than white; no pane is white, no pane glows, no pane is a bright rectangle. The daylight that comes through them is feeble and cold: it lifts the roof trusses, the upper steel and the tops of the pipes just out of black into a faint cold grey, gives the mezzanine floor and the yellow railing nearest the windows a thin dull grey edge — no bright patch on the mezzanine, no lit railing, no pool of daylight anywhere — and puts a faint cold sheen on the water and the fish. It casts no shadows, no rays, no shafts, no beams through dust; below the mezzanine and on the ground floor it is almost gone. The interior stays dark; the windows do not light the hall.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They do not light the room.
- THE RED ALARM LAMPS — ON THE STEEL STRUCTURE, AT THE BEAM–COLUMN JOINTS, NOT ON THE WALLS: about ten to twelve small red signal lamps of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011, all identical, all fixed to the steel frame of the hall on flat brackets at its structural joints: one at every column along the FRONT EDGE BEAM of the mezzanine, just beneath the floor grating and the yellow railing, so they form a short chain receding along the mezzanine edge; three on the OUTER STRINGER of the staircase — at its top, at mid-height and at its foot — following the diagonal of the stairs; two on the nearest columns high up, where the columns meet the roof beams; one on the right-hand column at mezzanine level. Every lamp is small: about 15 cm tall, no bigger than a coffee can, narrower than the tube of the yellow handrails; a grey cylindrical body with a ribbed red plastic cover, fixed flush to the steel member — not on a post, not on a stand, not on a pedestal, not free-standing. Each reads as a small red point with a soft red halo. They are lit, caught mid-flash, out of sync: a few at full brightness, the rest dimmer. Their light is LOCAL: the glowing red cover, a soft halation, a faint red patch on the steel within about a metre around each lamp, and a thin red streak in the water below it. They do not light the hall, the mezzanine, the stairs or the cabinets. None anywhere else: NO lamp on the far wall, none beside the windows, none above or between the windows, none on the wall panels, none on any cabinet, none on the railing tubes, none in the middle of a beam away from a joint; all of them the same size.
- THE NEAR LAMP — ONE, LEFT EDGE, OUT OF FOCUS: the single deliberate exception — ONE more red signal lamp of exactly the same small type and size, mounted on a flat bracket on the nearest steel column at the extreme LEFT edge of the frame, about a metre above the water, so it sits within half a metre of the lens, far outside the depth of field. It is lit, at full brightness. Because it is so close to the lens it renders as a large, soft, fully defocused red bokeh disc with a wide soft halo, its body and bracket unreadable — only a glowing red circle hanging at the left edge, partly cut by the frame, in the upper left quarter of the image. Its light is local: a soft red glow on the column beside it and one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; it does not tint the room, the cabinets or the fish beyond the near left corner. It is the ONLY lamp near the camera; there is no second near lamp, none at the right edge, none in the centre.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised steel a cold dark grey under the window fill, the yellow railings a faint dull yellow where the fill touches them and near-black elsewhere, the red cable bundles deep and dull, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no light reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, faint olive, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no warm daylight; red exists only on the small lamps, their patches and their streaks. Saturation hierarchy: the near bokeh lamp at the left edge is the largest and most saturated colour area in the frame, soft and unfocused; then the small red lamp covers on the structure; then the green and amber indicator lamps and the small screens; the window fill is colourless dark grey; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the window panes dim grey showing cloud texture — never white, never clipped; the red lamp covers and the indicator lamps the only near-clipped points, soft halation around them, the near bokeh disc bright but not burned to white at its centre. Heavy grain in the shadows. Documentary, still, silent — the aftermath, not the wave.

A long corridor with windows inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the REVERSE SHOT of Image 1: the same corridor photographed from its opposite end, looking back. March 11, 2011, late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. The earthquake has shaken the building, the lighting power is out, the red rotating alarm beacons are running — and outside, at this very moment, the TSUNAMI is surging across the quay below the windows. Inside the corridor there is no water. No people.

COMPOSITION — MIRRORED DIAGONAL: the same long, straight, narrow corridor as in Image 1, but seen from the other end, so everything is reversed left-to-right: the WINDOW WALL now runs along the RIGHT side of the frame and the DOOR WALL along the LEFT. Camera at human eye level, standing close to the RIGHT wall, looking down the full length of the corridor toward a single vanishing point slightly LEFT of centre, where the corridor ends in a closed pale blue door with a small window. The window wall recedes in steep perspective on the right, the door wall on the left. Wide lens, natural perspective, no fisheye. Every material, colour and fixture is identical to Image 1 — only the direction of view is reversed, and the earthquake has left its traces.

THE WINDOW WALL (RIGHT): a continuous band of large sliding windows in slim aluminium frames exactly as in Image 1, sill at about waist height, running the whole length of the corridor; cream-painted wall beneath, a red steel handrail on brackets along it. THE GLASS IS CRACKED BY THE QUAKE: several panes along the corridor carry fresh cracks — the nearest pane a large spider-web of radial cracks from an impact point near its lower corner, others long diagonal cracks running corner to corner, some branching, a few panes with only a single hairline — the cracked glass still held in its frames, no pane fallen out, no holes, no shards on the sill beyond a few tiny slivers; the cracks catch the grey daylight as thin bright lines and pick up the red beams as thin red threads. Between the cracks the glass is clean but not new, faint smears. No reflections of ceiling lights — they are dark.

THE VIEW THROUGH THE WINDOWS — THE TSUNAMI ON THE QUAY, LAYOUT FROM IMAGE 2: from this upper floor the windows look down onto the plant's waterfront quay of Image 2 — but the quay is being overrun. The harbour has risen over the quay edge and a turbulent surge of dirty grey-brown sea water, thick with mud, foam and debris, is pouring across the whole parking lot from the water toward the building, toward the wall directly beneath these windows; the lot's marked bays are gone under it, the guard rail along the quay edge shows only as a line of posts in the flow. The parked fleet of Image 2 is swamped: most cars are under the water, showing only as dark roofs and blurred shapes, some already shifted and drifting. THE RED CAR: the small red kei car of Image 2 is caught in the flow and being SWEPT TOWARD THE BUILDING — it is in the near-middle of the view, below the windows, closer to the building than the other cars, tilted and turning as the current carries it, ALMOST ENTIRELY UNDER WATER: only the top of its red roof and the upper edge of one window and a door frame break the surface, the churning water washing over the bonnet and boot, white foam and debris piling against its upstream side, its red paint the one clear colour in the grey-brown flood; the same red car as in Image 2 — same colour, same small boxy shape — nothing else about it changed. Along the quay edge the single straight line of identical grey street-lamp posts still stands in the water at equal spacing, one sodium luminaire each, lit warm amber, receding along the waterfront. Beyond, the harbour is a heaving grey-green mass; across it the long straight rubble-mound breakwater with grey concrete tetrapods on its seaward face is being overtopped — sea pouring over its crown, grey-white spray bursting high, its small red marker lights and the green light at its end still showing between the bursts; the open grey-green sea with white caps and a flat grey horizon beyond, the dark headland far off, flattened by haze. No reactor buildings, no stack in this view — they are behind the camera. The exterior light is exactly as in Image 2: dull, flat, fully diffused, the sky a narrow band of mid to dark greys, no sun, no bright patch. The view is seen through the cracked panes, the cracks laid over it as fine lines.

THE DOOR WALL (LEFT): cream-painted wall with a few flush steel doors in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as in Image 1, each with a small wired-glass window, spaced far apart — fewer doors than window bays. The rooms behind the doors are DARK: every small door window is black, no glow, no light behind any door. Between the doors, the same wall decor as Image 1, reversed to this wall: a cork notice board, a few small Japanese safety notices (安全第一, 禁煙), a wall telephone, a red fire extinguisher, a fire-hose cabinet.

THE ROTATING BEACONS — LIT: high along the door wall, close to the ceiling, the red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011 — one beacon per two doors, evenly spaced, receding down the corridor. Each is small: about 15 cm tall, a short cylindrical cream-beige plastic base on a grey wall bracket, a smooth dome of clear transparent RED plastic on top, inside it a small incandescent bulb and a curved chrome reflector that ROTATES around it. They are running, and this is a frozen instant of their sweep: each beacon throws a NARROW RED BEAM that turns in a circle, caught at a different phase — one beam raking along the ceiling, one across the door wall, one down onto the floor and up the window wall; the dome bright on the side the reflector faces, dark translucent red on the other; where a beam lands it lays a thin red band of light a few metres long with soft edges. The beams are narrow and weak: bands and streaks, never a red flood, never a red wash over the corridor; between the beams the walls keep the grey daylight.

EARTHQUAKE TRACES — SHAKEN, NOT DESTROYED: the corridor is intact in structure but visibly shaken. Several ceiling panels have dropped: two or three hang open at an angle from one edge, one lies on the floor; a fine fall of plaster dust and grit lies on the linoleum along the walls and on the handrail and window sills; hairline cracks run through the paint at the wall–ceiling joint and around door frames; the window glass is cracked as described above; the cork notice board hangs askew from one corner with papers scattered on the floor beneath it; the fire extinguisher has toppled and lies on its side; a door stands a hand's width ajar. THE BROKEN TUBE: on the floor in the near half of the corridor, under one of the ceiling fixtures, lies a long fluorescent TUBE that has fallen out of the fixture and shattered — the tube broken into two or three long pieces, the milky white glass split open, a scatter of fine white glass fragments and pale phosphor powder around it on the pale green linoleum, one metal end cap lying apart; the fixture above it is still in place in the ceiling, its diffuser dropped open on one side, the socket empty and dark. The tube is dead, unlit, dusty. A thin haze of dust still hangs in the air, catching the red beams. No rubble, no collapse, no blocked corridor, no fire, no water inside.

CEILING AND FLOOR: the same flat panelled ceiling as Image 1 with a line of recessed rectangular fluorescent fixtures down the centre, evenly spaced, receding — all fixed in place, ALL DARK, dead grey tubes, no glow; the one above the broken tube with its diffuser open and its socket empty; a PA loudspeaker high on the door wall. Pale green linoleum floor, slightly worn, dry, with a soft reflective sheen carrying the grey window light and the red bands of the beacons; dust, grit and the broken tube on it.

THE LIGHT: the windows are the ONLY steady source — cold, flat, non-directional grey daylight from the right, falling across the corridor from RIGHT to LEFT: the floor and the window sills lightest, the door wall on the left darker, the far end sinking into gloom; no sun, no directional shadows, no hard edges. No ceiling light, no light from the doors, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight. The rotating beacons are the only practicals: their thin red beams and the red bands they lay on the walls, ceiling and floor, strongest near the camera, fading down the corridor. Shading under the handrail and along the base of the walls.

ATMOSPHERE: a thin dust haze inside, made visible where the red beams cut through it; outside, damp sea haze and wind-blown spray over the surge, softening the breakwater and flattening the sea toward the sky tone.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours, only desaturated by the overcast: cream walls, pale green floor, powder-blue doors, aluminium frames, cool grey-white daylight, plaster dust and broken tube glass pale grey-white; the flood outside dirty grey-brown with grey-white foam, the harbour grey-green — never blue. Saturation hierarchy: the red beacon domes and their beams are the most saturated elements in the frame; then the RED handrail; then the red roof of the car in the flood — the one clear colour outside; then the powder-blue doors; then the small exterior lights seen through the glass — amber street lamps, red and green navigation lights; every other surface muted. Shadows cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. No golden cast; warmth only in the tiny exterior lights.

TONE: low contrast, flat overcast curve, lifted shadows, no crushed blacks, the sky through the windows held well below white, no blown highlights on the glass, the cracks reading as fine bright lines, not glare; the foam outside grey-white, not blown out. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint, dull overcast daylight seeps in through the small high windows, small red rotating alarm beacons sweep their beams across the steel structure of the hall, one more such beacon glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark, heavily overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the beacons and the camera.

THE WINDOWS — EXACTLY AS IN IMAGE 1, SMALL: the far wall carries ONE row of SMALL rectangular windows set high up just under the roof, exactly the same number, size, proportion, spacing and positions as in Image 1 — each only about 1.5 m wide and 1 m high, framed in steel, separated by wide fields of corrugated metal wall; they occupy only a small part of the wall, most of the wall is solid panel. There is NO other glazing anywhere: no glass wall, no curtain wall, no large windows, no floor-to-ceiling glazing, no enlarged windows, no extra windows, no clerestory band. Each pane is a flat, dull, dim grey — dirty, salt-streaked glass on a dark overcast day — with NOTHING visible through it: no sky, no clouds, no view, no detail; just flat grey glass.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of small dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the small windows as faint, broken dark-grey smears, the red beams of the beacons as thin trembling red streaks and bands wherever a beam reaches the water, and the near beacon at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the ones a beacon beam passes over flash a red glint on their wet flanks; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — MAIN LIGHTING DEAD, A FAINT DULL WINDOW FILL, ROTATING BEACONS, SMALL INDICATORS:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight.
- THE WINDOW LIGHT — DULL, VERY WEAK: the small panes are DIM — mid-to-dark grey, only a little lighter than the grey wall panels around them, about as bright as the small screens on the cabinets, far darker than white; no pane is white, no pane glows, no pane is a bright rectangle. The daylight that comes through them is feeble and cold: it lifts the roof trusses, the upper steel and the tops of the pipes just out of black into a faint cold grey, gives the mezzanine floor and the yellow railing nearest the windows a thin dull grey edge — no bright patch on the mezzanine, no lit railing, no pool of daylight anywhere — and puts a faint cold sheen on the water and the fish. It casts no shadows, no rays, no shafts, no beams through dust; below the mezzanine and on the ground floor it is almost gone. The windows do not light the hall.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They do not light the room.
- THE ROTATING BEACONS — ON THE STEEL STRUCTURE, AT THE BEAM–COLUMN JOINTS, NOT ON THE WALLS: about ten to twelve small red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011, all identical, all fixed to the steel frame of the hall on flat brackets at its structural joints: one at every column along the FRONT EDGE BEAM of the mezzanine, just beneath the floor grating and the yellow railing, so they form a short chain receding along the mezzanine edge; three on the OUTER STRINGER of the staircase — at its top, at mid-height and at its foot — following the diagonal of the stairs; two on the nearest columns high up, where the columns meet the roof beams; one on the right-hand column at mezzanine level. THE DEVICE: small — about 15 cm tall, no bigger than a coffee can, narrower than the tube of the yellow handrails — a short cylindrical base in cream-beige plastic on a flat bracket bolted flush to the steel member, and on top a smooth dome of clear transparent RED plastic; inside the dome a small incandescent bulb and a curved chrome reflector that ROTATES around it. Not on a post, not on a stand, not on a pedestal, not free-standing, not a vehicle light. THE LIGHT: because the reflector turns, each beacon does not glow evenly — it throws a NARROW RED BEAM that sweeps around in a circle, and this is a frozen instant of that sweep: from every beacon a slim red fan of light is visible in the damp air of the hall, pointing in whatever direction its reflector faces at this moment — each beacon caught at a different phase, so the beams point different ways; the dome is bright on the side the reflector faces and dark, translucent red on the opposite side; where a beam lands it lays a thin red band of light across a column, a beam, the underside of the mezzanine, a railing or the water, a few metres long, with soft edges. The beams are weak and narrow: they reach a few metres and fade; they are bands and streaks, never floods, never a red wash over the hall; between the beams the steel stays dark. None anywhere else: NO beacon on the far wall, none beside the windows, none above or between the windows, none on the wall panels, none on any cabinet, none on the railing tubes, none in the middle of a beam away from a joint; all of them the same size.

It is lit and turning. Because it is so close to the lens it renders as a large, soft, fully defocused red dome — a red bokeh disc with a wide soft halo, its base and bracket unreadable — hanging at the left edge, partly cut by the frame, in the upper left quarter of the image. Its beam at this instant sweeps across the near left corner, away from the lens: a soft red band on the column beside it and one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; it does not point into the lens and does not tint the cabinets or the fish beyond the near left corner. It is the ONLY beacon near the camera; there is no second near beacon, none at the right edge, none in the centre.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised steel a cold dark grey under the window fill, the yellow railings a faint dull yellow where the fill touches them and near-black elsewhere, the red cable bundles deep and dull, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no light reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, faint olive, never blue, never teal. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. 35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint, dull overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, small red alarm lamps flash on the steel structure of the hall, one more red alarm lamp glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark, heavily overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken dark-grey smears, the small red lamps on the structure as thin trembling red streaks scattered where the lamps stand above the water, and the near lamp at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the few nearest the left edge catch a faint red glint from the near lamp; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

Every lamp is small: about 15 cm tall, no bigger than a coffee can, narrower than the tube of the yellow handrails; a grey cylindrical body with a ribbed red plastic cover, fixed flush to the steel member — not on a post, not on a stand, not on a pedestal, not free-standing. It is lit, at full brightness. Where no light reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, faint olive, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no warm daylight; red exists only on the small lamps, their patches and their streaks. Saturation hierarchy: the near bokeh lamp at the left edge is the largest and most saturated colour area in the frame, soft and unfocused; then the small red lamp covers on the structure; then the green and amber indicator lamps and the small screens; the window fill is colourless dark grey; everything else desaturated and dark.

The guard rail is under. Only the single straight line of identical grey street-lamp posts still stands out of the water at equal spacing along the quay edge, one sodium luminaire each, lit warm amber, receding along the waterfront. The water is a violent, restless mass in the minutes right after the wave struck: dirty grey-brown, churned with foam, silt and debris — planks, plastic, torn sheet metal — heaving, surging, crossed by fast currents, spray in the air. Beyond it the harbour is a heaving grey-green mass; across it the long straight rubble-mound breakwater with grey concrete tetrapods on its seaward face is still being hit — waves slamming into it and pouring over its crown, grey-white spray bursting high, its small red marker lights and the green light at its end showing between the bursts; the open grey-green sea with white caps and a flat grey horizon beyond, the dark headland far off, flattened by haze. 走廊已经受损：近处部分窗玻璃破碎缺失，窗框边缘残留少量碎玻璃，地上散落玻璃、灰尘与掉落的天花板板材，一块吊顶倾斜悬挂，墙面局部开裂，红色扶手有一处弯曲。保留原走廊的结构与辨识度，不要变成完全坍塌的废墟。近处破损窗洞提供清楚的向下视线。

窗外下方是海啸已经淹没的同一停车场。灰褐色不透明洪水完全覆盖地面与停车线，车辆被冲离车位、方向凌乱。主要红车位于画面右下方的室外中景，约占整幅画面宽度十分之一至七分之一，足够辨认，但不是汽车特写。从第三层楼明显俯视红车，以车顶和引擎盖为主要可见表面，只露出较少的一侧车身，不能呈现平视汽车的正面视角。轮胎完全淹没，水线接近车门上缘。车身略微倾斜，前部较低，车尾浮起；一个前角被水流压在邻近工业建筑突出的混凝土墙角上。前翼子板与引擎盖一角明显凹折，保险杠局部脱落。墙角、车头接触点与浮起的车尾关系清晰，水流绕过车身，接触处聚集局部白沫。表现一辆已经被冲坏、仍由洪水托着的沉重汽车，不是正常停在水中。

红车后方有少量半淹车辆、漂浮碎木与杂物，路灯杆从洪水中伸出。更远处在窗外景物的上部保留一条灰暗海面、防波堤以及成排混凝土消波块，停车场与向下视线占据主要室外画面，天空仅少量出现，它们局部被浪沫冲刷但仍能辨认。空间由近到远明确连续：受损走廊与窗框—楼下淹没的停车场和红车—海边防波堤与消波块—远处海面与阴云。保持真实楼层高度和俯视角度，不把停车场抬到窗户同一高度。

阴天冷灰色自然光从右侧窗外照入较暗的走廊，室内破损细节仍然可读，外部水面不过曝。少量暖色路灯倒影散落在浑水中，红车是远一些的小面积色彩焦点。电影实拍质感，真实湿混凝土、浑水与受损金属，前景到远景有自然层次，停车场和海岸仍清晰可辨，不要过度虚化。无人物，无巨浪水墙，无爆炸，无火焰，无游戏渲染感，无拼贴，无字幕。

Ultra-wide 21:9 cinematic shot from inside a Japanese boiling water nuclear reactor pressure vessel during an emergency shutdown, Fukushima Daiichi, March 2011.

The camera is positioned inside the enormous reactor pressure vessel, looking horizontally and slightly downward across the upper section of the nuclear fuel assemblies. Dense rows of long, precisely arranged vertical fuel assemblies and metallic structural components extend deep into the frame, industrial, complex, heavy, realistic nuclear engineering, no futuristic design.

The reactor has already been SCRAMmed, but decay heat continues to generate intense heat. The cooling system has failed after a total station blackout.

The most important visual element: the reactor water level has fallen dangerously low. A clearly visible horizontal waterline cuts across the frame. The lower portions of the fuel assemblies remain submerged in dark, turbulent water, while the upper portions are beginning to emerge above the water surface and are surrounded by extremely dense hot steam.

The water is violently agitated by residual heat, turbulent and unstable, with streams of bubbles and vapor rising between the fuel assemblies. It should NOT look like a cooking pot or an explosion. It is a huge pressurized industrial system undergoing loss of cooling.

Above the waterline, the exposed metal is wet, dark and extremely hot, partially obscured by thick white-gray steam. Subtle heat distortion in the air and steam. No flames. No visible radiation. No blue Cherenkov glow. No glowing green material. No molten lava. The fuel rods are NOT bright red or orange.

Lighting is extremely realistic and motivated only by the environment: dim, oppressive industrial darkness, faint cold gray-blue ambient light filtering through the dense steam, subtle metallic reflections from wet stainless steel surfaces. Most of the reactor interior falls into deep shadow. The steam catches the limited light and creates volumetric depth, but the image must not look stylized or theatrical.

Color palette: desaturated steel gray, dark graphite, dirty silver, cold gray-blue water, pale steam. Almost no saturated colors. Natural photographic contrast, slightly underexposed, realistic dynamic range, subtle film grain.

The composition should communicate scale: the fuel assemblies dominate the foreground and middle distance, disappearing into steam and darkness. The visible waterline is unmistakable and dramatically low, suggesting that the water is continuing to recede and expose the reactor core.

Documentary realism, historical disaster reconstruction, grounded Japanese industrial engineering, physically plausible materials, physically plausible lighting, physically plausible steam and water behavior. Shot as if for an expensive serious historical drama, not a disaster blockbuster.

35mm cinema lens, low camera position close to the water surface, strong foreground depth, subtle atmospheric perspective, restrained cinematic composition, photorealistic, extremely detailed, natural textures, realistic stainless steel, realistic water physics, realistic condensation.

Mood: silent, mechanical, inevitable, deeply unsettling. Nothing is exploding yet. The horror comes entirely from understanding that the cooling water is disappearing while the reactor continues producing decay heat.

NO people, NO control room, NO text, NO warning graphics, NO gauges, NO sci-fi reactor glow, NO flames, NO explosion, NO dramatic orange lighting, NO fantasy machinery, NO cyberpunk elements, NO Chernobyl-style graphite blocks, NO visible molten core.
