35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, there is NO daylight — the hall has no windows — red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1, WITHOUT THE WINDOWS: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. ONE deliberate difference: the far wall is SOLID — unbroken corrugated metal panels from floor to roof, NO windows, no openings, no skylights, no glazing anywhere; the row of windows visible in Image 1 does not exist here. Nothing else is redesigned; the other differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the solid far wall and the dark roof trusses close the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches — the rest of the surface is black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — NO DAYLIGHT, NO MAIN LIGHTING, PRACTICALS ONLY:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight, no daylight from anywhere — no windows, no doors ajar, no skylights, no glow from outside. Between the practicals the hall is black.
- THE RED ALARM BEACONS — THE KEY LIGHT, BACKGROUND ONLY: mounted high in the BACKGROUND — on the far wall's steel columns and corrugated panels, and on the rear columns of the mezzanine — three to five red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011: a small grey cylindrical base with a ribbed red polycarbonate dome on a short wall bracket, an incandescent rotating lamp inside. They are caught mid-flash: the dome lit from within in warm deep red with soft red halation, and each flash throws a real sweep of red light onto the wall panels and columns around it, the underside of the mezzanine, the nearest railings and pipes, and down onto the water — deep red, falling off quickly into darkness, so the hall is revealed in separate pools of red with black between them. They flash out of sync: one or two at full brightness, the others dimmer, mid-rotation. They are small and far away, always in the background, never on the cabinets, never in the foreground. The red is strongest at the far wall and weakens toward the camera; the foreground water and the nearest cabinets are lit only by the faint tail of the sweeps and by the indicators.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They are the only light near the camera; they do not light the room.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised grey steel turned dark rose-grey under the red, the yellow railings reading as dull orange-brown in the flashes and near-black outside them, the red cable bundles nearly invisible against the red-washed doors, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no practical reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no white light anywhere. Saturation hierarchy: the beacon domes themselves are the most saturated points; then the red sweeps on the walls and the red streaks on the water; then the green and amber indicator lamps; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the beacon domes the only near-clipped points, soft halation around the beacons and the indicator lamps, the red pools falling off smoothly into shadow. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, a row of small red alarm lamps flashes on the far wall, one more red alarm lamp glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears, the small red lamps of the far wall as three thin trembling red streaks far away below the far wall, and the near lamp at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the few nearest the left edge catch a faint red glint from the near lamp; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, a row of small red alarm lamps flashes on the far wall, one more red alarm lamp glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears, the small red lamps of the far wall as three thin trembling red streaks far away below the far wall, and the near lamp at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the few nearest the left edge catch a faint red glint from the near lamp; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight.

This weak grey light barely reaches into the hall: it lifts the upper steel, the roof trusses and the tops of the pipes just out of black into a faint cold grey, gives the mezzanine a thin grey edge, and puts a faint cold sheen on the water and the fish — a fill that lets the structure be read, no more. They do not light the room.
- THE RED ALARM LAMPS — ONE ROW, IDENTICAL, FAR WALL ONLY: exactly THREE small red signal lamps of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011, mounted on the steel columns of the FAR WALL in ONE straight horizontal line, all at the SAME height — just above the top edge of the windows — one lamp per column bay, at equal spacing. Each lamp is small: about 15 cm tall, no bigger than a coffee can, narrower than the tube of the yellow handrails, many times smaller than a single window pane; a grey cylindrical body with a ribbed red plastic cover, fixed on a flat wall bracket flush to the column — not on a post, not on a stand, not on a pedestal, not free-standing. At this distance each reads as a small red point with a soft red halo. They are lit, caught mid-flash, out of sync: one at full brightness, the other two dimmer. Their light is LOCAL: the glowing red cover, a soft halation, a faint red patch on the wall panel within about a metre around each lamp, and one thin red streak in the water below the far wall. They do not light the hall, the mezzanine, the stairs or the cabinets. Nowhere else in the room: no red lamp on any cabinet, none on the railings, none on the stairs, none on a post, none in the middle ground; all three are the same size and at the same height.
- THE NEAR LAMP — ONE, LEFT EDGE, OUT OF FOCUS: the single deliberate exception — ONE more red signal lamp of exactly the same small type and size, mounted on a flat bracket on the nearest steel column at the extreme LEFT edge of the frame, about a metre above the water, so it sits within half a metre of the lens, far outside the depth of field. It is lit, at full brightness. Because it is so close to the lens it renders as a large, soft, fully defocused red bokeh disc with a wide soft halo, its body and bracket unreadable — only a glowing red circle hanging at the left edge, partly cut by the frame, in the upper left quarter of the image. Its light is local: a soft red glow on the column beside it and one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; it does not tint the room, the cabinets or the fish beyond the near left corner. It is the ONLY lamp near the camera; there is no second near lamp, none at the right edge, none in the centre.

No golden cast, no warm daylight; red exists only on the four lamps, their patches and their streaks. 35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, there is NO daylight — the hall has no windows — red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1, WITHOUT THE WINDOWS: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. ONE deliberate difference: the far wall is SOLID — unbroken corrugated metal panels from floor to roof, NO windows, no openings, no skylights, no glazing anywhere; the row of windows visible in Image 1 does not exist here. Nothing else is redesigned; the other differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the solid far wall and the dark roof trusses close the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches — the rest of the surface is black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — NO DAYLIGHT, NO MAIN LIGHTING, PRACTICALS ONLY:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight, no daylight from anywhere — no windows, no doors ajar, no skylights, no glow from outside. Between the practicals the hall is black.
- THE RED ALARM BEACONS — THE KEY LIGHT, BACKGROUND ONLY: mounted high in the BACKGROUND — on the far wall's steel columns and corrugated panels, and on the rear columns of the mezzanine — three to five red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011: a small grey cylindrical base with a ribbed red polycarbonate dome on a short wall bracket, an incandescent rotating lamp inside. They are caught mid-flash: the dome lit from within in warm deep red with soft red halation, and each flash throws a real sweep of red light onto the wall panels and columns around it, the underside of the mezzanine, the nearest railings and pipes, and down onto the water — deep red, falling off quickly into darkness, so the hall is revealed in separate pools of red with black between them. They flash out of sync: one or two at full brightness, the others dimmer, mid-rotation. They are small and far away, always in the background, never on the cabinets, never in the foreground. The red is strongest at the far wall and weakens toward the camera; the foreground water and the nearest cabinets are lit only by the faint tail of the sweeps and by the indicators.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They are the only light near the camera; they do not light the room.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised grey steel turned dark rose-grey under the red, the yellow railings reading as dull orange-brown in the flashes and near-black outside them, the red cable bundles nearly invisible against the red-washed doors, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no practical reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no white light anywhere. Saturation hierarchy: the beacon domes themselves are the most saturated points; then the red sweeps on the walls and the red streaks on the water; then the green and amber indicator lamps; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the beacon domes the only near-clipped points, soft halation around the beacons and the indicator lamps, the red pools falling off smoothly into shadow. Heavy grain in the shadows. Documentary, still, silent — the aftermath, not the wave.

AVOID: windows, any window, glazing, skylights, daylight, a lit wall opening, a doorway with light behind it, sunlight, sun rays, light shafts, god rays, lit fluorescent tubes, ceiling lights on, emergency white lights, flashlights, any white light source, blue tint, teal, golden cast, a uniform red tint over the whole frame with no dark areas, an evenly red-lit room, a black frame with nothing readable, beacons on the cabinets, beacons in the foreground, beacons everywhere, white or amber or blue beacons, modern LED strobe bars, police-style light bars, a close-up of the fish, a macro shot, fish filling the frame, large fish, tuna, salmon, koi, tropical fish, living fish, a clean mirror-like water surface, clear blue water, swimming-pool water, a wave, splashing, rushing water, people, bodies, a different room, a redesigned room, missing mezzanine, missing yellow railings, a camera from above, a high angle, a dry floor, fire, smoke, text overlays, watermark, 3d render, cgi.

生成一张16:9横向电影写实静帧，画面铺满，无黑边。

参考分工：<<<a0bafed2-2c1d-45e5-a7c9-16e5c83e2a6b>>> 用于核电站建筑风格、沿海工业环境与阴沉天气；<<<39d3785f-f508-42f5-99b0-0f779d72b15f>>> 用于同一停车场的建筑外墙、路灯、车辆尺度和空间关系；<<<eb05414b-175f-4163-a9f6-635cbfd8d9ed>>> 用于一辆红色高车身五门日本轻型汽车的外形、比例、红色车漆与黄色车牌19-17。不要复制三视图或摄影棚背景。

视点在电站建筑二楼的窗内，像站在窗边的人向斜下方看院内停车场。画面左侧仅露出一小条失焦的深色窗框，底部露出少量窗台；玻璃反光极弱，外面清晰可见。以受损红车和邻楼混凝土墙角为视觉中心，红车约占画面宽度三分之一，看见车顶、前部和一侧车身。不是航拍，不是停车场全景。

海啸已经冲入停车场，地面和停车线完全被不透明的灰褐色洪水淹没。水流裹着淤泥、碎木和少量工业碎片，在建筑之间形成不规则流纹和旋涡。红车已经浮起并冲离原来的车位，斜向横在水流中，车头略低、车身轻微侧倾，轮胎完全没入浑水，水线接近车门上缘，车顶与大部分车窗仍露在水面上。呈现沉重车身被洪水托起的重量感，不是正常停在浅水里，也不是悬空。

画面右侧是邻近工业建筑的厚重混凝土外墙与突出墙角，底部被洪水淹没。红车一个前角刚撞上墙角，被水流斜着压住，车尾仍浮在水中。接触位置清楚可见：前翼子板凹陷、引擎盖一角折起、保险杠一端脱落，侧面有擦伤，挡风玻璃局部开裂，车型仍可辨认。水在车身和墙角之间挤出局部白沫与短促水花，绕过车尾形成旋涡。以真实碰撞痕迹表达冲击。

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches, and the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears — barely there; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows and red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — MAIN LIGHTING DEAD, A FAINT WINDOW FILL, PRACTICALS AS THE KEY:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight.
- THE WINDOWS — VERY WEAK FILL: through the high windows of the far wall comes only a very faint, cold, sunless overcast daylight — the sky outside is dark and heavy, so the panes read as dim mid-grey rectangles, dull, held far below white, and the beacon domes are brighter than the panes. 从参考走廊的另一端反向观看：实体墙与门在画面左侧，连续窗户与红色扶手在右侧。根据反向机位重新建立真实透视，不要简单镜像参考图或反转文字。摄影机位于约第三层楼的走廊内，距停车场地面约8至10米，靠近右侧窗户，斜向右外侧，以明显的高位俯角向下看停车场。不是二楼的轻微俯视，也不是垂直航拍。宽阔的环境全景：左侧约三分之一画面保留受损走廊的墙、局部天花板、地面及纵深；右侧约三分之二通过近处宽大的窗洞看向外面。窗框形成自然前景，但不要遮住红车。不是只拍走廊尽头，也不是把室内和室外拼接成两幅画。

走廊已经受损：近处部分窗玻璃破碎缺失，窗框边缘残留少量碎玻璃，地上散落玻璃、灰尘与掉落的天花板板材，一块吊顶倾斜悬挂，墙面局部开裂，红色扶手有一处弯曲。保留原走廊的结构与辨识度，不要变成完全坍塌的废墟。近处破损窗洞提供清楚的向下视线。

窗外下方是海啸已经淹没的同一停车场。灰褐色不透明洪水完全覆盖地面与停车线，车辆被冲离车位、方向凌乱。主要红车位于画面右下方的室外中景，约占整幅画面宽度十分之一至七分之一，足够辨认，但不是汽车特写。从第三层楼明显俯视红车，以车顶和引擎盖为主要可见表面，只露出较少的一侧车身，不能呈现平视汽车的正面视角。轮胎完全淹没，水线接近车门上缘。车身略微倾斜，前部较低，车尾浮起；一个前角被水流压在邻近工业建筑突出的混凝土墙角上。前翼子板与引擎盖一角明显凹折，保险杠局部脱落。墙角、车头接触点与浮起的车尾关系清晰，水流绕过车身，接触处聚集局部白沫。表现一辆已经被冲坏、仍由洪水托着的沉重汽车，不是正常停在水中。

红车后方有少量半淹车辆、漂浮碎木与杂物，路灯杆从洪水中伸出。更远处在窗外景物的上部保留一条灰暗海面、防波堤以及成排混凝土消波块，停车场与向下视线占据主要室外画面，天空仅少量出现，它们局部被浪沫冲刷但仍能辨认。空间由近到远明确连续：受损走廊与窗框—楼下淹没的停车场和红车—海边防波堤与消波块—远处海面与阴云。保持真实楼层高度和俯视角度，不把停车场抬到窗户同一高度。

阴天冷灰色自然光从右侧窗外照入较暗的走廊，室内破损细节仍然可读，外部水面不过曝。少量暖色路灯倒影散落在浑水中，红车是远一些的小面积色彩焦点。电影实拍质感，真实湿混凝土、浑水与受损金属，前景到远景有自然层次，停车场和海岸仍清晰可辨，不要过度虚化。无人物，无巨浪水墙，无爆炸，无火焰，无游戏渲染感，无拼贴，无字幕。

Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, there is NO daylight — the hall has no windows — red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1, WITHOUT THE WINDOWS: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. ONE deliberate difference: the far wall is SOLID — unbroken corrugated metal panels from floor to roof, NO windows, no openings, no skylights, no glazing anywhere; the row of windows visible in Image 1 does not exist here. Nothing else is redesigned; the other differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the solid far wall and the dark roof trusses close the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches — the rest of the surface is black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — NO DAYLIGHT, NO MAIN LIGHTING, PRACTICALS ONLY:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight, no daylight from anywhere — no windows, no doors ajar, no skylights, no glow from outside. Between the practicals the hall is black.
- THE RED ALARM BEACONS — THE KEY LIGHT, BACKGROUND ONLY: mounted high in the BACKGROUND — on the far wall's steel columns and corrugated panels, and on the rear columns of the mezzanine — three to five red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011: a small grey cylindrical base with a ribbed red polycarbonate dome on a short wall bracket, an incandescent rotating lamp inside. They are caught mid-flash: the dome lit from within in warm deep red with soft red halation, and each flash throws a real sweep of red light onto the wall panels and columns around it, the underside of the mezzanine, the nearest railings and pipes, and down onto the water — deep red, falling off quickly into darkness, so the hall is revealed in separate pools of red with black between them. They flash out of sync: one or two at full brightness, the others dimmer, mid-rotation. They are small and far away, always in the background, never on the cabinets, never in the foreground. The red is strongest at the far wall and weakens toward the camera; the foreground water and the nearest cabinets are lit only by the faint tail of the sweeps and by the indicators.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They are the only light near the camera; they do not light the room.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised grey steel turned dark rose-grey under the red, the yellow railings reading as dull orange-brown in the flashes and near-black outside them, the red cable bundles nearly invisible against the red-washed doors, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no practical reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no white light anywhere. Saturation hierarchy: the beacon domes themselves are the most saturated points; then the red sweeps on the walls and the red streaks on the water; then the green and amber indicator lamps; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the beacon domes the only near-clipped points, soft halation around the beacons and the indicator lamps, the red pools falling off smoothly into shadow. Heavy grain in the shadows. Documentary, still, silent — the aftermath, not the wave.

视点在电站建筑二楼的窗内，像站在窗边的人向斜下方看院内停车场。画面左侧仅露出一小条失焦的深色窗框，底部露出少量窗台；玻璃反光极弱，外面清晰可见。以受损红车和邻楼混凝土墙角为视觉中心，红车约占画面宽度三分之一，看见车顶、前部和一侧车身。不是航拍，不是停车场全景。

海啸已经冲入停车场，地面和停车线完全被不透明的灰褐色洪水淹没。水流裹着淤泥、碎木和少量工业碎片，在建筑之间形成不规则流纹和旋涡。红车已经浮起并冲离原来的车位，斜向横在水流中，车头略低、车身轻微侧倾，轮胎完全没入浑水，水线接近车门上缘，车顶与大部分车窗仍露在水面上。呈现沉重车身被洪水托起的重量感，不是正常停在浅水里，也不是悬空。

画面右侧是邻近工业建筑的厚重混凝土外墙与突出墙角，底部被洪水淹没。红车一个前角刚撞上墙角，被水流斜着压住，车尾仍浮在水中。接触位置清楚可见：前翼子板凹陷、引擎盖一角折起、保险杠一端脱落，侧面有擦伤，挡风玻璃局部开裂，车型仍可辨认。水在车身和墙角之间挤出局部白沫与短促水花，绕过车尾形成旋涡。以真实碰撞痕迹表达冲击。

后景保留同一停车场的少量路灯、浅色工业外墙，以及两三辆被冲乱方向、仅露出车顶和部分车窗的车辆。背景适度柔化但空间可读。冷灰色阴天散射光，少量暖色路灯倒影被浑水打碎，红车是主要色彩焦点。湿混凝土、泥水、受损金属和玻璃具有真实摄影质感，克制、压迫、可信的灾难电影画面。

无人物，无巨浪水墙，无爆炸或火焰，无夸张巨型飞溅，无清澈海水，无玩具感或游戏渲染感，无拼贴，无字幕。

Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches, and the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears — barely there; the rest of the surface is near-black. THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows and red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. This weak grey light barely reaches into the hall: it lifts the upper steel, the roof trusses and the tops of the pipes just out of black into a faint cold grey, gives the mezzanine a thin grey edge, and puts a faint cold sheen on the water and the fish — a fill that lets the structure be read, no more. It casts no shadows, no rays, no shafts, no beams through dust; below the mezzanine and on the ground floor it is almost gone.

They flash out of sync: one or two at full brightness, the others dimmer, mid-rotation. They are small and far away, always in the background, never on the cabinets, never in the foreground. The red is strongest at the far wall and weakens toward the camera; the foreground water and the nearest cabinets are lit only by the faint tail of the sweeps, the faint window fill and the indicators.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They are the strongest light near the camera; they do not light the room.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised grey steel turned dark rose-grey under the red and cold grey under the window fill, the yellow railings reading as dull orange-brown in the flashes and as a faint dull yellow where only the window fill touches them, the red cable bundles nearly invisible against the red-washed doors, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no light reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, faint olive, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no warm daylight. Saturation hierarchy: the beacon domes themselves are the most saturated points; then the red sweeps on the walls and the red streaks on the water; then the green and amber indicator lamps; the window fill is colourless grey; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the window panes dull mid-grey, the beacon domes the only near-clipped points, soft halation around the beacons and the indicator lamps, the red pools falling off smoothly into the grey-black. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the red beacon flashes as long trembling red streaks across the dark water, the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the red-washed steel as broken red patches, and the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears — barely there; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows and red highlights where the beacon flashes catch their wet bellies; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — MAIN LIGHTING DEAD, A FAINT WINDOW FILL, PRACTICALS AS THE KEY:
- DEAD: every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; no ceiling light, no wall light, no emergency white lighting, no flashlight.
- THE WINDOWS — VERY WEAK FILL: through the high windows of the far wall comes only a very faint, cold, sunless overcast daylight — the sky outside is dark and heavy, so the panes read as dim mid-grey rectangles, dull, held far below white, and the beacon domes are brighter than the panes. This weak grey light barely reaches into the hall: it lifts the upper steel, the roof trusses and the tops of the pipes just out of black into a faint cold grey, gives the mezzanine a thin grey edge, and puts a faint cold sheen on the water and the fish — a fill that lets the structure be read, no more. It casts no shadows, no rays, no shafts, no beams through dust; below the mezzanine and on the ground floor it is almost gone.
- THE RED ALARM BEACONS — THE KEY LIGHT, BACKGROUND ONLY: mounted high in the BACKGROUND — on the far wall's steel columns and corrugated panels below and between the windows, and on the rear columns of the mezzanine — three to five red rotating alarm beacons of the type used in Japanese plants in 2011: a small grey cylindrical base with a ribbed red polycarbonate dome on a short wall bracket, an incandescent rotating lamp inside. They are caught mid-flash: the dome lit from within in warm deep red with soft red halation, and each flash throws a real sweep of red light onto the wall panels and columns around it, the underside of the mezzanine, the nearest railings and pipes, and down onto the water — deep red, falling off quickly into darkness, so the hall is revealed in separate pools of red with faint grey and black between them. They flash out of sync: one or two at full brightness, the others dimmer, mid-rotation. They are small and far away, always in the background, never on the cabinets, never in the foreground. The red is strongest at the far wall and weakens toward the camera; the foreground water and the nearest cabinets are lit only by the faint tail of the sweeps, the faint window fill and the indicators.
- THE CABINET INDICATORS — LIT: the switchgear cabinets are still alive: their small pilot lamps, indicator LEDs and small panel displays glow exactly as in Image 1 — small points of green, red and amber, and the dim glow of the little screens — sharp, tiny, local, each throwing a faint glow onto the grey door around it and a small dot onto the water below. They are the strongest light near the camera; they do not light the room.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours where light reaches them — galvanised grey steel turned dark rose-grey under the red and cold grey under the window fill, the yellow railings reading as dull orange-brown in the flashes and as a faint dull yellow where only the window fill touches them, the red cable bundles nearly invisible against the red-washed doors, the grey cabinets, the black-green water, the pewter fish. Where no light reaches, everything falls to near-black with faint detail — cool neutral black, faint olive, never blue, never teal. No golden cast, no warm daylight. Saturation hierarchy: the beacon domes themselves are the most saturated points; then the red sweeps on the walls and the red streaks on the water; then the green and amber indicator lamps; the window fill is colourless grey; everything else desaturated and dark.

TONE: very dark, low-key, exposed for the practicals so that the steel structure, the cabinets and the fish remain faintly readable in the dark — not a black frame; lifted blacks with detail, the window panes dull mid-grey, the beacon domes the only near-clipped points, soft halation around the beacons and the indicator lamps, the red pools falling off smoothly into the grey-black. Heavy grain in the shadows. Documentary, still, silent — the aftermath, not the wave.

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, every light in the building is dead, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, cold overcast daylight outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead lights and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin rainbow oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples; it reflects the pale windows and the yellow railings as broken, wobbling patches, never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, bright silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus silver shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear silver bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

THE LIGHT — ALL ARTIFICIAL LIGHT DEAD, WINDOWS ONLY: the power is gone. Every fluorescent tube in the roof and on the mezzanine is dark grey glass; every indicator lamp, screen and pilot light on the cabinets is off; no emergency lighting, no flashlight, no glow anywhere inside. The ONLY light is cold, flat, sunless overcast daylight through the high windows of the far wall — pale grey, textured with cloud, the brightest area of the frame but NOT burned to white. It falls steeply downward from the windows: the upper steel, the underside of the roof and the tops of the pipes catch a dim grey wash; the mezzanine throws deep shadow beneath itself; the ground-floor cabinets are lit only by what reaches down between the structures; the water surface picks up the windows as pale reflections and becomes the second-brightest surface. Everything away from the windows sinks into gloom; the far corners are nearly black. No directional sun, no rays, no light shafts, no beams through dust.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours, only darkened and cooled by the dim daylight — galvanised grey steel, the yellow railings still readable as yellow but muted in the gloom, the red cable bundles deep and dull, the grey cabinets, the grey-green turbid water, the silver of the fish. Shadows shift to cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. No golden or amber cast anywhere; no artificial colour. Saturation hierarchy: the yellow railings nearest the windows and the silver fish catching the window light are the only bright notes; the red cables muted below them; everything else low.

TONE: dark, low-key, low contrast within the shadows, lifted blacks with detail, the windows held just below white, the water reflections soft. Faint grain, heaviest in the shadows. Documentary, still, silent — the aftermath, not the wave.

参考分工：<<<a0bafed2-2c1d-45e5-a7c9-16e5c83e2a6b>>> 用于核电站建筑风格、沿海工业环境与阴沉天气；<<<39d3785f-f508-42f5-99b0-0f779d72b15f>>> 用于同一停车场的建筑外墙、路灯、车辆尺度和空间关系；<<<eb05414b-175f-4163-a9f6-635cbfd8d9ed>>> 用于一辆红色高车身五门日本轻型汽车的外形、比例、红色车漆与黄色车牌19-17。不要复制三视图或摄影棚背景。

视点在电站建筑二楼的窗内，像站在窗边的人向斜下方看院内停车场。画面左侧仅露出一小条失焦的深色窗框，底部露出少量窗台；玻璃反光极弱，外面清晰可见。以受损红车和邻楼混凝土墙角为视觉中心，红车约占画面宽度三分之一，看见车顶、前部和一侧车身。不是航拍，不是停车场全景。

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, red alarm beacons are flashing on the walls, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the flashing beacons and the camera.

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, a row of small red alarm lamps flashes on the far wall, one more red alarm lamp glows out of focus right beside the lens at the left edge of the frame, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears, the small red lamps of the far wall as three thin trembling red streaks far away below the far wall, and the near lamp at the left edge as one soft red smear on the water in the near left corner; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

35mm film still, fine visible grain, 16:9. Image 1 is the reference for the ROOM: the same two-level electrical switchgear hall inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the same steel structure, materials, layout and equipment — but photographed from a completely different camera position, minutes after the tsunami: the whole ground level is flooded with sea water, the main lighting of the building is dead, only a very faint overcast daylight seeps in through the high windows, a row of small red alarm lamps flashes on the far wall, and dead fish float on the water. March 11, 2011, about 16:00, a dark overcast afternoon outside. No people.

THE ROOM — CONSISTENT WITH IMAGE 1: the identical hall: galvanised steel columns and beams, the open-grid steel mezzanine with its yellow-painted tubular handrails, the steel staircase with yellow rails, the large lagged pipes and ducts, the corrugated grey metal wall panels, the row of high windows along the far wall in the same positions, the grey switchgear cabinets on the ground floor with their bundles of red cables, the cable reels, the small yellow-and-black warning sign, the roof trusses with their dark fluorescent tubes. Same proportions, same material colours, same wear. Nothing is redesigned; the only differences are the water, the fish, the dead main lights, the small red lamps and the camera.

CAMERA — FROM THE WATER SURFACE, LOOKING UP: the lens sits a few centimetres above the water surface on the flooded ground floor, among the switchgear cabinets, tilted upward by about 20 degrees. Wide lens, about 24 mm equivalent — a WIDE SHOT, not a close-up: the water plane fills the lower part of the frame, the half-submerged cabinets rise in the middle distance, the mezzanine, railings, staircase and pipes stand above them, and the far wall with its row of dim windows sits near the top of the frame. Strong upward perspective: verticals converge upward, the underside of the mezzanine and the roof trusses loom overhead. Focus is on the cabinets and the mezzanine; anything within half a metre of the lens is out of focus.

THE WATER: the ground floor is flooded with SEA WATER about 1–1.2 metres deep — the cabinets stand in it with their lower third submerged, a dark wet tide-line on their doors a hand above the surface where the water has already dropped slightly. The water is not clean: turbid grey-green sea water clouded with silt, a thin oil film in patches, streaks of dirty foam, small floating debris — paper, a plastic bottle, splinters. The surface is almost calm but alive: a slow low swell from the receding wave, small ripples. It reflects only what is lit: the cabinet indicator lamps as tiny coloured dots, the dim windows as faint, broken grey smears, and the small red lamps of the far wall as three thin trembling red streaks far away, below the far wall; the rest of the surface is near-black. Never a clean mirror. In the FOREGROUND the water surface runs right up to the lens, softly out of focus.

THE DEAD FISH: dozens of dead JAPANESE SARDINES (maiwashi, Sardinops melanostictus) — small, 15–20 cm, slim, silver with a blue-grey back and a row of dark spots along the flank — float on the surface, belly-up or on their sides, eyes clouded, some half-submerged, some caught against the cabinets and the debris, scattered across the whole flooded floor and drifting slowly with the swell. In this light their silver reads as dull pewter with a faint cold sheen from the windows; the ones beside the cabinets pick up tiny green and amber glints from the indicator lamps; the ones in darkness are only faint pale shapes. The nearest ones, right in front of the lens, are large soft out-of-focus shapes; further away they sharpen into small clear bodies. No other species, no large fish, no living fish.

右侧不同办公室陆续有人出来，他们先让过已有的人流，随即转向并加入同一前进方向。男女员工分散在不同位置，速度与动作不同步。部分人在移动中举帽戴上，其他人继续露着头发。
摄影机接近玻璃时逐渐减速，停住脚步。奔跑级别的大幅晃动收住，但保留轻微、不规则的手持起伏、呼吸与构图修正。窗前整个观察和转焦过程都有这种微小的活的运动。

先看海啸，工程师尚未出现：
摄影机先到窗前，对焦窗外的海浪与第一道防波堤。此时画面里没有工程师，也没有他的倒影。先让观众清楚看见正在发生的灾难。
其他工作人员仍从摄影机后方沿走廊跑过，他们柔化的倒影掠过玻璃。有人在倒影里边跑边戴帽，有人直接通过。
巨大而厚重的海水前缘逼近从海侧遇到的第一道防波堤，在堤前堆高，然后猛烈撞击固定结构，沿堤线翻起宽阔、不规则的白色水墙和喷雾。推进、堆积、撞击与翻落连续发生。

工程师只在玻璃倒影中到达：
海浪仍然清楚、焦点仍在窗外时，工程师才从摄影机后侧来到窗边。他的模糊倒影从玻璃画面边缘进入，逐渐接近并站定。
他的真人身体始终在这一构图之外，不走进摄影机与玻璃之间，不直接遮住窗外景象。观众只能通过倒影看见他。
摄影机与玻璃的角度让倒影形成足够紧的脸部近景：脸、眼镜和上部肩膀占据主要画面，而不是远处一个小小的全身倒影。工程师靠近窗户，帽子仍拿在手里，可以在构图下缘之外。优先保留脸部表演。
先让这个近处倒影仍处于模糊状态。只有工程师站定后，焦点才从远处海啸平顺转向倒影中的眼睛。海浪逐渐柔化，倒影里的脸与眼镜变清楚。
严格顺序：海啸清晰且没有工程师，模糊的工程师倒影进入，倒影站定，然后转焦。摄影机保持微小手持呼吸，不用突然换机位获得近景。

倒影里的恐惧：
通过清楚的反射近景看他的反应。工程师意识到这片水可能很快杀死自己。他的眼睛锁住窗外，呼吸突然卡住，嘴唇略张，喉结轻动。想深吸气平静下来，吸气却浅而断续。下颌紧绷，眼神短暂无法从威胁上移开。
这是对死亡迫近的真实恐惧。他努力不让自己失控，但观众能看见压抑失败的细节。表演集中，不夸张，也不拖成长时间静止凝视。
在他清楚的反射肩膀后面，其他工作人员仍以柔焦倒影陆续跑过。有人独自经过，有人间隔着跟上，方向一致。只有工程师暂时停下，背景不冻结、不清空。

明确加入同向人流：
几名员工继续从工程师身旁经过，向走廊前方跑去。工程师用力收回视线，从窗边退开，转向这些人刚刚跑去的方向，跟在他们背后追上。
他的目标是追随前方员工的背影。先让几个人通过，再让他加入他们后面，以实际动作说明方向，而不只是抽象地说“跟随人流”。
摄影机随他离开玻璃，后移并沿短弧转向，从倒影连续找到真人。窗框、扶手与经过的员工保持空间可追踪。进入直接拍摄后，摄影机移到他的侧面，与他同向、同速前进。

摄影机跟着脚步强烈晃动，出现上下冲击和横向补偿，并持续找回他的眼睛。他努力调节呼吸，但无法完全平静：吸气短促，嘴唇略张，眼睛急切检查前方，下颌与颈部紧张。
前方员工先转过一个拐角，工程师跟着同一组背影转入无窗内走廊。摄影机在身侧同步转弯，保持连续路线。

无窗内走廊与戴帽：
新的内走廊由普通实墙、办公室门和顶灯构成。人流仍向前，摄影机继续与工程师侧面并行。
工程师在急行中举起同一顶安全帽，戴上，双手来到下巴附近，将下巴带卡扣接合、扣紧，再短促拉紧一下。动作急切，手有紧张感，但接触关系清楚：戴帽、找到卡扣、接合、收紧、放手。
摄影机短暂保留脸、下巴和双手的空间，看到动作完成，随后实际靠近侧脸。

眼镜旁的极近侧面特写：
眼镜框、镜片后的近侧眼睛、太阳穴和一部分脸颊几乎占满画面。保持严格侧面轮廓，帽檐只局部进入上缘。镜头与他并行移动，不绕到正前方。
脸部比例自然，焦点锁住镜片后的眼睛，反光有层次。背景的墙、门、灯和同向奔跑人员强烈虚化。
近景仍受到奔跑冲击，摄影机不断补偿找回眼睛。他真实地喘息、紧张，试图镇定却没有完全成功。这里是运动中的极近景，不是稳定悬浮的肖像。

低于肩部的画外接触：
极近侧面构图保持收紧。一次来自画面外、低于肩线的突然接触阻住他的上身，使胸腹与躯干先短促减速，随后头和眼镜因惯性一晃，呼吸被打断。
接触对象比工程师矮，但始终完全位于画外，不为解释接触而扩展构图。观众只看到极近侧脸的一次突然失衡，无法确认与谁发生了碰撞。
摄影机立即受这个动作带动，从眼镜旁猛然向下俯摇。快速、大幅度的tilt-down形成强烈连续的纵向运动模糊，衣服和墙面拉成竖向色带。保持同一个摄影机动作，不切换到独立地面机位。

钥匙与结束：
一串金属钥匙从画外落入视野，沿自然轨迹掉到鞋边，触地发出清楚的金属碰响，可以有一次小幅弹跳。钥匙来源保持在画外。
工程师补一步恢复平衡。钥匙触地已经可理解，而摄影机仍向下运动、画面仍带残余纵向模糊时立即结束。用这个向下的模糊衔接下一场，不停成钥匙静物，不抬回人物。

摄影机从参考中的机位和斜向前下方的观察角度开始，从第一帧就平缓、连续地将镜头向下俯转，逐渐将正下方的沙地带入画面中心，完成光轴垂直朝下的顶视。开场机位高度保持不变，这只是摄影机在原位逐渐低头看向沙地，不是起重机下降，也不向前靠近海床。这个俯转发生在低频轰鸣逐渐增强的过程中，第一下猛烈冲击到来时已完成顶视；从冲击这一刻才开始沿光轴反方向向后退离，也就是向上升高，持续看着下方沙地。  皇带鱼在海床上方自然向左游过。沿背部延伸的长背鳍连续起伏，银色带状身体保持柔韧、克制的弯曲，细长鳍条被水流轻轻拖动。画面中所有小鱼从第一帧就自然游动：近处海床上方、石块与海带之间以及远处水体中的小鱼都轻摆尾鳍，以各自不同的方向和速度缓缓穿行，偶尔自然转向，形成持续而细微的生命活动，没有静止悬挂的鱼。稀薄悬浮物掠过前景，冷色漫射光从上方偏左斜穿水体，只在银色鱼身、砂砾和贝壳碎片上留下有限亮度。  开场平静的游动中，一股深沉的水下低频轰鸣从微弱逐渐增强、变厚，压力持续积累；紧接着，第一次突然、极其猛烈而沉重的整体冲击穿过画面。整片可见海床与岩石结构发生大幅、急促的横向错动并猛然上顶；摄影机因水体和自身惯性滞后，底部从它下方剧烈移位，原本稳定的空间关系瞬间被打破。紧接着摄影机受到一次沉重的轴向顿挫，开始沿光轴反方向向后退离海床，仿佛被冲击推离沙地。机位向上升高，光轴始终垂直朝下，不转向、不侧倾。  细砾、贝壳碎片和松动的小石块同时跳离接触面，落下后继续滑移与碰撞；大块岩石随周围底部共同震动。海带根部被海床突然带动，长叶片因水体阻力滞后，随后猛烈拖向另一侧。  皇带鱼在冲击到来的瞬间突然受惊，身体短促收曲，头部立即转向画面左侧靠近镜头的逃离路径。背鳍起伏迅速加快，柔韧的长身紧随头部猛然加速，一次连续的逃离动作从镜头前近距离斜掠而过，银色鱼身形成短促的方向性运动模糊，尾部沿同一条弯曲路径最后掠出画面左侧。整条鱼迅速离开；同一瞬间，画面中所有小鱼也受到惊吓，包括近处海床上方、石块与海带之间以及远处水体中的小鱼。它们迅速摆尾、突然转向，沿各自不同的逃离路径四散加速，游出画框或逃向更远的水体，在泥云遮住它们之前清楚呈现从平静游动到惊慌逃散的变化，没有小鱼停在原处或继续悠闲游动。摄影机继续向上退离，同时垂直朝下看着海床，不追随鱼转向。  覆盖海床的松散细泥在同一个冲击中被大范围猛烈掀离底部。贴地浑浊迅速增厚为沿整片海床翻卷的灰褐色沉积云，岩石之间的细泥相互连成一片，大片底部纹理迅速消失。少量细小气泡从石块之间被扰动的沉积层中断续释放，向上穿过泥云。冲击表现为地面的整体运动与沉积层脱离，不出现孤立喷口、爆炸火团或放射状泥柱。  冲击扰动的局部水流裹挟大量细泥向上翻涌，追上已经上升的摄影机。摄影机被同一股上涌水流带动，向上的速度骤然增加，保持垂直朝下的顶视而不侧倾；近处颗粒与海带快速滑过画框，底部明显加速远离。摄影机在被带向上方的同时保持垂直朝下的观察方向。水流推动摄影机，泥沙随水流翻卷，两者具有不同的惯性与相对速度。  初始大冲击之后，数次沉重而间隔不规则的震动继续穿过底部。细石反复跳动，泥层持续脱离，摄影机承受沿退离轴线的短促震动，保持垂直朝下的光轴和向上退离的路径，不横向甩动或改变角度。  0:04–0:07｜垂直俯视加速远离，翻卷泥层包围摄影机 摄影机保持已经完成的顶视，光轴垂直朝下，延续被上涌水流带动后的较快上升速度。石块、海带根部和海床纹理迅速缩小，近处海带从画框边缘快速滑过，海床被涌起的细泥逐层覆盖，明确显示摄影机真的加速离开了底部。  细泥在水中扩散、翻卷并被局部水流带高；较重砂粒在短暂抬起后重新下沉，较轻淤泥保持悬浮。镜头前有近处快速划过的颗粒、中层成片翻卷的泥云和最后消失的海床暗影。少量细小气泡穿过泥云，沿镜头附近上升。密度持续增加，最后整个画面被灰褐色流体占据。  水下摄影机受到不规则的沉重轴向短促震动，但仍沿同一条向上的撤离路径运动。震动只影响退离的瞬时速度，不改变垂直朝下的光轴与连续上升的主方向。能见度消失时，地理标志与尺度同时消失，摄影机保持垂直朝下的光轴。快速上升继续发生在厚重、持续翻卷的浑水内部，直到0:08之前画面始终被流体完全包围。  0:07–0:08｜泥、水泡、深色液体 镜头附近的泥粒与细小气泡继续经过。背景先变深，随后前景颗粒也逐渐失去轮廓，最后几个气泡的微弱反光被深褐色流体吞没。摄影机保持连续的上升速度和朝下的光轴，黑暗只是一层正在经过的浑水，而不是停留的黑场。整个画面仍被深色液体占据，尺度尚不可辨认。  0:08–0:09｜直接拉出咖啡，刚认出杯子便结束 遮住视线的液膜从镜头前退开：黑咖啡、冷白色反光与白瓷杯沿几乎在同一个向上拉出的动作中出现。摄影机已经位于杯口正上方，光轴垂直朝下，圆形杯沿完整而自然，杯柄随杯沿进入画面，桌面只在四周短暂露出。  液体内部的运动直接延续为杯中已经发生的激烈晃动。杯子仍在震动的桌面上，冷白色顶灯在咖啡表面留下局部反光。没有单独展示海面、波峰或液体变形的段落，也没有慢动作停顿。最终构图只包含杯中咖啡、白瓷杯沿、杯柄和四周少量桌面。观众刚认出这是一杯咖啡，镜头立即结束在仍然持续的上升运动与震动中。  声音： 全程只有连续环境声与动作声。开场先有从微弱逐渐增强、越来越厚重的水下低频轰鸣，在第一次冲击之前持续积累压力，随后骤然爆发为极其强烈而沉重的第一下冲击。突然的沉重水下低频冲击伴随连续轰鸣、砂石猛烈接触和沉闷水流，后续不规则冲击保持压力与重量；摄影机被水流带向上方时，近处翻涌的浑水声迅速增强。浑水变深时声音被包裹，杯口揭示的瞬间直接进入贴身的建筑震响、瓷杯与桌面的轻碰及杯内液体拍击。声音不因空间揭示而停顿，结束时仍有持续地震与液体晃动声。

左侧长窗和红色扶手、右侧办公室门与设备清楚建立空间。摄影机继续从后方追上并超过人员，靠近左侧一块无遮挡的窗玻璃。
右侧不同办公室陆续有人出来，他们先让过已有的人流，随即转向并加入同一前进方向。男女员工分散在不同位置，速度与动作不同步。部分人在移动中举帽戴上，其他人继续露着头发。
摄影机接近玻璃时逐渐减速，停住脚步。奔跑级别的大幅晃动收住，但保留轻微、不规则的手持起伏、呼吸与构图修正。窗前整个观察和转焦过程都有这种微小的活的运动。

先看海啸，工程师尚未出现：
摄影机先到窗前，对焦窗外的海浪与第一道防波堤。此时画面里没有工程师，也没有他的倒影。先让观众清楚看见正在发生的灾难。
其他工作人员仍从摄影机后方沿走廊跑过，他们柔化的倒影掠过玻璃。有人在倒影里边跑边戴帽，有人直接通过。
巨大而厚重的海水前缘逼近从海侧遇到的第一道防波堤，在堤前堆高，然后猛烈撞击固定结构，沿堤线翻起宽阔、不规则的白色水墙和喷雾。推进、堆积、撞击与翻落连续发生。
以 <<<39621b4e-f235-4418-830f-9af547bbdc04>>> 的规模、暗色水体和白色浪顶为依据。建筑与防波堤固定，提供尺度。水有质量，喷雾随重力回落并受风吹散。摄影机留在室内同一个窗口，透过完整玻璃观察，不改变到室外机位。

工程师只在玻璃倒影中到达：
海浪仍然清楚、焦点仍在窗外时，工程师才从摄影机后侧来到窗边。他的模糊倒影从玻璃画面边缘进入，逐渐接近并站定。
他的真人身体始终在这一构图之外，不走进摄影机与玻璃之间，不直接遮住窗外景象。观众只能通过倒影看见他。
摄影机与玻璃的角度让倒影形成足够紧的脸部近景：脸、眼镜和上部肩膀占据主要画面，而不是远处一个小小的全身倒影。工程师靠近窗户，帽子仍拿在手里，可以在构图下缘之外。优先保留脸部表演。
先让这个近处倒影仍处于模糊状态。只有工程师站定后，焦点才从远处海啸平顺转向倒影中的眼睛。海浪逐渐柔化，倒影里的脸与眼镜变清楚。
严格顺序：海啸清晰且没有工程师，模糊的工程师倒影进入，倒影站定，然后转焦。摄影机保持微小手持呼吸，不用突然换机位获得近景。

倒影里的恐惧：
通过清楚的反射近景看他的反应。工程师意识到这片水可能很快杀死自己。他的眼睛锁住窗外，呼吸突然卡住，嘴唇略张，喉结轻动。想深吸气平静下来，吸气却浅而断续。下颌紧绷，眼神短暂无法从威胁上移开。
这是对死亡迫近的真实恐惧。他努力不让自己失控，但观众能看见压抑失败的细节。表演集中，不夸张，也不拖成长时间静止凝视。
在他清楚的反射肩膀后面，其他工作人员仍以柔焦倒影陆续跑过。有人独自经过，有人间隔着跟上，方向一致。只有工程师暂时停下，背景不冻结、不清空。

明确加入同向人流：
几名员工继续从工程师身旁经过，向走廊前方跑去。工程师用力收回视线，从窗边退开，转向这些人刚刚跑去的方向，跟在他们背后追上。
他的目标是追随前方员工的背影。先让几个人通过，再让他加入他们后面，以实际动作说明方向，而不只是抽象地说“跟随人流”。
摄影机随他离开玻璃，后移并沿短弧转向，从倒影连续找到真人。窗框、扶手与经过的员工保持空间可追踪。进入直接拍摄后，摄影机移到他的侧面，与他同向、同速前进。

严格侧面跟跑：
工程师朝前方员工奔跑，摄影机在他身侧并行。镜头的观看方向横向对着他的侧脸，接近垂直于他的行进方向。保持真正的侧面轮廓，而不是从正前方倒退拍他迎面跑来。
摄影机跟着脚步强烈晃动，出现上下冲击和横向补偿，并持续找回他的眼睛。他努力调节呼吸，但无法完全平静：吸气短促，嘴唇略张，眼睛急切检查前方，下颌与颈部紧张。
前方员工先转过一个拐角，工程师跟着同一组背影转入无窗内走廊。摄影机在身侧同步转弯，保持连续路线。

无窗内走廊与戴帽：
新的内走廊由普通实墙、办公室门和顶灯构成。人流仍向前，摄影机继续与工程师侧面并行。
工程师在急行中举起同一顶安全帽，戴上，双手来到下巴附近，将下巴带卡扣接合、扣紧，再短促拉紧一下。动作急切，手有紧张感，但接触关系清楚：戴帽、找到卡扣、接合、收紧、放手。
摄影机短暂保留脸、下巴和双手的空间，看到动作完成，随后实际靠近侧脸。

眼镜旁的极近侧面特写：
眼镜框、镜片后的近侧眼睛、太阳穴和一部分脸颊几乎占满画面。保持严格侧面轮廓，帽檐只局部进入上缘。镜头与他并行移动，不绕到正前方。
脸部比例自然，焦点锁住镜片后的眼睛，反光有层次。背景的墙、门、灯和同向奔跑人员强烈虚化。
近景仍受到奔跑冲击，摄影机不断补偿找回眼睛。他真实地喘息、紧张，试图镇定却没有完全成功。这里是运动中的极近景，不是稳定悬浮的肖像。

低于肩部的画外接触：
极近侧面构图保持收紧。一次来自画面外、低于肩线的突然接触阻住他的上身，使胸腹与躯干先短促减速，随后头和眼镜因惯性一晃，呼吸被打断。
接触对象比工程师矮，但始终完全位于画外，不为解释接触而扩展构图。观众只看到极近侧脸的一次突然失衡，无法确认与谁发生了碰撞。
摄影机立即受这个动作带动，从眼镜旁猛然向下俯摇。快速、大幅度的tilt-down形成强烈连续的纵向运动模糊，衣服和墙面拉成竖向色带。保持同一个摄影机动作，不切换到独立地面机位。

一串金属钥匙从画外落入视野，沿自然轨迹掉到鞋边，触地发出清楚的金属碰响，可以有一次小幅弹跳。钥匙来源保持在画外。
工程师补一步恢复平衡。钥匙触地已经可理解，而摄影机仍向下运动、画面仍带残余纵向模糊时立即结束。用这个向下的模糊衔接下一场，不停成钥匙静物，不抬回人物。

摄影与声音：
开场明确向右约100度快速转动，短暂运动模糊但同一空间可追踪。摄影机实际跑到远处出口并经过连接通道；窗前停住脚步，但保持轻微手持呼吸；先观察海啸，再等待工程师模糊倒影进入，转焦后通过反射近景读出恐惧；随后与工程师同向侧面奔跑，最终收至眼镜旁极近轮廓。
供电已恢复，强震已明显平息。大幅摄影机晃动来自实际奔跑、避让与身体惯性。窗前与奔跑段的运动幅度有清楚对比。
工业顶灯与冷色窗光从侧上方塑造皮肤和眼镜。进入内走廊后由室内顶灯维持自然曝光和层次阴影。浅景深突出眼睛与情绪，保留背景行动的空间感。
整段唯一可辨认的对白是开场一次画外“Tsunami!”。其余声音来自设备低鸣、远处警报、不同步的脚步、呼吸、衣料和门声。窗前加入海啸低沉轰鸣与撞击水声，倒影近景中能感到工程师短促的呼吸。

写实灾难电影，21:9宽银幕。日本福岛核电站。一个连续长镜头：从控制室内主工程师的脸部近景开始，摄影机快速向右转，跟随人员从控制室跑出，经过短连接通道进入有窗走廊。摄影机先来到玻璃前观察海啸，工程师稍后才以模糊倒影出现。焦点转到倒影中的脸，读出他对死亡迫近的恐惧。随后他加入同向人流，摄影机严格从侧面跟随他跑进无窗内走廊，戴好并扣紧安全帽，收至眼镜旁的极近侧面特写。最后一次画外接触打断动作，摄影机猛然向下俯摇至掉落的钥匙。动作紧凑、空间连续，没有可见剪辑或瞬移。

人物与方向：
工作人员有自然可见的头发、不同的短发或束发造型、年龄和面貌，穿普通蓝色长袖工作服。多数为男性，也有少量女性。

人流有一个始终明确的前进方向：离开控制室，经过短连接通道，沿有窗走廊向前，再转入无窗内走廊。办公室出来的员工也汇入这个方向。通过连续出现的前方人员背影建立路线。工程师最后必须追随这些人的背影前进。

开场：
首帧近距离看工程师的脸。他看向控制室设备，眼神紧张，主照明已经恢复。画面刚出现，立即从画外传来一次喊声：
“Tsunami!”
摄影机快速向右转约100度，方向以摄影机自身视线为准。转动带短暂、自然的横向运动模糊，但观众仍能追踪掠过的控制柜、人员与门口，感到摄影机仍在同一间控制室。
转向完成后，出口在前方较远处。摄影机需要经过实际室内距离才能到达。出口后是短连接通道，再通过打开的门进入有窗主走廊。

从控制室跑出：
工作人员从控制室内部经过摄影机前方，背朝摄影机向出口跑。摄影机从后面追上。门框逐渐接近，家具产生真实视差，清楚呈现从原位置到出口的完整路线。
门口有小规模拥挤。三四个人先通过，另几人随后汇入，有人收半步、侧身、扶门框再继续。所有人慌张、急迫，仍保留可通过的空隙。
摄影机主动离开主工程师，不等他动身。他比先行人员和摄影机晚一些离开，暂时留在画外。摄影机前方只看见其他员工的背影。
摄影机抱持式奔跑，明显上下冲击、横向偏移和惯性补偿。近处肩膀、后脑、背部与手臂擦过画面，摄影机利用真实空隙穿行。被背部短暂遮挡后仍沿同一路线前进，焦点从近处肩背自然找到门洞。
短连接通道只用于向外通过。摄影机跟着人群背影穿过同一个打开的门，进入大走廊。

有窗主走廊：
左侧长窗和红色扶手、右侧办公室门与设备清楚建立空间。摄影机继续从后方追上并超过人员，靠近左侧一块无遮挡的窗玻璃。
右侧不同办公室陆续有人出来，他们先让过已有的人流，随即转向并加入同一前进方向。男女员工分散在不同位置，速度与动作不同步。部分人在移动中举帽戴上，其他人继续露着头发。
摄影机接近玻璃时逐渐减速，停住脚步。奔跑级别的大幅晃动收住，但保留轻微、不规则的手持起伏、呼吸与构图修正。窗前整个观察和转焦过程都有这种微小的活的运动。

先看海啸，工程师尚未出现：
摄影机先到窗前，对焦窗外的海浪与第一道防波堤。此时画面里没有工程师，也没有他的倒影。先让观众清楚看见正在发生的灾难。
其他工作人员仍从摄影机后方沿走廊跑过，他们柔化的倒影掠过玻璃。有人在倒影里边跑边戴帽，有人直接通过。
巨大而厚重的海水前缘逼近从海侧遇到的第一道防波堤，在堤前堆高，然后猛烈撞击固定结构，沿堤线翻起宽阔、不规则的白色水墙和喷雾。推进、堆积、撞击与翻落连续发生。
以 <<<39621b4e-f235-4418-830f-9af547bbdc04>>> 的规模、暗色水体和白色浪顶为依据。建筑与防波堤固定，提供尺度。水有质量，喷雾随重力回落并受风吹散。摄影机留在室内同一个窗口，透过完整玻璃观察，不改变到室外机位。

工程师只在玻璃倒影中到达：
海浪仍然清楚、焦点仍在窗外时，工程师才从摄影机后侧来到窗边。他的模糊倒影从玻璃画面边缘进入，逐渐接近并站定。
他的真人身体始终在这一构图之外，不走进摄影机与玻璃之间，不直接遮住窗外景象。观众只能通过倒影看见他。
摄影机与玻璃的角度让倒影形成足够紧的脸部近景：脸、眼镜和上部肩膀占据主要画面，而不是远处一个小小的全身倒影。工程师靠近窗户，帽子仍拿在手里，可以在构图下缘之外。优先保留脸部表演。
先让这个近处倒影仍处于模糊状态。只有工程师站定后，焦点才从远处海啸平顺转向倒影中的眼睛。海浪逐渐柔化，倒影里的脸与眼镜变清楚。
严格顺序：海啸清晰且没有工程师，模糊的工程师倒影进入，倒影站定，然后转焦。摄影机保持微小手持呼吸，不用突然换机位获得近景。

倒影里的恐惧：
通过清楚的反射近景看他的反应。工程师意识到这片水可能很快杀死自己。他的眼睛锁住窗外，呼吸突然卡住，嘴唇略张，喉结轻动。想深吸气平静下来，吸气却浅而断续。下颌紧绷，眼神短暂无法从威胁上移开。

工程师在急行中举起同一顶安全帽，戴上，双手来到下巴附近，将下巴带卡扣接合、扣紧，再短促拉紧一下。动作急切，手有紧张感，但接触关系清楚：戴帽、找到卡扣、接合、收紧、放手。
摄影机短暂保留脸、下巴和双手的空间，看到动作完成，随后实际靠近侧脸。

眼镜旁的极近侧面特写：
眼镜框、镜片后的近侧眼睛、太阳穴和一部分脸颊几乎占满画面。保持严格侧面轮廓，帽檐只局部进入上缘。镜头与他并行移动，不绕到正前方。
脸部比例自然，焦点锁住镜片后的眼睛，反光有层次。背景的墙、门、灯和同向奔跑人员强烈虚化。
近景仍受到奔跑冲击，摄影机不断补偿找回眼睛。他真实地喘息、紧张，试图镇定却没有完全成功。这里是运动中的极近景，不是稳定悬浮的肖像。

低于肩部的画外接触：
极近侧面构图保持收紧。一次来自画面外、低于肩线的突然接触阻住他的上身，使胸腹与躯干先短促减速，随后头和眼镜因惯性一晃，呼吸被打断。
接触对象比工程师矮，但始终完全位于画外，不为解释接触而扩展构图。观众只看到极近侧脸的一次突然失衡，无法确认与谁发生了碰撞。
摄影机立即受这个动作带动，从眼镜旁猛然向下俯摇。快速、大幅度的tilt-down形成强烈连续的纵向运动模糊，衣服和墙面拉成竖向色带。保持同一个摄影机动作，不切换到独立地面机位。

钥匙与结束：
一串金属钥匙从画外落入视野，沿自然轨迹掉到鞋边，触地发出清楚的金属碰响，可以有一次小幅弹跳。钥匙来源保持在画外。
工程师补一步恢复平衡。钥匙触地已经可理解，而摄影机仍向下运动、画面仍带残余纵向模糊时立即结束。用这个向下的模糊衔接下一场，不停成钥匙静物，不抬回人物。

摄影与声音：
开场明确向右约100度快速转动，短暂运动模糊但同一空间可追踪。摄影机实际跑到远处出口并经过连接通道；窗前停住脚步，但保持轻微手持呼吸；先观察海啸，再等待工程师模糊倒影进入，转焦后通过反射近景读出恐惧；随后与工程师同向侧面奔跑，最终收至眼镜旁极近轮廓。
供电已恢复，强震已明显平息。大幅摄影机晃动来自实际奔跑、避让与身体惯性。窗前与奔跑段的运动幅度有清楚对比。
工业顶灯与冷色窗光从侧上方塑造皮肤和眼镜。进入内走廊后由室内顶灯维持自然曝光和层次阴影。浅景深突出眼睛与情绪，保留背景行动的空间感。
整段唯一可辨认的对白是开场一次画外“Tsunami!”。其余声音来自设备低鸣、远处警报、不同步的脚步、呼吸、衣料和门声。窗前加入海啸低沉轰鸣与撞击水声，倒影近景中能感到工程师短促的呼吸。
扣帽时有轻微卡扣声。结尾是衣料接触、被打断的呼吸、鞋底摩擦与钥匙触地声。背景交流不可辨认，没有配乐、旁白、字幕或人为运镜音效。

写实灾难电影，21:9宽银幕。日本福岛核电站。一个连续长镜头：从控制室内主工程师的脸部近景开始，摄影机快速向右转，跟随人员从控制室跑出，经过短连接通道进入有窗走廊。摄影机先来到玻璃前观察海啸，工程师稍后才以模糊倒影出现。焦点转到倒影中的脸，读出他对死亡迫近的恐惧。随后他加入同向人流，摄影机严格从侧面跟随他跑进无窗内走廊，戴好并扣紧安全帽，收至眼镜旁的极近侧面特写。最后一次画外接触打断动作，摄影机猛然向下俯摇至掉落的钥匙。动作紧凑、空间连续，没有可见剪辑或瞬移。

人物与方向：
工作人员有自然可见的头发、不同的短发或束发造型、年龄和面貌，穿普通蓝色长袖工作服。多数为男性，也有少量女性。
所有人最初从控制室跑出时尚未戴安全帽，头发可见。进入后面的有窗走廊后，部分员工才在移动中戴帽，动作不同步。主工程师在窗前仍未戴帽。
人流有一个始终明确的前进方向：离开控制室，经过短连接通道，沿有窗走廊向前，再转入无窗内走廊。办公室出来的员工也汇入这个方向。通过连续出现的前方人员背影建立路线。工程师最后必须追随这些人的背影前进。

开场：
首帧近距离看工程师的脸。他看向控制室设备，眼神紧张，主照明已经恢复。画面刚出现，立即从画外传来一次喊声：
“Tsunami!”
摄影机快速向右转约100度，方向以摄影机自身视线为准。转动带短暂、自然的横向运动模糊，但观众仍能追踪掠过的控制柜、人员与门口，感到摄影机仍在同一间控制室。
转向完成后，出口在前方较远处。摄影机需要经过实际室内距离才能到达。出口后是短连接通道，再通过打开的门进入有窗主走廊。

从控制室跑出：
工作人员从控制室内部经过摄影机前方，背朝摄影机向出口跑。摄影机从后面追上。门框逐渐接近，家具产生真实视差，清楚呈现从原位置到出口的完整路线。
门口有小规模拥挤。三四个人先通过，另几人随后汇入，有人收半步、侧身、扶门框再继续。所有人慌张、急迫，仍保留可通过的空隙。
摄影机主动离开主工程师，不等他动身。他比先行人员和摄影机晚一些离开，暂时留在画外。摄影机前方只看见其他员工的背影。
摄影机抱持式奔跑，明显上下冲击、横向偏移和惯性补偿。近处肩膀、后脑、背部与手臂擦过画面，摄影机利用真实空隙穿行。被背部短暂遮挡后仍沿同一路线前进，焦点从近处肩背自然找到门洞。
短连接通道只用于向外通过。摄影机跟着人群背影穿过同一个打开的门，进入大走廊。

有窗主走廊：
左侧长窗和红色扶手、右侧办公室门与设备清楚建立空间。摄影机继续从后方追上并超过人员，靠近左侧一块无遮挡的窗玻璃。
右侧不同办公室陆续有人出来，他们先让过已有的人流，随即转向并加入同一前进方向。男女员工分散在不同位置，速度与动作不同步。部分人在移动中举帽戴上，其他人继续露着头发。
摄影机接近玻璃时逐渐减速，停住脚步。奔跑级别的大幅晃动收住，但保留轻微、不规则的手持起伏、呼吸与构图修正。窗前整个观察和转焦过程都有这种微小的活的运动。

先看海啸，工程师尚未出现：
摄影机先到窗前，对焦窗外的海浪与第一道防波堤。此时画面里没有工程师，也没有他的倒影。先让观众清楚看见正在发生的灾难。
其他工作人员仍从摄影机后方沿走廊跑过，他们柔化的倒影掠过玻璃。有人在倒影里边跑边戴帽，有人直接通过。
巨大而厚重的海水前缘逼近从海侧遇到的第一道防波堤，在堤前堆高，然后猛烈撞击固定结构，沿堤线翻起宽阔、不规则的白色水墙和喷雾。推进、堆积、撞击与翻落连续发生。
以 <<<39621b4e-f235-4418-830f-9af547bbdc04>>> 的规模、暗色水体和白色浪顶为依据。建筑与防波堤固定，提供尺度。水有质量，喷雾随重力回落并受风吹散。摄影机留在室内同一个窗口，透过完整玻璃观察，不改变到室外机位。

工程师只在玻璃倒影中到达：
海浪仍然清楚、焦点仍在窗外时，工程师才从摄影机后侧来到窗边。他的模糊倒影从玻璃画面边缘进入，逐渐接近并站定。
他的真人身体始终在这一构图之外，不走进摄影机与玻璃之间，不直接遮住窗外景象。观众只能通过倒影看见他。
摄影机与玻璃的角度让倒影形成足够紧的脸部近景：脸、眼镜和上部肩膀占据主要画面，而不是远处一个小小的全身倒影。工程师靠近窗户，帽子仍拿在手里，可以在构图下缘之外。优先保留脸部表演。
先让这个近处倒影仍处于模糊状态。只有工程师站定后，焦点才从远处海啸平顺转向倒影中的眼睛。海浪逐渐柔化，倒影里的脸与眼镜变清楚。
严格顺序：海啸清晰且没有工程师，模糊的工程师倒影进入，倒影站定，然后转焦。摄影机保持微小手持呼吸，不用突然换机位获得近景。

倒影里的恐惧：
通过清楚的反射近景看他的反应。工程师意识到这片水可能很快杀死自己。他的眼睛锁住窗外，呼吸突然卡住，嘴唇略张，喉结轻动。想深吸气平静下来，吸气却浅而断续。下颌紧绷，眼神短暂无法从威胁上移开。
这是对死亡迫近的真实恐惧。他努力不让自己失控，但观众能看见压抑失败的细节。表演集中，不夸张，也不拖成长时间静止凝视。
在他清楚的反射肩膀后面，其他工作人员仍以柔焦倒影陆续跑过。有人独自经过，有人间隔着跟上，方向一致。只有工程师暂时停下，背景不冻结、不清空。

明确加入同向人流：
几名员工继续从工程师身旁经过，向走廊前方跑去。工程师用力收回视线，从窗边退开，转向这些人刚刚跑去的方向，跟在他们背后追上。
他的目标是追随前方员工的背影。先让几个人通过，再让他加入他们后面，以实际动作说明方向，而不只是抽象地说“跟随人流”。

右侧不同办公室陆续有人出来，他们先让过已有的人流，随即转向并加入同一前进方向。男女员工分散在不同位置，速度与动作不同步。部分人在移动中举帽戴上，其他人继续露着头发。
摄影机接近玻璃时逐渐减速，停住脚步。奔跑级别的大幅晃动收住，但保留轻微、不规则的手持起伏、呼吸与构图修正。窗前整个观察和转焦过程都有这种微小的活的运动。

前方员工先转过一个拐角，工程师跟着同一组背影转入无窗内走廊。摄影机在身侧同步转弯，保持连续路线。

工程师在急行中举起同一顶安全帽，戴上，双手来到下巴附近，将下巴带卡扣接合、扣紧，再短促拉紧一下。动作急切，手有紧张感，但接触关系清楚：戴帽、找到卡扣、接合、收紧、放手。
摄影机短暂保留脸、下巴和双手的空间，看到动作完成，随后实际靠近侧脸。

眼镜旁的极近侧面特写：
眼镜框、镜片后的近侧眼睛、太阳穴和一部分脸颊几乎占满画面。保持严格侧面轮廓，帽檐只局部进入上缘。镜头与他并行移动，不绕到正前方。
脸部比例自然，焦点锁住镜片后的眼睛，反光有层次。背景的墙、门、灯和同向奔跑人员强烈虚化。
近景仍受到奔跑冲击，摄影机不断补偿找回眼睛。他真实地喘息、紧张，试图镇定却没有完全成功。这里是运动中的极近景，不是稳定悬浮的肖像。

低于肩部的画外接触：

接触对象比工程师矮，但始终完全位于画外，不为解释接触而扩展构图。观众只看到极近侧脸的一次突然失衡，无法确认与谁发生了碰撞。
摄影机立即受这个动作带动，从眼镜旁猛然向下俯摇。快速、大幅度的tilt-down形成强烈连续的纵向运动模糊，衣服和墙面拉成竖向色带。保持同一个摄影机动作，不切换到独立地面机位。

钥匙与结束：
一串金属钥匙从画外落入视野，沿自然轨迹掉到鞋边，触地发出清楚的金属碰响，可以有一次小幅弹跳。钥匙来源保持在画外。
工程师补一步恢复平衡。钥匙触地已经可理解，而摄影机仍向下运动、画面仍带残余纵向模糊时立即结束。用这个向下的模糊衔接下一场，不停成钥匙静物，不抬回人物。
