最重要的视觉事件是强烈、持续的地震。在刻度下降回绿色区域、主照明恢复之前，摄影机和建筑始终猛烈震动，不因喝咖啡、说话、行走、停电或拍摄仪表而变稳。明显的不规则横向位移、竖向颠簸与倾斜持续打断构图；较大幅度的摇晃中叠加密集细震。摄影师只能部分补偿，尚未完全恢复就再次震偏。桌沿和门框在画面边缘明显摆动，背景虚化灯点快速、不规则地移动，纸张滑落，椅子自行移动，松散物件震动。人的身体也在持续摇晃，抓住桌沿、屈膝、调整脚下重心，竭力站稳。震动在关闭声音观看时也必须清楚可见。人物不被突然抛向一侧，没有夸张扑动、跌倒或喜剧表演。只有刻度回到绿色区域且主照明恢复以后，地震才开始减弱。

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: medium-wide shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay a few metres in front of the end wall of a service building. The camera is SQUARE-ON to that wall: the wall is FRONTAL, parallel to the picture plane, flat across the LEFT third of the frame — it does NOT recede in perspective, no steep angle, no vanishing lines along it. Its right-hand corner stands roughly one third in from the left edge; past that corner, to the RIGHT, the view opens onto the parking lot, and beyond the lot the harbour water and the breakwater. Two planes: MIDDLE — the frontal wall with its door on the left, and the nearest rows of the parking lot with the red kei car on the right, sharp; BACKGROUND — the harbour, the breakwater and the grey sea, softened by haze. Nothing in the near foreground — the bottom of the frame is the open quay surface. Lens about 40–50 mm equivalent, natural perspective, a tighter frame than a full establishing shot — the door and the red car read large; horizon a little above centre. DEPTH OF FIELD: the door, the wall and the near cars crisp, the far lot and the breakwater gently softening with distance.

THE BUILDING (LEFT, FRONTAL): a low, plain plant service building seen head-on — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel end wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; a downpipe, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. Set into the wall, facing the camera directly, roughly four to five metres away, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. ABOVE THE DOOR, A CANOPY: a small flat rectangular canopy of painted steel, slightly wider than the door, projecting out from the wall about a metre over the step, supported on two short brackets, its top and edge weathered with rust streaks. The door lamp is mounted on the UNDERSIDE of this canopy — a rectangular fluorescent fixture fixed flat to the canopy's underside, pointing straight down at the door and the step. There is NO lamp on the wall face itself, nothing mounted on the wall above the door except the canopy.

THE PARKING LOT (RIGHT AND MIDDLE) — THREE ORDERLY ROWS, HALF FULL:
- LAYOUT: a flat concrete / asphalt quay-top lot with faded white bay lines, laid out as EXACTLY THREE straight parallel rows of marked bays, the rows running across the frame roughly parallel to the quay edge, one behind the other, with a driving lane between each pair of rows. The frame shows the lot from its near corner: the nearest row large on the right, the second and third rows behind it, smaller, toward the water. The rows are clearly readable as rows — every parked car sits squarely inside a bay, aligned with its neighbours, none parked at odd angles.
- OCCUPANCY: the lot is only about half full. The cars are distributed RANDOMLY along the rows: in places two or three cars stand side by side, then one empty bay, then a car, then two empty bays, then another car — an irregular, natural rhythm of cars and gaps in every row, never a solid unbroken line, never evenly spaced. Roughly 12–16 cars in the lot, not all of them in frame.
- THE RED CAR'S ROW: the nearest row contains THE RED KEI CAR from the reference image — the same car, same red paint, same details, same yellow Japanese plate 福島 580 / あ 19-17, same small parking scuffs on the bumpers. EVERY car in this row is parked nose-first toward the waterfront, all pointing the same way at the harbour, so from the camera they show their rear quarters and flanks. The red car stands with its RIGHT side toward the camera and its nose toward the water. It is the ONLY red car in the entire lot.
- THE OTHER CARS: a mixed everyday Japanese workplace fleet of the 2000s — boxy kei cars, compact hatchbacks, a few sedans, two white company minivans with sliding doors, a small white van. Colours varied but ordinary: white, silver, light grey, dark grey, black, dark blue, a beige one, a pale metallic gold one, plus a couple of YELLOW cars — a small kei car in muted mustard yellow and a compact in pale lemon-cream yellow, both clearly yellow but faded, everyday, not neon — and a couple of GREEN cars — one in dark forest green and one in a soft mint / pale green, both muted. No second red car, all plain and unwashed, all with Japanese plates; no brand badges or readable logos on any car. The yellow and green cars sit in the two rear rows, not beside the red car, so the red car stays the single strongest colour. The other two rows may face either way, but within each row the cars are parallel and squared to the bays.
- ALL CARS ARE PARKED AND DARK: every car in the lot is switched off — no headlights, no position lights, no tail lights, no indicators, no interior cabin light in any car, the red car included; their lamps are dark glass, their windows dark, reflecting only the grey sky.
- THE STREET LAMPS — ONE STRAIGHT LINE, ALL IDENTICAL: the lot is lit by a SINGLE straight line of street-lamp posts standing along the quay edge, just inside the guard rail, parallel to the water and to the breakwater. Every post is IDENTICAL: the same plain grey galvanised steel pole, the same height (about 8 m), the same single short arm bent toward the parking lot, the same single box-shaped sodium luminaire on the end of the arm — ONE luminaire per pole, no double arms, no twin heads. The posts stand at EQUAL intervals, about 20–25 metres apart, three to five of them in frame, forming one clean row that recedes in perspective along the quay — the nearest post seen full height, the farther ones progressively smaller and closer together, all on the same line, all arms pointing the same way over the cars. NO lamp posts anywhere else: none between the rows of cars, none in the driving lanes, none next to the building, none in the foreground, none of a different height, shape or type.
- Wheel chocks in a few bays, a couple of traffic cones, a low steel guard rail along the quay edge with faded yellow-and-black paint. The lot is dry; NO visible earthquake damage — no cracks, no fallen objects, no displaced cars; only the ordinary wear of a working quay.

THE HARBOUR AND THE BREAKWATER (BACKGROUND, RIGHT): beyond the guard rail, the enclosed harbour basin — cold grey-green water, choppy under the wind: short steep chop, small waves slapping the quay wall, no white crests inside the basin, restless but not stormy. Across the basin, the plant's inner breakwater exactly as at Fukushima Daiichi: a long, dead-straight rubble-mound breakwater running across the harbour — a low concrete crown walkway with a plain parapet on top, and the seaward face armoured with a jumble of grey concrete TETRAPODS, weathered and salt-stained; on the sea side, waves breaking on the tetrapods throw up grey-white spray. Its near end may be hidden behind the building's corner. Beyond the breakwater, the open sea — darker grey-green with longer wind waves and scattered white caps — running out to a flat grey horizon; the dark forested headland far off to one side, flattened by haze. No cooling towers, no reactor buildings in this view — they are behind the camera.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under the cars, under the guard rail, under the canopy and along the base of the wall. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — car roofs and bonnets, the lot surface, the canopy top, the breakwater crown, the water. Vertical surfaces are clearly darker and darken toward the ground — the frontal building wall, the car flanks, the quay wall — with the wall's base and the ground between the cars sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, fast-moving, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, LOCAL, EACH WITH ITS OWN COLOUR:
- THE CANOPY LAMP: the fluorescent fixture under the canopy is ON — the same slightly warm-neutral fluorescent white as the corridor ceiling lights, an even soft rectangle of light on the canopy's underside throwing a weak pale wash straight down onto the door face and the step, the pool tight and local. Not sodium, not amber, not blue. No light on the wall above the canopy.
- THE STREET LAMPS: the single line of identical posts along the quay edge is ON, every one of them warm amber SODIUM — one receding chain of warm amber points at equal spacing along the waterfront, each dropping a weak amber pool onto the concrete beneath it, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight; the nearest sharp, the far ones blooming softly. Warm amber-orange, never yellow-green, never white. No other lamps over the lot.
- THE WINDOWS: a couple of small windows in the building lit with warm tungsten light from inside; most windows dark, reflecting grey sky.
- THE BREAKWATER: several small RED navigation / marker lights spaced along the breakwater crown, tiny sharp red points receding along its length, and at its far end a single GREEN navigation light, sharp against grey water.
- a small RED warning light on a distant crane boom or pylon.
- THE HORIZON: far out on the open sea, at the horizon line beyond the breakwater, the navigation and deck lights of several distant ships — tiny points, a few of them a cold blue-green MERCURY-VAPOUR white, only there, only on the horizon, only as specks; nothing of that colour anywhere closer.
- NO car lights of any kind.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze with wind-blown spray in the air over the breakwater. The wall, the door and the near cars clear; the far side of the lot slightly softened; the breakwater loses contrast; the open sea and headland flatten toward the sky tone, the ships' lights on the horizon reduced to faint specks. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours — only desaturated and cooled by the overcast, NOT re-tinted. Off-white walls read cool grey-white; the pale blue band and the pale blue door stay blue; the canopy the same weathered grey-white as the wall; the car paints stay their own colours, muted — the yellow cars read as dulled mustard and cream, the green cars as dulled forest and mint, never bright; the harbour reads grey-green, never blue; the tetrapods pale concrete grey with salt and rust stains. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, powder blue, dull grey-green, cool concrete grey, asphalt grey, weathered white, silver, black, dark blue, beige, muted mustard yellow, pale cream yellow, dark forest green, soft mint green, rust, with small accents of sodium amber, warm-neutral fluorescent white, tungsten amber, deep red, one green, and cold mercury blue-green confined to the horizon. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The daylight areas carry NO golden or amber cast; warmth exists only inside the lit windows and the lamp pools. 35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: medium-wide shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay a few metres in front of the end wall of a service building. The camera is SQUARE-ON to that wall: the wall is FRONTAL, parallel to the picture plane, flat across the LEFT third of the frame — it does NOT recede in perspective, no steep angle, no vanishing lines along it. Its right-hand corner stands roughly one third in from the left edge; past that corner, to the RIGHT, the view opens onto the parking lot, and beyond the lot the harbour water and the breakwater. Two planes: MIDDLE — the frontal wall with its door on the left, and the nearest rows of the parking lot with the red kei car on the right, sharp; BACKGROUND — the harbour, the breakwater and the grey sea, softened by haze. Nothing in the near foreground — the bottom of the frame is the open quay surface. Lens about 40–50 mm equivalent, natural perspective, a tighter frame than a full establishing shot — the door and the red car read large; horizon a little above centre. DEPTH OF FIELD: the door, the wall and the near cars crisp, the far lot and the breakwater gently softening with distance.

THE BUILDING (LEFT, FRONTAL): a low, plain plant service building seen head-on — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel end wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; a downpipe, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. Set into the wall, facing the camera directly, roughly four to five metres away, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. ABOVE THE DOOR, A CANOPY: a small flat rectangular canopy of painted steel, slightly wider than the door, projecting out from the wall about a metre over the step, supported on two short brackets, its top and edge weathered with rust streaks. The door lamp is mounted on the UNDERSIDE of this canopy — a rectangular fluorescent fixture fixed flat to the canopy's underside, pointing straight down at the door and the step. There is NO lamp on the wall face itself, nothing mounted on the wall above the door except the canopy.

- LAYOUT: a flat concrete / asphalt quay-top lot with faded white bay lines, laid out as EXACTLY THREE straight parallel rows of marked bays, the rows running across the frame roughly parallel to the quay edge, one behind the other, with a driving lane between each pair of rows. The frame shows the lot from its near corner: the nearest row large on the right, the second and third rows behind it, smaller, toward the water. The rows are clearly readable as rows — every parked car sits squarely inside a bay, aligned with its neighbours, none parked at odd angles.
- OCCUPANCY: the lot is only about half full. The cars are distributed RANDOMLY along the rows: in places two or three cars stand side by side, then one empty bay, then a car, then two empty bays, then another car — an irregular, natural rhythm of cars and gaps in every row, never a solid unbroken line, never evenly spaced. Roughly 12–16 cars in the lot, not all of them in frame.

EVERY car in this row is parked nose-first toward the waterfront, all pointing the same way at the harbour, so from the camera they show their rear quarters and flanks. 极近侧面构图保持收紧。一次来自画面外、低于肩线的突然接触阻住他的上身，使胸腹与躯干先短促减速，随后头和眼镜因惯性一晃。
接触对象比工程师矮，但始终完全位于画外，不为解释接触而扩展构图。观众只看到极近侧脸的一次突然失衡，无法确认与谁发生了碰撞。
摄影机立即受这个动作带动，从眼镜旁猛然向下俯摇。快速、大幅度的tilt-down形成强烈连续的纵向运动模糊，衣服和墙面拉成竖向色带。保持同一个摄影机动作，不切换到独立地面机位。

一串金属钥匙从画外落入视野，沿自然轨迹掉到鞋边，触地发出清楚的金属碰响，可以有一次小幅弹跳。钥匙来源保持在画外。
工程师补一步恢复平衡。钥匙触地已经可理解，而摄影机仍向下运动、画面仍带残余纵向模糊时立即结束。用这个向下的模糊衔接下一场，不停成钥匙静物，不抬回人物。

Its right-hand corner stands roughly one third in from the left edge; past that corner, to the RIGHT, the view opens onto the parking lot, and beyond the lot the harbour water and the breakwater. Three planes: near FOREGROUND — out of focus, a low steel pipe railing crossing the bottom of the frame; MIDDLE — the frontal wall with its door on the left, and the nearest rows of the parking lot with the red kei car on the right, sharp; BACKGROUND — the harbour, the breakwater and the grey sea, softened by haze. Lens about 40–50 mm equivalent, natural perspective, a tighter frame than a full establishing shot — the door and the red car read large; horizon a little above centre. DEPTH OF FIELD: moderate — the foreground railing clearly soft and blurred, the door, the wall and the near cars crisp, the far lot and the breakwater gently softening.

The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under the cars, under the guard rail, under the canopy and along the base of the wall. Nothing is evenly flooded.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: wide establishing shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay near the corner of a service building, looking diagonally across the parking lot toward the harbour and the breakwater. Three planes: LEFT FOREGROUND — the flat end wall of the building runs away from the camera along the left edge of the frame, with a steel door in it a few metres from the lens; MIDDLE — the parking lot, the red kei car among the parked cars; BACKGROUND — the restless harbour water and, across it, the long straight breakwater, with the open grey sea and sky beyond. Natural 28–35 mm perspective, no fisheye, horizon a little above centre.

THE BUILDING (LEFT FOREGROUND): a low, plain plant service building — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; downpipes, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. In the wall, roughly four to five metres from the camera, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. Above the door, a rectangular recessed-style fluorescent wall fixture of the same type as the corridor's ceiling lights. The wall recedes in steep perspective and is cut by the left edge of the frame.

THE PARKING LOT (MIDDLE GROUND) — THREE ORDERLY ROWS, HALF FULL:
- LAYOUT: a flat concrete / asphalt quay-top lot with faded white bay lines, laid out as EXACTLY THREE straight parallel rows of marked bays, the rows running across the frame roughly parallel to the quay edge, one behind the other, with a driving lane between each pair of rows. The rows are clearly readable as rows — every parked car sits squarely inside a bay, aligned with its neighbours, none parked at odd angles.
- OCCUPANCY: the lot is only about half full. The cars are distributed RANDOMLY along the rows: in places two or three cars stand side by side, then one empty bay, then a car, then two empty bays, then another car — an irregular, natural rhythm of cars and gaps in every row, never a solid unbroken line, never evenly spaced. Roughly 12–16 cars in total across the three rows.
- THE RED CAR'S ROW: the row nearest the camera-side lane contains THE RED KEI CAR from the reference image — the same car, same red paint, same details, same yellow Japanese plate 福島 580 / あ 19-17, same small parking scuffs on the bumpers. EVERY car in this row is parked nose-first toward the waterfront, all pointing the same way at the harbour, so from the camera they show their rear quarters and flanks. The red car stands with its RIGHT side toward the camera and its nose toward the water. It is the ONLY red car in the entire lot.
- THE OTHER CARS: a mixed everyday Japanese workplace fleet of the 2000s — boxy kei cars, compact hatchbacks, a few sedans, two white company minivans with sliding doors, a small white van. Colours varied but ordinary: white, silver, light grey, dark grey, black, dark blue, a beige one, a dark green one, a pale metallic gold one — no second red car, no bright colours, all plain and unwashed, all with Japanese plates; no brand badges or readable logos on any car. The other two rows may face either way, but within each row the cars are parallel and squared to the bays.
- STREET LAMPS: a proper row of ordinary steel street-lamp posts stands along the lot at regular intervals, following the driving lanes — plain grey poles with single cobra-head or box luminaires, period-correct sodium fixtures.
- Wheel chocks in a few bays, a couple of traffic cones, a low steel guard rail along the quay edge with faded yellow-and-black paint. The lot is dry; NO visible earthquake damage — no cracks, no fallen objects, no displaced cars; only the ordinary wear of a working quay.

THE HARBOUR AND THE BREAKWATER (BACKGROUND): beyond the guard rail, the enclosed harbour basin — cold grey-green water, choppy under the wind: short steep chop, small waves slapping the quay wall, no white crests inside the basin, restless but not stormy. Across the basin, the plant's inner breakwater exactly as at Fukushima Daiichi: a long, dead-straight rubble-mound breakwater running across the whole width of the harbour — a low concrete crown walkway with a plain parapet on top, and the seaward face armoured with a jumble of grey concrete TETRAPODS, weathered and salt-stained; on the sea side, waves breaking on the tetrapods throw up grey-white spray. Beyond the breakwater, the open sea — darker grey-green with longer wind waves and scattered white caps — running out to a flat grey horizon; the dark forested headland far off to one side, flattened by haze. No cooling towers, no reactor buildings in this view — they are behind the camera.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under the cars, under the guard rail and along the base of the wall. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — car roofs and bonnets, the lot surface, the breakwater crown, the water. Vertical surfaces are clearly darker and darken toward the ground — the building wall, the car flanks, the quay wall — with the wall's base and the ground between the cars sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: wide establishing shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay near the corner of a service building, looking diagonally across the parking lot toward the harbour and the breakwater. THE BUILDING (LEFT FOREGROUND): a low, plain plant service building — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; downpipes, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. In the wall, roughly four to five metres from the camera, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. 35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: wide establishing shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay near the corner of a service building, looking diagonally across the parking lot toward the harbour and the breakwater. Three planes: LEFT FOREGROUND — the flat end wall of the building runs away from the camera along the left edge of the frame, with a steel door in it a few metres from the lens; MIDDLE — the parking lot, the red kei car among the parked cars; BACKGROUND — the restless harbour water and, across it, the long straight breakwater, with the open grey sea and sky beyond. Natural 28–35 mm perspective, no fisheye, horizon a little above centre.

THE BUILDING (LEFT FOREGROUND): a low, plain plant service building — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; downpipes, a wall lamp, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. In the wall, roughly four to five metres from the camera, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. The wall recedes in steep perspective and is cut by the left edge of the frame.

THE PARKING LOT (MIDDLE GROUND) — THREE ORDERLY ROWS, HALF FULL:
- LAYOUT: a flat concrete / asphalt quay-top lot with faded white bay lines, laid out as EXACTLY THREE straight parallel rows of marked bays, the rows running across the frame roughly parallel to the quay edge, one behind the other, with a driving lane between each pair of rows. The rows are clearly readable as rows — every parked car sits squarely inside a bay, aligned with its neighbours, none parked at odd angles.
- OCCUPANCY: the lot is only about half full. The cars are distributed RANDOMLY along the rows: in places two or three cars stand side by side, then one empty bay, then a car, then two empty bays, then another car — an irregular, natural rhythm of cars and gaps in every row, never a solid unbroken line, never evenly spaced. Roughly 12–16 cars in total across the three rows.
- THE RED CAR'S ROW: the row nearest the camera-side lane contains THE RED KEI CAR from the reference image — the same car, same red paint, same details, same yellow Japanese plate 福島 580 / あ 19-17, same small parking scuffs on the bumpers. EVERY car in this row is parked nose-first toward the waterfront, all pointing the same way at the harbour, so from the camera they show their rear quarters and flanks. The red car stands with its RIGHT side toward the camera and its nose toward the water. It is the ONLY red car in the entire lot.
- THE OTHER CARS: a mixed everyday Japanese workplace fleet of the 2000s — boxy kei cars, compact hatchbacks, a few sedans, two white company minivans with sliding doors, a small white van. Colours varied but ordinary: white, silver, light grey, dark grey, black, dark blue, a beige one, a dark green one, a pale metallic gold one — no second red car, no bright colours, all plain and unwashed, all with Japanese plates; no brand badges or readable logos on any car. The other two rows may face either way, but within each row the cars are parallel and squared to the bays.
- Wheel chocks in a few bays, a couple of traffic cones, a low steel guard rail along the quay edge with faded yellow-and-black paint, a lamp post or two. The lot is dry; NO visible earthquake damage — no cracks, no fallen objects, no displaced cars; only the ordinary wear of a working quay.

THE HARBOUR AND THE BREAKWATER (BACKGROUND): beyond the guard rail, the enclosed harbour basin — cold grey-green water, choppy under the wind: short steep chop, small waves slapping the quay wall, no white crests inside the basin, restless but not stormy. Across the basin, the plant's inner breakwater exactly as at Fukushima Daiichi: a long, dead-straight rubble-mound breakwater running across the whole width of the harbour — a low concrete crown walkway with a plain parapet on top, and the seaward face armoured with a jumble of grey concrete TETRAPODS, weathered and salt-stained; on the sea side, waves breaking on the tetrapods throw up grey-white spray. A small navigation light at its end. Beyond the breakwater, the open sea — darker grey-green with longer wind waves and scattered white caps — running out to a flat grey horizon; the dark forested headland far off to one side, flattened by haze. No cooling towers, no reactor buildings in this view — they are behind the camera.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under the cars, under the guard rail and along the base of the wall. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — car roofs and bonnets, the lot surface, the breakwater crown, the water. Vertical surfaces are clearly darker and darken toward the ground — the building wall, the car flanks, the quay wall — with the wall's base and the ground between the cars sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, fast-moving, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, LOCAL:
- the wall lamp on the building, just coming on: a weak warm amber sodium pool on the panels and the ground by the door; one or two pole-mounted lamps over the lot, some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each a weak pool on the concrete, pools far apart; a lamp dead;
- a couple of small warm-lit windows in the building, most windows dark, reflecting grey sky;
- the tiny navigation light at the breakwater end — one green, sharp against grey water; a small red warning light on a distant crane boom or pylon;
- no car lights on; no headlights, no tail lights, no interior lights.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze with wind-blown spray in the air over the breakwater. The building and the near cars clear; the far side of the lot slightly softened; the breakwater loses contrast; the open sea and headland flatten toward the sky tone. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s — the waterfront service quay and its parking lot inside the plant's harbour. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy, a stiff onshore wind. Intact, in normal operation. No people anywhere.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION: wide establishing shot from human eye level (about 1.6 m), standing on the quay near the corner of a service building, looking diagonally across the parking lot toward the harbour and the breakwater. Natural 28–35 mm perspective, no fisheye, horizon a little above centre.

THE BUILDING (LEFT FOREGROUND): a low, plain plant service building — off-white / cool grey-white painted steel-panel wall with a pale blue band low down, exactly the plant's material canon; a few small square windows high up; downpipes, faint rust streaks at the panel joints, grime near the ground. In the wall, roughly four to five metres from the camera, a single flush steel door in the same pale, slightly greyed powder blue as the plant's buildings, with a small wired-glass vision panel, a lever handle and a small number plate beside it; a concrete step and a scuffed rubber mat at its foot. Above the door, a rectangular recessed-style fluorescent wall fixture of the same type as the corridor's ceiling lights. The wall recedes in steep perspective and is cut by the left edge of the frame.

The rows are clearly readable as rows — every parked car sits squarely inside a bay, aligned with its neighbours, none parked at odd angles.
- OCCUPANCY: the lot is only about half full. A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese TEPCO operators and engineers are distributed naturally around the room — the others mostly men aged 30–55, plus the young woman described below.

Her hair is straight, black, shoulder-length or slightly longer, neatly tied back low or left simply down with a straight fringe — plain and tidy, nothing fashionable or styled. Some of the others stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors — the young woman included: a real junior staff member, not a model.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

Create a highly photorealistic wide documentary photograph of the central control room of Reactor Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Japan, immediately before the March 2011 accident, based on the historically documented appearance of the room in late 2010 and January 2011.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese TEPCO operators and engineers are distributed naturally around the room — the others mostly men aged 30–55, plus the young woman described below.

THE CENTRAL FIGURE: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FRAME, AT FULL HEIGHT, FACING THE CAMERA FRONTALLY, STANDS A YOUNG JAPANESE WOMAN, ABOUT 24 YEARS OLD, A JUNIOR ENGINEER. She is beautiful in a natural, unstyled way — the look of a top university graduate of that era, 2011: a clean, intelligent, well-kept face with no visible makeup beyond the barest minimum, clear skin, straight dark brows, dark eyes. Her hair is straight, black, shoulder-length or slightly longer, neatly tied back low or left simply down with a straight fringe — plain and tidy, nothing fashionable or styled. Her expression is the heart of the picture: calm and composed, but her gaze is direct, open and quietly expressive — an earnest, thoughtful look with a trace of vulnerability that invites empathy, as if she is carrying something she has not said. Not smiling, not posing, not dramatic; a still, sincere, held moment. She stands upright, arms relaxed at her sides or one hand loosely holding a clipboard or logbook, wearing the same uniform as everyone else, slightly loose on her frame. She looks straight into the lens.

Some of the others stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

They all wear period-correct two-tone blue TEPCO industrial work uniforms: muted blue-grey work jackets with darker blue shoulder and outer-sleeve sections, matching saturated blue work trousers, black practical work shoes. No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors — the young woman included: a real junior staff member, not a model.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

No emergency condition.
No smoke.
No debris.
No flooding.
No protective equipment.
No dramatic behavior.

FLOOR:
Smooth muted grey-green institutional industrial flooring with a low satin finish. A subdued dark blue perimeter strip runs along the base of parts of the control consoles.

LIGHT:
Bright, functional, neutral fluorescent illumination typical of a Japanese technical facility around 2010.

The room is evenly illuminated from above. Light is broad and soft, with very little directional shadow. Pale green control panels retain their natural material color. Skin tones remain realistic — the young woman's face is lit by the same flat overhead fluorescent light as everything else, no beauty light, no portrait key, no rim light, no glow. Dark desks and blue uniforms remain readable without crushed blacks.

No cinematic colored lighting.
No teal-orange grade.
No blue neon.
No dramatic shadows.

COLOR:
Natural documentary color.

Muted pale sage-green control panels.
Cool grey-green floor.
Charcoal-grey workstation furniture.
Off-white and aged light-grey office equipment.
Period TEPCO blue uniforms.
Small red and green indicator lights providing restrained color accents.

The overall room should look slightly aged and institutional rather than freshly renovated. Surfaces show subtle wear, slightly faded paint, mildly yellowed plastics and small differences in equipment age.

CAMERA:
Full-frame documentary photography, approximately 28–32 mm lens.
Camera height about 1.6 metres.
Natural perspective.
No fisheye.
No exaggerated wide-angle distortion.

Keep both the foreground operator island and the control wall clearly readable. Moderate depth of field, not shallow portrait focus; the central figure is sharp but so is the room around her.

The composition should feel observational and slightly asymmetric, as though a professional documentary photographer stepped into the real Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 central control room during an ordinary working shift and made one wide photograph — with one young engineer who happened to look up at the camera.

PHOTOGRAPHIC CHARACTER:
Real live-action photography.
Subtle organic film-like grain.
Natural optical softness.
Moderate microcontrast.
Soft highlight rolloff from fluorescent lighting.
No HDR.
No oversharpening.
No CGI cleanliness.
No architectural-visualization look.

The most important goal is historical plausibility and the dense, practical, slightly cluttered reality of the Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 central control room shortly before March 2011.

Create a highly photorealistic wide documentary photograph of the central control room of Reactor Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Japan, immediately before the March 2011 accident, based on the historically documented appearance of the room in late 2010 and January 2011.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese TEPCO operators and engineers are distributed naturally around the room — the others mostly men aged 30–55, plus the young woman described below.

THE CENTRAL FIGURE: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FRAME, AT FULL HEIGHT, FACING THE CAMERA FRONTALLY, STANDS A YOUNG JAPANESE WOMAN, ABOUT 24 YEARS OLD, A JUNIOR ENGINEER. She is beautiful in a natural, unstyled way — the look of a top university graduate of that era, 2011: a clean, intelligent, well-kept face with no visible makeup beyond the barest minimum, clear skin, straight dark brows, dark eyes. Her hair is straight, black, shoulder-length or slightly longer, neatly tied back low or left simply down with a straight fringe — plain and tidy, nothing fashionable or styled. Her expression is the heart of the picture: calm and composed, but her gaze is direct, open and quietly expressive — an earnest, thoughtful look with a trace of vulnerability that invites empathy, as if she is carrying something she has not said. Not smiling, not posing, not dramatic; a still, sincere, held moment. She stands upright, arms relaxed at her sides or one hand loosely holding a clipboard or logbook, wearing the same uniform as everyone else, slightly loose on her frame. She looks straight into the lens.

Some of the others stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

They all wear period-correct two-tone blue TEPCO industrial work uniforms: muted blue-grey work jackets with darker blue shoulder and outer-sleeve sections, matching saturated blue work trousers, black practical work shoes. No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors — the young woman included: a real junior staff member, not a model.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese male TEPCO operators and engineers, mostly 30–55 years old, are distributed naturally around the room.

ONE OF THE CONTROL ROOM WORKERS STANDS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FRAME, AT FULL HEIGHT, FACING THE CAMERA FRONTALLY.

Some stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

They wear period-correct two-tone blue TEPCO industrial work uniforms: muted blue-grey work jackets with darker blue shoulder and outer-sleeve sections, matching saturated blue work trousers, black practical work shoes. No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

No emergency condition.
No smoke.
No debris.
No flooding.
No protective equipment.
No dramatic behavior.

FLOOR:
Smooth muted grey-green institutional industrial flooring with a low satin finish. A subdued dark blue perimeter strip runs along the base of parts of the control consoles.

LIGHT:
Bright, functional, neutral fluorescent illumination typical of a Japanese technical facility around 2010.

The room is evenly illuminated from above. Light is broad and soft, with very little directional shadow. Pale green control panels retain their natural material color. Skin tones remain realistic. Dark desks and blue uniforms remain readable without crushed blacks.

No cinematic colored lighting.
No teal-orange grade.
No blue neon.
No dramatic shadows.

COLOR:
Natural documentary color.

Muted pale sage-green control panels.
Cool grey-green floor.
Charcoal-grey workstation furniture.
Off-white and aged light-grey office equipment.
Period TEPCO blue uniforms.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese male TEPCO operators and engineers, mostly 30–55 years old, are distributed naturally around the room.

ONE OF THE CONTROL ROOM WORKERS STANDS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FRAME, AT FULL HEIGHT, FACING THE CAMERA FRONTALLY.

Some stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

They wear period-correct two-tone blue TEPCO industrial work uniforms: muted blue-grey work jackets with darker blue shoulder and outer-sleeve sections, matching saturated blue work trousers, black practical work shoes. No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

No emergency condition.
No smoke.
No debris.
No flooding.
No protective equipment.
No dramatic behavior.

Smooth muted grey-green institutional industrial flooring with a low satin finish. A subdued dark blue perimeter strip runs along the base of parts of the control consoles.

Bright, functional, neutral fluorescent illumination typical of a Japanese technical facility around 2010.

The room is evenly illuminated from above. Light is broad and soft, with very little directional shadow. Pale green control panels retain their natural material color. Skin tones remain realistic. Dark desks and blue uniforms remain readable without crushed blacks.

No cinematic colored lighting.
No teal-orange grade.
No blue neon.
No dramatic shadows.

Natural documentary color.

Cool grey-green floor.
Charcoal-grey workstation furniture.
Off-white and aged light-grey office equipment.

Natural perspective.

Create a highly photorealistic wide documentary photograph of the central control room of Reactor Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Japan, immediately before the March 2011 accident, based on the historically documented appearance of the room in late 2010 and January 2011.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. Its surface is filled naturally with early-2000s office and control equipment: thick-bezel computer monitors, older LCD displays, keyboards, several off-white landline telephones, a white laser printer, vertical binders, folders, printed manuals, loose papers, notebooks, pens and small office supplies.

The central desk should feel genuinely occupied and operational, with believable working clutter rather than decorative set dressing.

Approximately 7–9 Japanese male TEPCO operators and engineers, mostly 30–55 years old, are distributed naturally around the room.

ONE OF THE CONTROL ROOM WORKERS STANDS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FRAME, AT FULL HEIGHT, FACING THE CAMERA FRONTALLY.

Some stand directly in front of the control panels examining instruments. One operator is seated at the central workstation. Others stand in small loose groups, facing equipment rather than posing for the camera; only the central figure faces the camera.

They wear period-correct two-tone blue TEPCO industrial work uniforms: muted blue-grey work jackets with darker blue shoulder and outer-sleeve sections, matching saturated blue work trousers, black practical work shoes. No helmets, no respirators, no protective suits. One senior operator may wear a white supervisory armband with narrow colored stripes.

The employees must feel like ordinary working engineers captured during a normal shift, not models or actors.

The room is fully operational and undamaged, before the earthquake and tsunami.

No emergency condition.
No smoke.
No debris.
No flooding.
No protective equipment.
No dramatic behavior.

FLOOR:
Smooth muted grey-green institutional industrial flooring with a low satin finish. A subdued dark blue perimeter strip runs along the base of parts of the control consoles.

LIGHT:
Bright, functional, neutral fluorescent illumination typical of a Japanese technical facility around 2010.

The room is evenly illuminated from above. Light is broad and soft, with very little directional shadow. Pale green control panels retain their natural material color. Skin tones remain realistic. Dark desks and blue uniforms remain readable without crushed blacks.

No cinematic colored lighting.
No teal-orange grade.
No blue neon.
No dramatic shadows.

COLOR:
Natural documentary color.

Muted pale sage-green control panels.
Cool grey-green floor.
Charcoal-grey workstation furniture.
Off-white and aged light-grey office equipment.
Period TEPCO blue uniforms.
Small red and green indicator lights providing restrained color accents.

The overall room should look slightly aged and institutional rather than freshly renovated. Surfaces show subtle wear, slightly faded paint, mildly yellowed plastics and small differences in equipment age.

CAMERA:
Full-frame documentary photography, approximately 28–32 mm lens.
Camera height about 1.6 metres.
Natural perspective.
No fisheye.
No exaggerated wide-angle distortion.

Keep both the foreground operator island and the control wall clearly readable. Moderate depth of field, not shallow portrait focus.

The composition should feel observational and slightly asymmetric, as though a professional documentary photographer stepped into the real Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 central control room during an ordinary working shift and made one wide photograph.

PHOTOGRAPHIC CHARACTER:
Real live-action photography.
Subtle organic film-like grain.
Natural optical softness.
Moderate microcontrast.
Soft highlight rolloff from fluorescent lighting.
No HDR.
No oversharpening.
No CGI cleanliness.
No architectural-visualization look.

The most important goal is historical plausibility and the dense, practical, slightly cluttered reality of the Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 central control room shortly before March 2011.

AVOID:
modern command center, futuristic interfaces, giant touchscreen walls, cyberpunk, blue neon, dramatic cinematic lighting, sterile minimalist desks, modern laptops, tablets, smartphones, thin-bezel monitors, clean empty room, symmetrical staging, emergency equipment, helmets, protective suits, smoke, destruction, water, debris, HDR, CGI, 3D render, concept art.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. A long corridor with windows inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people.

Create a highly photorealistic wide documentary photograph of the central control room of Reactor Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Japan, immediately before the March 2011 accident, based on the historically documented appearance of the room in late 2010 and January 2011.

16:9 horizontal frame. Shot on 35mm colour negative film, fine-grained daylight stock pushed slightly for the interior — clearly visible organic grain throughout.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall. The ceiling is included in the upper part of the frame.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

THE ANNUNCIATOR PANELS — LIT: along the top of the control wall runs a continuous row of large black rectangular annunciator panels, each a dense grid of small rectangular backlit tile windows, roughly 6–8 rows of tiles per panel. The windows are ILLUMINATED, as in normal operation: the majority glow a warm amber / orange-yellow from behind, a scattering of them glow red, and a smaller number are dark and unlit. The lit tiles read as bright, evenly backlit rectangles with a soft warm glow spilling slightly at their edges, sitting in the matte black of the panel, so the whole row across the top of the wall reads as a long band of warm glowing tiles punctuated by red ones, receding along the curve of the wall — the near panels crisp and individual, the far panels compressing into a warm speckled strip. Amber = warm orange-yellow, never yellow-green, never white. Red = deep signal red, never pink, never orange. In the middle of the row a small red LED numeric readout. These lit annunciators are the strongest and most saturated colour in the entire frame.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control wall, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the wall projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

CEILING — TWO LEVELS:
1. THE CENTRAL LUMINOUS CEILING: a large raised rectangular light-ceiling over the middle of the room — one continuous glowing surface made of translucent diffuser panels with a soft corrugated, wave-like texture: gentle parallel horizontal ripples running across the whole surface, like ribbed milky acrylic. It glows evenly from within; no individual lamps or tubes are visible, only uniform soft illumination with a faint ripple pattern. Warm-neutral white with a slight fluorescent yellow tint, held textured rather than blown white.
2. THE PERIMETER SOFFIT: around the raised light-ceiling, a lower flat dropped ceiling band runs along the room's outline, following the horseshoe curve of the control panels. Matte pale grey-green / off-white. Set flush into it, in rows, are rectangular recessed fluorescent troffer fixtures — separate bright rectangles with a slightly cooler, greener white than the central light-ceiling; a few tubes marginally dimmer than the rest.
3. THE STEP: where the raised luminous centre meets the lower soffit there is a clean stepped edge — a vertical riser with a softly rounded corner, casting a faint soft shadow line onto the soffit.
Nothing else on the ceiling: no exposed pipes or ducts, no pendant lamps, no grid of perforated metal panels, no acoustic tile grid.

THE CENTRAL WORK AREA — A SMALL GROUP OF PLAIN STEEL OFFICE DESKS, NOT A CONSOLE:
In the middle of the room, a modest amount of ordinary Japanese office furniture, with open floor around it: two or three standard light-grey steel office desks — pale grey laminate tops with rounded grey steel edging, grey steel frames, built-in front drawer pedestals — pushed together into one loose group, plus one matching cream / beige steel multi-drawer filing pedestal beside them. The rest of the middle floor stays clear; the room must not look crowded with furniture.

CHAIRS: one office swivel chair upholstered in royal-blue fabric on a black five-star base with casters, and two black high-backed office swivel chairs, pulled out at different angles.

SCREENS: two thick-bezel early-2000s computer monitors in light grey / beige — one larger LCD angled toward the viewer, one smaller CRT-style beige monitor showing pale cyan text on a black screen — and one old thick black laptop lying open.

1. BRIGHTEST: the luminous ceiling and the troffers. They stop clearly short of pure white and hold their ripple texture and their faint yellow-green tint inside them. NOTHING in the frame clips to clean white
2. the desk tops, the console tops and the operators' shoulders — the lit horizontal planes
3. THE CONTROL SURFACE OF THE PICTURE: the pale sage-green panel wall and the light-grey desk tops. These are nominally pale, and they must render clearly below the ceiling, holding every label, seam, scuff and yellowed edge. If either blows out, the whole frame is wrong
4. the blue uniforms, the vertical faces of the consoles, the floor
5. DARKEST: the matte black of the annunciator panels between the lit tiles, the recesses beneath the desks and the console overhang. Even here nothing approaches pure black — the darkest tone is an open, slightly milky charcoal with texture visible in it
The bulk of the frame sits in the middle of this short range. Contrast is flat and even; density comes from grain and material, never from contrast.
THE ONE EXCEPTION: the lit annunciator tiles sit above this ladder as small self-luminous sources, their centres just reaching white while the black panel around them stays deep. They are the only bright points in the picture.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, LOCAL:
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small, dim warm rectangles, scattered, not every window; most windows dark, reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight. A few lamps dead.
- WALL FLOODLIGHTS on the turbine hall end walls, washing faintly down the panelling.
- Small red warning lights on the tall lattice transmission pylons and on a crane boom; a slow amber beacon on a gantry crane.
- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays and small navigation lights at the breakwater ends — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against grey water.
- Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings on a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings off-white panelled walls with a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind, deep green muted toward olive-grey and darkening in the gloom.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze. Near structures clear; further ones lose contrast and colour, going pale grey-green; the furthest structures and the headland flatten into soft grey silhouettes. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing shot from the sea side looking in toward the shore, slightly off-axis so the row of buildings runs diagonally across the frame, holding the whole row, the harbour and the hills.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours — only desaturated and cooled by the overcast, NOT re-tinted. Off-white walls read cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; hills stay green dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, dull grey-green, olive-grey, cool concrete grey, rust, weathered white, with small accents of tungsten amber, mercury blue-green, a little deep red and a single green. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The daylight areas carry NO golden or amber cast; warmth exists only inside the lit windows and the sodium pools. Saturation hierarchy: the warm lit windows are the most saturated thing in the frame, then the small pylon and navigation lights; every large surface is muted and low.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. A long corridor with windows inside Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast outside, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people.

COMPOSITION: a long, straight, narrow service corridor receding to a single vanishing point slightly right of centre, ending in a closed door with a small window at the far end. Camera at human eye level, standing close to the LEFT wall and looking down the length of the corridor, so the window wall runs away in steep perspective along the left side of the frame and the door wall along the right. Wide lens, natural perspective, no fisheye.

THE WINDOW WALL (LEFT): a continuous band of large sliding windows in slim aluminium frames, sill at about waist height, running the whole length of the corridor; cream-painted wall beneath. The glass is clean but not new, with faint smears and reflections of the ceiling lights.

THE HANDRAIL — PAINTED RED: below the sills, a continuous tubular steel handrail on short steel wall brackets runs the full length of the window wall, receding with the perspective. It is painted a MUTED VERMILION RED — the same slightly orange, weathered industrial red used on the plant's painted steelwork; not fire-engine scarlet, not maroon, not pink. The paint is old: slightly chalky, worn to bare metal on the top where hands run along it, small chips at the brackets. It is the strongest colour inside the corridor.

THE VIEW OUTSIDE — THE WATERFRONT WITH ITS LIGHTS: through the windows, the plant's seafront: concrete quays and a harbour basin, the breakwater with tetrapod armour blocks, cold grey-green sea with low swell and dull grey-white foam, and above it a dense, low, storm-grey cloud deck. At the edges of the view, parts of plant structures — a pale panelled building wall with its pale blue band, pipe racks, a light grey lattice pylon — and the dark forested headland far off. The sun is entirely hidden: no disc, no bright patch, no glow; the sky through the glass is held in mid to dark greys, darker than white. Cold damp sea haze flattens the far structures into soft grey silhouettes.
PRACTICALS OUTSIDE, seen small and sharp through the glass, the only live colour in the view — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it:
- warm tungsten light in a few windows of the buildings on the quay, small dim rectangles, most windows dark;
- yard lamps just coming on along the quay and internal roads: some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each a weak pool on wet concrete, pools far apart, a lamp or two dead;
- a faint wall floodlight on a building end wall;
- small red warning lights on the lattice pylon and on a crane boom;
- at the breakwater ends, two tiny navigation lights, one green, one red, sharp against the grey water.

THE DOOR WALL (RIGHT): cream / pale beige painted wall with a dark skirting, and a row of flush steel doors set at intervals, some with a small wired-glass vision panel and a lever handle. Small room-number plates beside each door.

If its presence is perceptible at all, it exists only as a very weak, broad, pale area of higher luminance behind the cloud layer near one side of the upper edge of the frame — never centred, never a distinct solar disc.

The daylight is cold but naturally overcast rather than artificially blue. The whole station is illuminated by a large soft sky source: diffuse, broad, quiet light arriving from the cloud ceiling, wrapping around structures rather than striking them. Vertical surfaces receive soft cool-grey illumination; horizontal surfaces catch slightly more of the pale sky. Recesses, undersides and gaps between buildings remain open and readable instead of falling into black.

No hard sun shadows. No rim light. No shafts of sunlight. No golden-hour effect.

LOCAL COLOUR — PRESERVE THE REAL MATERIAL COLOURS:
Do not recolour the location into a stylized palette. Every material retains its natural local colour and is shifted only by the cold overcast illumination.

The main industrial buildings remain aged off-white, light neutral grey and weathered warm-white, approximately within #E2DFD5–#F1F3F2 before the effect of the sky light. Their faded pale blue and blue-grey painted areas remain restrained and slightly chalky, around a weathered #C6D8EC family — never cyan, never turquoise, never vivid blue.

Galvanized steel structures, latticework and exposed metal read as pale silver-grey with a slight cool reflection from the cloud ceiling, not blue-painted metal.

Concrete aprons, seawalls and service structures remain old mineral grey with faint beige warmth underneath, approximately #C4C0AF in their local colour. Under the overcast sky that warmth is suppressed but not erased.

Roads and asphalt are muted dirty grey and grey-khaki, never deep black.

Vegetation keeps its real colour: subdued olive, moss green and deep forest green. The cold sky reduces its warmth and saturation but does NOT turn the landscape teal, cyan or blue-green. Near vegetation is darker and richer; distant vegetation becomes softer and slightly cooler through atmospheric haze.

The sea and harbor water retain a restrained medium teal-blue / steel-blue local colour, approximately around #3F7999, made duller and greyer by the cloudy sky. No tropical cyan water.

VENTILATION STACKS:
The tall lattice ventilation stacks retain their period-correct alternating RED AND WHITE horizontal painted sections. The uppermost section / top edge of every stack is always RED. The red is weathered industrial red — muted oxide red / faded signal red rather than bright scarlet, orange-red or neon. The white sections are aged industrial white, slightly greyed by weather and the cold sky.
