Create a highly photorealistic wide documentary photograph of the central control room of Reactor Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, Japan, immediately before the March 2011 accident, based on the historically documented appearance of the room in late 2010 and January 2011.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control panel bank. The upper part of the frame includes the ceiling architecture.

This must be a historically grounded reconstruction of the real Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 central control room, not a generic modern control room and not a futuristic command center.

SPATIAL ARCHITECTURE — CRITICAL:
The room is a larger hall-like technical space. The long pale green control panel bank is NOT the outer wall of the room and NOT the back wall itself. It is a tall freestanding internal equipment structure placed inside a larger room. Operators stand and work in front of it, but the architectural room continues above it and beyond it.

The control panel bank should read like a large internal island-wall of instrumentation inside a spacious hall.

Most importantly:
— the ceiling must continue past and beyond the control panel bank;
— the room extends farther behind the panels;
— the top edge of the panel bank ends clearly below the ceiling;
— above the panels there is visible open air volume / empty space / upper room volume;
— the ceiling does NOT spring directly from the top edge of the control panel bank;
— the panel bank must not visually merge into the ceiling;
— the viewer must feel that the people working at the panels are in one part of a larger room.

Do not depict the control panel as if it seals off the room.
Do not depict the ceiling as if it touches the top of the panels.
Do not depict the panel as a continuation into the architecture.
The room continues behind the panel line.

MAIN CONTROL PANEL BANK:
A very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel bank extends laterally across almost the entire frame and gently curves around the operator area. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation:
— large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows;
— clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles;
— vertical meters;
— chart recorders;
— small numerical displays;
— red and green indicator lamps;
— switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls;
— Japanese technical labels and placards;
— several larger black display screens integrated into upper areas.

The panel bank remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.
The lower section projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

The panel color is muted pale institutional sage-green / grey-green enamel, slightly aged and matte, around the #A7B59D to #B0BDA9 family. It should feel like old Japanese industrial equipment, not fresh mint green and not modern pastel design.

PANEL-TO-CEILING RELATIONSHIP — ABSOLUTE REQUIREMENT:
The top of the control panel bank is clearly visible as a finished top edge below the ceiling.
Above that top edge, there is a visible band of air and room volume.
Behind and beyond the panel bank, the ceiling continues deeper into the room.
The control panel bank should therefore feel shorter than the full room height.
Even if the space behind the bank is not fully exposed, the geometry must clearly imply that the hall continues beyond it.

CEILING — LARGE ROOM CEILING, NOT PANEL EXTENSION:
The ceiling belongs to the larger hall, not to the panel bank.

It has a distinctive two-level system:

1. CENTRAL LUMINOUS CEILING:
A large raised rectangular light-ceiling over the middle of the room — one continuous glowing surface made of translucent diffuser panels with a soft corrugated, ribbed, wave-like texture. Gentle parallel ripples run across the whole surface like ribbed milky acrylic. It glows evenly from within; no individual bulbs or tubes are visible. Warm-neutral white with a slight fluorescent yellow cast, held textured rather than blown out.

This luminous central ceiling hovers over the central operator area and continues in perspective across the larger hall. It must feel like a ceiling plane suspended over the room, not connected to the control panel bank.

2. PERIMETER SOFFIT:
Around the raised luminous center, a lower flat dropped ceiling band runs along the room’s outline. Matte pale grey-green / off-white. Set into it are rectangular recessed fluorescent troffer fixtures — separate bright rectangles with a slightly cooler, greener white than the central luminous ceiling. The soffit follows the broader room architecture and continues around the hall independently of the control panel bank.

3. THE STEP:
Where the raised luminous center meets the lower soffit there is a clean stepped edge — a vertical riser with a softly rounded corner, casting a faint soft shadow line onto the soffit.

4. DEPTH OF THE ROOM:
The ceiling must visibly recede in perspective beyond the panel bank. The upper architecture must communicate that the hall extends farther than the panel line. The viewer must sense more room volume behind the panels.

Nothing else on the ceiling:
— no exposed ducts;
— no acoustic tile grid;
— no perforated metal ceiling field;
— no pendant lights;
— no modern office drop-ceiling look;
— no ceiling touching the panels.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is therefore completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

- RED AVIATION WARNING LIGHTS on the stacks: a hard point of deep red burning at the very top of each stack and at intermediate levels down the lattice, plus the same red points on the tall transmission pylons and on the crane booms. Small, sharp, steady, with a tight red halation, deep red — never pink, never orange.
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small warm rectangles, dim, scattered, not every window, most windows dark and reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: a scattering of pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, the pools far apart and much weaker than daylight. A few lamps dead.

- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays, and small navigation lights at the ends of the breakwaters — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against the grey water.
- A slow amber beacon on a gantry crane. Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.

NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE STACKS: tall lattice exhaust stacks between the units, painted in alternating RED and WHITE bands of roughly equal height all the way down, the TOP section always RED with a red crowning head. Muted vermilion, not scarlet, not maroon; the white dirty and weathered with rust streaks. Under this dull light the painted bands read subdued and greyed.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind, deep green muted toward olive-grey and darkening in the gloom.

35mm film still shot on daylight-balanced colour negative, fine-grained stock, clearly visible organic grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold overcast weather. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — ONE VAST OVERCAST SOURCE, ALMOST SHADOWLESS: the entire cloud deck is the light source, huge and soft, wrapping everything. No visible sun disc, no shafts, no rays, no sparkle. Behind the solid cloud, a slightly brighter patch of veiled sun sits high in the UPPER LEFT of the frame, just at the top edge — a diffuse pale glow with no hard edge, marginally warmer than the rest of the sky and only in its immediate area. The light therefore arrives from above and from the left: the left faces of the buildings, stacks and pylons are a little brighter, the right faces sink into soft shade.
THE LIGHTING RATIO IS VERY LOW — the shaded side of any wall sits barely one stop below its lit side, and often less. Shadows are long, very soft-edged, falling away from that glow, barely more than gradations on the concrete and the roads. Every shadow stays fully open with all its detail and surface texture legible inside it.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: because the light comes from the sky dome, horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea. Vertical walls are noticeably darker and darken further toward the ground; the undersides of pipe racks, gantries and the harbour structures sit in soft shadow. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE TONAL LADDER — A SHORT, FLAT SCALE FROM END TO END: this is a deliberately narrow-range picture, roughly five stops from the brightest sky to the deepest shade, and no more. Build it in this order:
1. BRIGHTEST: the veiled glow at the upper left of the cloud deck. It stops clearly short of pure white and holds a faint tone and a faint warmth — NOTHING in the frame reaches clean white and nothing clips
2. the rest of the sky, then the flat roofs, the quay decks and the sea — the light horizontal planes
3. the off-white reactor walls are the CONTROL SURFACE of the picture: nominally white, they must render as a cool grey-white sitting comfortably below the sky, with their panel joints, staining and weathering all clearly readable. If they blow out, the whole frame is wrong
4. the shaded right faces, the pale blue mottling, the grey turbine halls
5. DARKEST: the undersides of the pipe racks and gantries and the shadowed harbour structures. Even here nothing approaches black — the darkest tone in the picture is an open, slightly milky grey with texture still visible in it
The bulk of the frame sits in the middle of this short range. Contrast is flat and even throughout; density comes from grain and material, never from contrast.

THE SKY: a full unbroken cloud deck, dense and low, with structure and tonality in it — grey banks, subtle darker striations — never a blown-out white void. It grades from the pale veiled glow at the upper left to heavier, colder, denser grey toward the right and lower edge.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings along a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings are off-white panelled walls carrying a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls are light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, transmission pylons of light grey lattice behind. Every surface carries its age: salt bloom and rust bleeding from fixings, dark rain-streaking down the panel joints, patched and mismatched roofing, concrete stained green-black where water runs, paint chalked and faded on the seaward faces.

THE STACKS: tall lattice exhaust stacks rising between the units, painted in alternating RED and WHITE bands of roughly equal height all the way down. — the room extends farther behind the panels;

— the viewer must feel that the people working at the panels are in one part of a larger room.

The ceiling starts farther back and higher up, behind the line of the control panels, not directly from the top edge of the panels.
The ceiling should read as a separate architectural element hovering above the central room, while the control wall remains below it.
This separation must be clearly visible in the image.

16:9 horizontal frame.

A wide establishing interior shot from approximately human eye level, looking across the main working area toward the long curved Unit 3 control wall. The ceiling is included in the upper part of the frame.

The rear of the room is occupied by a very large continuous pale sage-green / grey-green analog control panel extending across almost the entire frame and gently curving around the room. It is densely populated with authentic late-20th-century Japanese nuclear instrumentation: large black annunciator panels filled with many small rectangular status windows, clusters of white circular analog gauges with black needles, vertical meters, chart recorders, small numerical displays, red and green indicator lamps, switches, pushbuttons, rotary controls and Japanese technical labels.

THE PANELS ARE FREE-STANDING CABINETS OF FINITE HEIGHT, NOT PART OF THE CEILING: the control panels are floor-standing vertical cabinets about 2.3–2.5 metres tall with a flat, clearly defined top edge. They do NOT reach the ceiling and do NOT merge into it. Above the top edge of the panels there is a clear band of empty space — a plain, smooth, flat wall in a pale grey-green / off-white tone, roughly one metre high, with nothing mounted on it — and only above that wall does the ceiling begin. The ceiling plane continues over the panels and beyond them, extending past the top of the control wall toward the back of the room, so the panels stand in front of the wall as furniture, and the ceiling is a separate surface higher up and further back.

Several larger black display screens are integrated into the upper portions of the control panels, but the room remains overwhelmingly analog and physical rather than digital.

The lower section of the panels projects outward as a continuous operator console covered with dense switches and instrumentation.

1. THE CENTRAL LUMINOUS CEILING: a large raised rectangular light-ceiling over the middle of the room — one continuous glowing surface made of translucent diffuser panels with a soft corrugated, wave-like texture: gentle parallel horizontal ripples running across the whole surface, like ribbed milky acrylic. It glows evenly from within; no individual lamps or tubes are visible, only uniform soft illumination with a faint ripple pattern. Warm-neutral white with a slight fluorescent yellow tint, held textured rather than blown white.

Matte pale grey-green / off-white. Set flush into it, in rows, are rectangular recessed fluorescent troffer fixtures — separate bright rectangles with a slightly cooler, greener white than the central light-ceiling; a few tubes marginally dimmer than the rest. This soffit sits well above the top of the control panels, separated from them by the band of plain wall, and extends beyond the panels toward the room's outer walls.
3. THE STEP: where the raised luminous centre meets the lower soffit there is a clean stepped edge — a vertical riser with a softly rounded corner, casting a faint soft shadow line onto the soffit.
Nothing else on the ceiling: no exposed pipes or ducts, no pendant lamps, no grid of perforated metal panels, no acoustic tile grid.

In the foreground and middle ground is a large dark charcoal-grey central operator workstation island, broad and irregularly curved, visibly used and practical rather than sleek. 35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavily overcast weather. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — ONE VAST DULL OVERCAST SOURCE: a thick, dense, unbroken cloud layer is the only light source — heavy and grey, completely sealing the sky. The sun is fully buried behind it and does NOT burn through: no sun disc, no bright hot spot, no glowing core, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. Its position is only faintly implied by a very subtle, barely perceptible lightening of the cloud toward the UPPER LEFT of the frame — a soft tonal gradient of a fraction of a stop, not a light source, with no defined shape or edge and no glow around it. The overall level is low and dull, like a grey winter afternoon before rain.

DIRECTION — VERY WEAK: because that faint lightening sits upper left, the light arrives slightly from above and from the left. The difference is minimal: left faces of buildings, stacks and pylons are a touch lighter, right faces a touch darker. Shadows are extremely soft, long and weak — barely readable gradations on concrete and roadways, no defined shadow edges anywhere.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground; undersides of pipe racks, gantries, jetties and harbour structures sit in soft shade. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a full, dense, low cloud deck occupying the upper part of the frame, held in a NARROW tonal range of mid to dark greys — grey banks, layered striations, ragged lower edges, a sense of weight and moisture. It must stay clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no blown-out white, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings on a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings are off-white panelled walls carrying a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE STACKS: tall lattice exhaust stacks rising between the units, painted in alternating RED and WHITE bands of roughly equal height all the way down. The TOP section is always RED — the crowning head at the very top is red. The red is a muted vermilion, not fire engine scarlet and not maroon; the white is dirty and weathered, with rust streaks lower down. Under this dull light the red bands are subdued but remain the only relatively saturated thing in the frame.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam breaking on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind the plant, deep green muted toward olive-grey.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze. Near units clear; further units lose contrast and colour, going pale grey-green; the furthest structures and the headland flatten into soft grey silhouettes. Depth is built by haze, not by light.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing shot from the sea side looking in toward the shore, slightly off-axis so the row of buildings runs diagonally across the frame. Deep enough to hold the whole row, the stacks, the harbour and the hills.

Off-white walls stay off-white reading cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; the red stack bands stay red; hills stay green dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, dull grey-green, olive-grey, cool concrete grey, rust, weathered white, muted vermilion. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The whole frame is cold and neutral: NO golden or amber cast anywhere, not even near the faint lightening in the cloud. Saturation rationed and low overall.

TONE: low contrast, flat dull overcast curve, lifted shadows, no crushed blacks, compressed highlights with the sky held well below white. No specular highlights, no glare, no glowing areas, no halation. Faint grain, heaviest in the shadows. Restrained documentary photographic feel, slightly underexposed rather than bright.

THE LIGHT — ONE VAST OVERCAST SOURCE, ALMOST SHADOWLESS: the entire cloud deck is the light source, huge and soft, wrapping everything. No visible sun disc, no shafts, no rays, no sparkle. Behind the solid cloud, a slightly brighter patch of veiled sun sits high in the UPPER LEFT of the frame, just at the top edge — a diffuse pale glow with no hard edge, marginally warmer than the rest of the sky and only in its immediate area. The light therefore arrives from above and from the left: the left faces of the buildings, stacks and pylons are a little brighter, the right faces sink into soft shade.
THE LIGHTING RATIO IS VERY LOW — the shaded side of any wall sits barely one stop below its lit side, and often less. Shadows are long, very soft-edged, falling away from that glow, barely more than gradations on the concrete and the roads. Every shadow stays fully open with all its detail and surface texture legible inside it.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: because the light comes from the sky dome, horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea. Vertical walls are noticeably darker and darken further toward the ground; the undersides of pipe racks, gantries and the harbour structures sit in soft shadow. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE TONAL LADDER — A SHORT, FLAT SCALE FROM END TO END: this is a deliberately narrow-range picture, roughly five stops from the brightest sky to the deepest shade, and no more. Build it in this order:
1. BRIGHTEST: the veiled glow at the upper left of the cloud deck. It stops clearly short of pure white and holds a faint tone and a faint warmth — NOTHING in the frame reaches clean white and nothing clips
2. the rest of the sky, then the flat roofs, the quay decks and the sea — the light horizontal planes
3. the off-white reactor walls are the CONTROL SURFACE of the picture: nominally white, they must render as a cool grey-white sitting comfortably below the sky, with their panel joints, staining and weathering all clearly readable. If they blow out, the whole frame is wrong
4. the shaded right faces, the pale blue mottling, the grey turbine halls

The bulk of the frame sits in the middle of this short range. Contrast is flat and even throughout; density comes from grain and material, never from contrast.

THE SKY: a full unbroken cloud deck, dense and low, with structure and tonality in it — grey banks, subtle darker striations — never a blown-out white void. It grades from the pale veiled glow at the upper left to heavier, colder, denser grey toward the right and lower edge.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings along a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings are off-white panelled walls carrying a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls are light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. Every surface carries its age: salt bloom and rust bleeding from fixings, dark rain-streaking down the panel joints, patched and mismatched roofing, concrete stained green-black where water runs, paint chalked and faded on the seaward faces.

Both ends of the scale are pulled in — no clipped highlight anywhere, no crushed black anywhere.

Off-white walls stay off-white and read cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; the red stack bands stay red; the hills stay green, dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Wide establishing shot of Units 1–4 of a 1970s-era Japanese coastal nuclear power station, BEFORE any accident — fully intact, normal operation, calm and clean.

SUBJECT: FOUR boxy reactor units standing in a straight row along a flat coastal terrace beside the sea. Each unit = a tall rectangular concrete-and-steel reactor building (roughly cube-like, flat-roofed, off-white/pale grey cladding) with a lower, longer turbine hall in front of it, on the seaward side. STYLE: utilitarian industrial architecture, weathered concrete, metal panels, beige/grey/off-white tones; realistic late-20th-century look, no modern glass. Documentary realism.

MOOD & LIGHT: ordinary soft daylight, slightly overcast, neutral cool palette; only thin steam/vapour, absolutely no smoke, fire, damage or debris; quiet and orderly.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing angle (drone/hillside view), three-quarter so all four units, their turbine halls, the stacks, the sea and the green slope read clearly. Deep focus, photorealistic, sharp, natural colours, high dynamic range. No text, no watermark, no close-up people.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, LOCAL:
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small, dim warm rectangles, scattered, not every window; most windows dark, reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight. A few lamps dead.
- WALL FLOODLIGHTS on the turbine hall end walls, washing faintly down the panelling.
- Small red warning lights on the tall lattice transmission pylons and on a crane boom; a slow amber beacon on a gantry crane.
- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays and small navigation lights at the breakwater ends — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against grey water.
- Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

THE STACKS — WHITE, WITH A PALE BLUE HEAD, AND COMPLETELY UNLIT: tall, slender lattice exhaust towers rising between the units, tapering slightly toward the top, built of horizontal tiers and diagonal cross-bracing. The entire lattice tower is WHITE — a plain, uniform white/very light grey from base to top, with NO stripes, NO bands, NO red, NO alternating colours anywhere on the structure; just weathering, grey grime and faint rust staining. The only colour is at the very top: the exhaust duct emerging above the lattice is capped by a short section painted PALE BLUE / soft grey-turquoise, a small cool blue head occupying roughly the top tenth of the tower's height. Against the grey sky the white towers read as pale grey skeletal lines, the blue cap slightly cooler still.
The stacks carry NO LIGHTING WHATSOEVER: no red aviation warning lights, no lamps, no beacons, no glowing points, nothing lit at the top or anywhere on the lattice. They are completely dark and unlit.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, AND NOT ON THE STACKS:
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small, dim warm rectangles, scattered, not every window; most windows dark, reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight. A few lamps dead.
- WALL FLOODLIGHTS on the turbine hall end walls, washing faintly down the panelling.
- Small red warning lights on the tall lattice transmission pylons and on a crane boom; a slow amber beacon on a gantry crane.
- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays and small navigation lights at the breakwater ends — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against grey water.
- Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings on a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings off-white panelled walls with a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind, deep green muted toward olive-grey and darkening in the gloom.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze. Near units clear; further units lose contrast and colour, going pale grey-green; the furthest structures and the headland flatten into soft grey silhouettes; the white lattice stacks fade toward the sky tone with distance. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing shot from the sea side looking in toward the shore, slightly off-axis so the row of buildings runs diagonally across the frame, holding the whole row, the stacks, the harbour and the hills.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours — only desaturated and cooled by the overcast, NOT re-tinted. Off-white walls read cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; the stack heads stay pale blue; hills stay green dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, soft grey-turquoise, dull grey-green, olive-grey, cool concrete grey, rust, weathered white, with small accents of tungsten amber, mercury blue-green, a little deep red and a single green. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The daylight areas carry NO golden or amber cast; warmth exists only inside the lit windows and the sodium pools. Saturation hierarchy: the warm lit windows are the most saturated thing in the frame, then the small pylon and navigation lights; every large surface is muted and low.

TONE: low contrast, flat dull overcast curve, lifted shadows, no crushed blacks, compressed highlights with the sky held well below white. No specular highlights on daylight surfaces, no glare. Tight controlled halation ONLY around the practical lights. Faint grain, heaviest in the shadows. Restrained documentary photographic feel, slightly underexposed rather than bright.

A photo, September 2010, TEPCO workers in the central control room of Unit 3 at Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. Wide shot, camera at human eye level.

Wide establishing shot of Units 1–4 of a 1970s-era Japanese coastal nuclear power station, BEFORE any accident — fully intact, normal operation, calm and clean.

SUBJECT: FOUR boxy reactor units standing in a straight row along a flat coastal terrace beside the sea. Each unit = a tall rectangular concrete-and-steel reactor building (roughly cube-like, flat-roofed, off-white/pale grey cladding) with a lower, longer turbine hall in front of it, on the seaward side. Unit 1 (far end) is noticeably SMALLER and older-looking; Units 2, 3 and 4 are LARGER and similar in size to each other. Tall red-and-white banded lattice exhaust/vent stacks rise between the units (about one stack shared per pair of units). NO cooling towers (seawater-cooled).

SITE: the four units sit on a low cut platform just above the Pacific; a steep green forested slope/bluff rises directly behind them; pipe racks, gantry cranes, service roads, parking and switchyard gear around the buildings; transmission pylons and power lines running inland behind the plant; a breakwater, seawater intake/outfall channels and a calm blue sea with gentle surf in the foreground.

STYLE: utilitarian industrial architecture, weathered concrete, metal panels, beige/grey/off-white tones; realistic late-20th-century look, no modern glass. Documentary realism.

MOOD & LIGHT: ordinary soft daylight, slightly overcast, neutral cool palette; only thin steam/vapour, absolutely no smoke, fire, damage or debris; quiet and orderly.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing angle (drone/hillside view), three-quarter so all four units, their turbine halls, the stacks, the sea and the green slope read clearly. Deep focus, photorealistic, sharp, natural colours, high dynamic range. No text, no watermark, no close-up people.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, LOCAL:
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small, dim warm rectangles, scattered, not every window; most windows dark, reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight. A few lamps dead.
- WALL FLOODLIGHTS on the turbine hall end walls, washing faintly down the panelling.
- Small red warning lights on the tall lattice transmission pylons and on a crane boom; a slow amber beacon on a gantry crane.
- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays and small navigation lights at the breakwater ends — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against grey water.
- Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings on a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings off-white panelled walls with a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind, deep green muted toward olive-grey and darkening in the gloom.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze. Near structures clear; further ones lose contrast and colour, going pale grey-green; the furthest structures and the headland flatten into soft grey silhouettes. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing shot from the sea side looking in toward the shore, slightly off-axis so the row of buildings runs diagonally across the frame, holding the whole row, the harbour and the hills.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours — only desaturated and cooled by the overcast, NOT re-tinted. Off-white walls read cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; hills stay green dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, dull grey-green, olive-grey, cool concrete grey, rust, weathered white, with small accents of tungsten amber, mercury blue-green, a little deep red and a single green. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The daylight areas carry NO golden or amber cast; warmth exists only inside the lit windows and the sodium pools. Saturation hierarchy: the warm lit windows are the most saturated thing in the frame, then the small pylon and navigation lights; every large surface is muted and low.

TONE: low contrast, flat dull overcast curve, lifted shadows, no crushed blacks, compressed highlights with the sky held well below white. No specular highlights on daylight surfaces, no glare. Behind the solid cloud, a slightly brighter patch of veiled sun sits high in the UPPER LEFT of the frame, just at the top edge — a diffuse pale glow with no hard edge, marginally warmer than the rest of the sky and only in its immediate area. The light therefore arrives from above and from the left: the left faces of the buildings, stacks and pylons are a little brighter, the right faces sink into soft shade.

Shadows are long, very soft-edged, falling away from that glow, barely more than gradations on the concrete and the roads. Every shadow stays fully open with all its detail and surface texture legible inside it.

The bulk of the frame sits in the middle of this short range. Contrast is flat and even throughout; density comes from grain and material, never from contrast.

THE SKY: a full unbroken cloud deck, dense and low, with structure and tonality in it — grey banks, subtle darker striations — never a blown-out white void. It grades from the pale veiled glow at the upper left to heavier, colder, denser grey toward the right and lower edge.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings along a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Every surface carries its age: salt bloom and rust bleeding from fixings, dark rain-streaking down the panel joints, patched and mismatched roofing, concrete stained green-black where water runs, paint chalked and faded on the seaward faces.

THE STACKS: tall lattice exhaust stacks rising between the units, painted in alternating RED and WHITE bands of roughly equal height all the way down. The TOP section is always RED — the crowning head at the very top is red. The red is a muted vermilion-orange, not fire engine scarlet and not maroon; the white is dirty and weathered. They also mark the depth: the nearest stack holds its red clearly, the next reads paler and softer, the furthest is reduced to a faint pink-grey thread against the cloud.

35mm film still, fine visible grain. Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, 2000s. Late afternoon, about 16:00, cold heavy overcast, gloomy. Intact, in normal operation. No people, no vehicles.

THE LIGHT — DULL, FLAT, FULLY DIFFUSED: a thick, dense, unbroken storm-grey cloud layer seals the sky completely. The sun is entirely hidden — no disc, no hot spot, no glow, no lightening anywhere in the cloud, no halo, no bloom, no flare, no rays. The daylight is completely non-directional: soft, dim, ambient light falling from the whole sky dome. NO shadows with direction; only faint soft occlusion shading under overhangs, pipe racks, gantries and jetties. The overall level is low and grey, like the hour before rain.

FALLOFF TOP TO BOTTOM: light comes from the sky dome, so horizontal surfaces read lightest — flat roofs, quay decks, roadways, the sea surface. Vertical walls are clearly darker and darken further toward the ground, the lower parts of the buildings sinking into gloom. Nothing is evenly flooded.

THE SKY: a dense, low, layered cloud deck in a NARROW band of mid to dark greys — heavy banks, ragged lower edges, a sense of moisture and weight. Clearly darker than white: no bright sky, no luminous patch, no break in the cloud, no blue.

THE STACKS — WHITE, WITH A PALE BLUE HEAD, AND COMPLETELY UNLIT: tall, slender lattice exhaust towers rising between the units, tapering slightly toward the top, built of horizontal tiers and diagonal cross-bracing. The entire lattice tower is WHITE — a plain, uniform white/very light grey from base to top, with NO stripes, NO bands, NO red, NO alternating colours anywhere on the structure; just weathering, grey grime and faint rust staining. The only colour is at the very top: the exhaust duct emerging above the lattice is capped by a short section painted PALE BLUE / soft grey-turquoise, a small cool blue head occupying roughly the top tenth of the tower's height. Against the grey sky the white towers read as pale grey skeletal lines, the blue cap slightly cooler still.
The stacks carry NO LIGHTING WHATSOEVER: no red aviation warning lights, no lamps, no beacons, no glowing points, nothing lit at the top or anywhere on the lattice. They are completely dark and unlit.

PRACTICALS — SMALL, FEW, AND NOT ON THE STACKS:
- WARM LIT WINDOWS: in a few windows of the service and control buildings and along a row of high windows in the turbine halls, warm tungsten light glows from inside — small, dim warm rectangles, scattered, not every window; most windows dark, reflecting only grey sky.
- YARD LIGHTING just coming on: pole-mounted lamps along the internal roads and over the switchyard — some warm amber sodium, some cold blue-green mercury vapour, each throwing a weak pool onto wet concrete, pools far apart and much weaker than the daylight. A few lamps dead.
- WALL FLOODLIGHTS on the turbine hall end walls, washing faintly down the panelling.
- Small red warning lights on the tall lattice transmission pylons and on a crane boom; a slow amber beacon on a gantry crane.
- HARBOUR: dim lighting along the quays and small navigation lights at the breakwater ends — one green, one red, tiny and sharp against grey water.
- Small greenish-white lamps over a few doorways.
All practicals are SMALL and LOCAL — they punctuate the scene, they do not illuminate it. Daylight still dominates.

THE PLANT: a row of boxy reactor buildings on a flat coastal terrace, each with a long lower turbine hall on the seaward side. Reactor buildings off-white panelled walls with a distinctive pale blue mottled camouflage pattern across the upper section; turbine halls light grey with a pale blue band low down; flat roofs dull grey-green. NO cooling towers. Pipe racks, tanks, gantry cranes, service roads, light grey lattice transmission pylons behind.

THE SEA AND SHORE: cold grey-green water, low swell, dull grey-white foam on the breakwaters and tetrapods; concrete quays and armour blocks in cool pale grey; steep forested hills behind, deep green muted toward olive-grey and darkening in the gloom.

ATMOSPHERE: cold damp sea haze. Near units clear; further units lose contrast and colour, going pale grey-green; the furthest structures and the headland flatten into soft grey silhouettes; the white lattice stacks fade toward the sky tone with distance. Depth is built by haze, not by sunlight.

CAMERA: elevated wide establishing shot from the sea side looking in toward the shore, slightly off-axis so the row of buildings runs diagonally across the frame, holding the whole row, the stacks, the harbour and the hills.

COLOUR: materials keep their own colours — only desaturated and cooled by the overcast, NOT re-tinted. Off-white walls read cool grey-white; the blue mottling stays blue; the stack heads stay pale blue; hills stay green dulled toward olive-grey; the sea reads grey-green, never blue. Palette: cool grey-white, pale blue-grey, soft grey-turquoise, dull grey-green, olive-grey, cool concrete grey, rust, weathered white, with small accents of tungsten amber, mercury blue-green, a little deep red and a single green. Shadows shift toward cool neutral grey and faint olive — never blue, never teal. The daylight areas carry NO golden or amber cast; warmth exists only inside the lit windows and the sodium pools. Saturation hierarchy: the warm lit windows are the most saturated thing in the frame, then the small pylon and navigation lights; every large surface is muted and low.

TONE: low contrast, flat dull overcast curve, lifted shadows, no crushed blacks, compressed highlights with the sky held well below white. No specular highlights on daylight surfaces, no glare. Tight controlled halation ONLY around the practical lights. Faint grain, heaviest in the shadows. Restrained documentary photographic feel, slightly underexposed rather than bright.

水位缓慢而持续地上涨。镜头清楚显示积水从低处一点点漫上座椅，再逐渐淹到她的身体。水中混合着泥沙、细小碎屑和漂浮的泡沫，水线始终可见。

女员工急切地摸索安全带锁扣，反复按压并扯动带子，但卡扣没有松开。她又抓住身旁的车门把手，用力拉动并顶门，贴着地面的驾驶座车门始终无法打开。她的身体仍被安全带限制在原来的座位上。她越来越慌，呼吸急促，继续用力挣扎。

浑水不断从前方流入，水线在她身上逐渐升高。她被刚才扑面的水呛得咳嗽，一边扯动安全带，一边抬高下巴寻找空气。随着水位上涨，每次挣扎激起的水花都会扑到她嘴边，她咳嗽着把脸抬起，大口喘息。

摄影机始终留在她肩膀后方的同一个车内位置。上涨的水面逐渐触及镜头下缘，再慢慢升到镜头中央。画面下半部分浸在灰褐色污水中，受到泥沙、气泡和折射干扰；上半部分仍能看到她抬起的脸和挣扎的肩膀。水线在同一个镜头前真实晃动。

画面结束时，汽车仍然侧躺在右侧车身上，前挡风玻璃的破口继续进水，车厢里的水位仍在缓慢上涨。她头上已经没有安全帽，安全带仍将她困在驾驶座上。她不断尝试挣脱，一边咳嗽，一边抬头抢夺空气。摄影机保持在她肩膀后方，镜头半浸在水中，车厢尚未完全灌满。

所有声音均为现场同步声：厂房门被推开的撞击声、奔跑脚步和急促呼吸、机械钥匙和车锁声、隔着二楼玻璃听不清内容的谈话、女员工在画面外打开驾驶座车门和坐进汽车的声音、一次画外驾驶座车门关闭声、安全帽被摘下和放置的声音、安全带扣合声、发动机启动声、迅速逼近的洪流轰鸣、水体撞上汽车和玻璃的沉重巨响、玻璃开裂与局部破碎声、车身侧翻撞地声。撞击过后，声音逐渐转为持续的进水声、车厢内的水声、安全带和车门把手被拉扯的声音，以及她急促的喘息和咳嗽。没有可辨认的对白。
